sources.title: Bitcoin Mining Difficulty Has Not Set a Record in 374 Days, Its Longest Gap on Record - Cryptonews.net
passages: Bitcoin’s mining difficulty has not printed a new all-time high in 374 days.
The metric stands at 148.36 trillion hashes after the retarget of 29 October 2026, which lifted it 5.54% from 140.58 trillion.
The record remains 155.97 trillion, set at block 921,312 on 29 October 2025 at 10:14 UTC, according to mempool.space difficulty data.
That leaves the network 4.88% below its peak, and spot Bitcoin at $75,577, down 2.5% over seven days and 7.6% over 30.
A year without a record is not a malfunction.

On daily difficulty samples, the current 356-day run below the record is the longest in the network’s history, ahead of the 348 days between August 2011 and July 2012, the 236 days from May 2021 to January 2022, and the 225 days from October 2018 to May 2019.
Neither result depends on a new difficulty record; both depend on the price of Bitcoin, which has fallen 7.6% in 30 days.

Put that $700 million annualized colocation book against the $12.4 billion the entire network earns from issuance each year, and one company’s real-estate and power business is worth about 5.6% of everything Bitcoin mining produces.
A halving cuts the same hashprice by half unless price doubles, and it lands before the next difficulty record decision is settled in any meaningful sense.

Until then, the correct read is a network consolidating below its ceiling while its publicly traded operators shift revenue toward contracted colocation and away from a hashprice that no longer covers high-cost power.
For traders, miner balance sheets are a supply variable to watch rather than a signal to chase.
For anyone modelling hashprice, $33.4 per petahash per day is the number the whole industry is currently underwriting.
Bitcoin recalculates difficulty every 2,016 blocks, roughly two weeks of mining.
The mechanism is self-limiting, which is why the record has held through a year of infrastructure building.
With Bitcoin near $75,577 and hashrate averaging about 1.02 ZH/s, miners have little incentive to add capacity, so the retargets of the past year have not been enough to clear the October 2025 peak.

extraction.body: Bitcoin’s mining difficulty has not printed a new all-time high in 374 days. The metric stands at 148.36 trillion hashes after the retarget of 29 October 2026, which lifted it 5.54% from 140.58 trillion. The record remains 155.97 trillion, set at block 921,312 on 29 October 2025 at 10:14 UTC, according to mempool.space difficulty data. That leaves the network 4.88% below its peak, and spot Bitcoin at $75,577, down 2.5% over seven days and 7.6% over 30. A year without a record is not a malfunction. Difficulty rises only when the network finds blocks faster than the ten-minute target, and it falls or stalls when hashrate growth slows or capital leaves. What makes this stretch unusual is its length. On daily difficulty samples, the current 356-day run below the record is the longest in the network’s history, ahead of the 348 days between August 2011 and July 2012, the 236 days from May 2021 to January 2022, and the 225 days from October 2018 to May 2019. Bitcoin recalculates difficulty every 2,016 blocks, roughly two weeks of mining. The protocol compares the time taken for that batch against the 20,160 minutes implied by ten-minute blocks, then scales the target proportionally. If the batch arrived in nine minutes per block, difficulty climbs about 11%. If blocks slowed to twelve minutes, it drops. The mechanism is self-limiting, which is why the record has held through a year of infrastructure building. Difficulty can only break out when hashrate expands faster than price. Between the record on 29 October 2025 and the most recent retarget exactly one year later, difficulty moved from 155.97 trillion to 148.36 trillion. Two separate retargets in the interim, on 3 October 2026 and 19 September 2026, produced 132.72 trillion and 132.76 trillion, so the network spent the northern autumn recovering ground it had already covered. Hashrate tells a similar story. Current network hashrate sits near 1.02 zettahashes per second, with the 30-day peak at 1.22 ZH/s, based on blockchain.info’s hash-rate series. A rising hashrate that outruns price does not raise difficulty indefinitely. It raises the cost of production instead, until marginal operators switch off and the retarget resets the field. Difficulty matters to miners because it converts into revenue per unit of computing power. The arithmetic is simple enough to run directly. Bitcoin issues 3.125 $BTC per block and produces roughly 144 blocks a day, so 450 $BTC enters the market daily. At $75,577, that is about $34.0 million of gross issuance value per day, or $12.4 billion annualized, before transaction fees. Divide that by the network’s 1.02 ZH/s, which is 1.017 million petahashes, and the industry earns roughly $33.4 per petahash per second per day. That figure is the hashprice in everything but name. A month ago, with Bitcoin near $81,750 by CoinGecko’s 30-day change, the same hashrate would have produced about $36.2 per PH/s per day. Difficulty barely moved. Revenue per unit of power fell 7.6%. That gap explains why miners did not respond to flat difficulty by adding machines. Adding hashrate when price falls simply lowers the industry’s return per petahash and raises the next difficulty adjustment in someone else’s favour. The rational move is to hold steady, sell coins, or repurpose the power. Revenue per petahash only means something against the cost of running one. Take a current-generation machine rated at 20 joules per terahash. One petahash of that hardware draws 20 kilowatts, which is 480 kilowatt-hours a day. Against $33.4 of daily issuance revenue, the break-even power price works out to about 7.0 cents per kilowatt-hour, before fees, cooling, staff and hosting. That single number explains most of the sector’s behaviour this year. An operator paying 4 cents keeps roughly $14 per petahash per day of gross margin. An operator paying 7.5 cents is losing money on the same machine at the same difficulty. Neither result depends on a new difficulty record; both depend on the price of Bitcoin, which has fallen 7.6% in 30 days. The clearest evidence of that shift came on 5 November, when Core Scientific reported third-quarter results that barely resemble a mining company. Colocation revenue rose nearly 60% sequentially to $215.4 million. The company billed for 485 megawatts as of 30 September, representing more than $700 million in average annualized colocation GAAP revenue. Net income reached $1.2 billion, a figure the filed earnings release attributes to “a non-cash gain in the change in fair value of warrants,” not to mining. Adjusted EBITDA more than tripled sequentially to $133.6 million on a 57% margin, up from 25%. “Our execution at scale is translating into results, with a significant sequential increase in GAAP colocation revenue,” chief executive Adam Sullivan said in the release. “We are nearing full delivery under our first colocation agreement while construction under our second is underway across five campuses.” He added: “With revenue growing and substantial contracted capacity still to deliver, we have built a strong foundation for our next phase of growth.” Put that $700 million annualized colocation book against the $12.4 billion the entire network earns from issuance each year, and one company’s real-estate and power business is worth about 5.6% of everything Bitcoin mining produces. The warrants-driven net income is worth flagging separately. A $1.2 billion profit that depends on the mark on warrants is a balance-sheet event, and investors who read it as operating strength will misprice the quarter. This is the pattern BlockchainReporter documented when miners’ AI pivot decoupled their shares from Bitcoin, and again when AI contracts gave listed miners a valuation edge over pure-play operators. Flat difficulty does not hurt a company that is paid per megawatt of high-density colocation. It hurts the operator whose entire revenue line is the $33.4 per petahash. A new record requires hashrate to grow faster than the protocol can absorb, and the next decision point is close. The next retarget falls at block 975,744, with the chain at 974,990 at the time of writing, which places it around 12 November. Difficulty would need to climb 5.1% from 148.36 trillion to clear 155.97 trillion. The 29 October adjustment delivered 5.54%, so the arithmetic is not exotic; it is a question of whether the hashrate behind it exists. Two conditions could produce it. A price recovery would restore miner margins and pull curtailed capacity back online, since the same machines become profitable at $81,750 that sit idle at $75,577. Alternatively, new capacity could come from operators with lower power costs or stranded energy contracts, which raises network hashrate without needing a higher Bitcoin price. Neither is visible in current data: the 30-day hashrate peak of 1.22 ZH/s has already faded to an average near 1.02 ZH/s. The longer calendar matters too. The subsidy has been 3.125 $BTC per block since April 2024, and the next halving sits at block 1,050,000. With the chain at 974,990, that is 75,010 blocks away, or roughly 521 days at the current pace of 144 blocks a day. A halving cuts the same hashprice by half unless price doubles, and it lands before the next difficulty record decision is settled in any meaningful sense. The invalidation is explicit. If difficulty closes an epoch above 155.97 trillion, the 374-day gap ends and the record resets. Until then, the correct read is a network consolidating below its ceiling while its publicly traded operators shift revenue toward contracted colocation and away from a hashprice that no longer covers high-cost power. For traders, miner balance sheets are a supply variable to watch rather than a signal to chase. For anyone modelling hashprice, $33.4 per petahash per day is the number the whole industry is currently underwriting. 148.36 trillion, set at the retarget of 29 October 2026. That is 4.88% below the all-time high of 155.97 trillion recorded on 29 October 2025 at block 921,312. Difficulty only rises when blocks arrive faster than the ten-minute target. With Bitcoin near $75,577 and hashrate averaging about 1.02 ZH/s, miners have little incentive to add capacity, so the retargets of the past year have not been enough to clear the October 2025 peak. Hashprice is daily revenue per unit of computing power. At 450 $BTC of daily issuance and $75,577 per coin, the network earns about $34.0 million a day, or roughly $33.4 per petahash per second per day before fees. Falling hashprice squeezes miners even when difficulty is flat. The next retarget falls at block 975,744. With the chain at 974,990 at the time of writing, that places the adjustment around 12 November 2026. Clearing the record would require a 5.1% increase. A Bitcoin price recovery that restores miner margins, or new low-cost capacity coming online from operators with cheaper power. The 30-day hashrate peak of 1.22 ZH/s shows the capacity exists, but it has not been sustained. Data: mempool.space, CoinGecko, Blockchain.com difficulty and hash-rate series. sources.title: Bitcoin’s Second-Ever Negative Difficulty Reading: AI Capital Does What China’s Mining Ban Did
passages: Only the Second Time in Bitcoin's History This Metric Has Gone Negative The 2021 China ban dropped difficulty by roughly 28% in its steepest single adjustment and pushed year-over-year difficulty growth negative.

Bitcoin's mining network has just crossed a threshold that has appeared only once before in the currency's entire history: network difficulty has fallen below where it stood a year ago, confirmed by Luxor's Hashrate Index on July 28, 2026.
The last time that happened was in mid-2021, when China's government forced roughly half of the world's mining operations offline in a matter of weeks.
Bitcoin's Self-Regulating Security Mechanism Designed for a Different Problem To understand why this moment matters, it helps to understand what mining difficulty actually measures.
Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism exists to keep that 10-minute cadence stable regardless of how much computing power joins or leaves the network.

The machines are shutting down because the same power infrastructure that runs a Bitcoin miner is worth more to artificial intelligence data centers — and the AI market is willing to pay three to 25 times more per megawatt than Bitcoin mining currently offers.
The April 2024 halving cut the block reward from 6.25 to 3.125 Bitcoin.
As of August 1, Bitcoin traded near $63,100 — down approximately 47% from that peak — meaning a block now yields roughly $197,000.

Publicly traded miners sold more than 32,000 Bitcoin in the first quarter of 2026 alone — a single-quarter record that exceeded the full-year total for 2025 and surpassed the roughly 20,000 Bitcoin sold during the 2022 Terra Luna collapse.

Bitcoin uses a cryptographic process called proof-of-work: miners compete to find a hash value — the output of the SHA-256 algorithm applied to a block of transaction data — that falls below a numerical target.

extraction.body: Bitcoin's mining network has just crossed a threshold that has appeared only once before in the currency's entire history: network difficulty has fallen below where it stood a year ago, confirmed by Luxor's Hashrate Index on July 28, 2026. The last time that happened was in mid-2021, when China's government forced roughly half of the world's mining operations offline in a matter of weeks. The machines are shutting down because the same power infrastructure that runs a Bitcoin miner is worth more to artificial intelligence data centers — and the AI market is willing to pay three to 25 times more per megawatt than Bitcoin mining currently offers. And it raises a question prior contractions never required asking: will the hashrate come back at all? Bitcoin's Self-Regulating Security Mechanism Designed for a Different Problem To understand why this moment matters, it helps to understand what mining difficulty actually measures. Bitcoin uses a cryptographic process called proof-of-work: miners compete to find a hash value — the output of the SHA-256 algorithm applied to a block of transaction data — that falls below a numerical target. The only way to find a qualifying hash is brute force: modern application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) miners attempt trillions of hash calculations per second, each one a lottery ticket, searching for the rare output that satisfies the network's current requirements. The Bitcoin Foundation's 2026 explainer on mining mechanics covers the underlying proof-of-work process in depth. At current difficulty of 126.23 trillion, only approximately one in 70 trillion random hash attempts produces a qualifying result. The network collectively performs roughly 868 quintillion such calculations every second — that is 868 exahashes per second — with the reward going to whichever miner finds a valid hash first, approximately once every ten minutes. Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism exists to keep that 10-minute cadence stable regardless of how much computing power joins or leaves the network. If the previous 2,016 blocks arrived faster than the 10-minute average implies, difficulty rises. The formula is simple: new target equals old target multiplied by the ratio of actual epoch time to the ideal 20,160-minute epoch. The adjustment is capped at four times in either direction to prevent wild swings. It assumes that economic incentives will always bring hashrate back when it leaves — that when difficulty falls, surviving miners find more blocks and earn more per unit of computing power, making the network more attractive to capital until equilibrium is restored. Only the Second Time in Bitcoin's History This Metric Has Gone Negative The 2021 China ban dropped difficulty by roughly 28% in its steepest single adjustment and pushed year-over-year difficulty growth negative. Within months, displaced miners had relocated to the United States, Kazakhstan, and other regions, and difficulty was climbing to new all-time highs. The current contraction has reproduced the year-over-year reading without any policy catalyst. Bitcoin's difficulty stands at 126.23 trillion as of the July 25 adjustment, roughly 1.1% below the 127.62 trillion it recorded one year earlier — only the second sub-zero year-over-year reading in the network's history, confirmed by Luxor's Hashrate Index on July 28, 2026. The decline from the November 2025 all-time high of 155.97 trillion is 19.1% — the third-deepest drawdown since dedicated ASIC hardware became the standard mining tool. Only the aftermath of the China ban and a 2018 bear market produced steeper declines. Bitcoin Magazine Pro's data shows the downward hashrate trend has now extended approximately 287 consecutive days. The seven-day average hashrate stood near 868 exahashes per second (EH/s) by late July, down from more than one zettahash per second at the network's late-2025 peak — a decline of roughly 12% from the all-time high. Three Forces Are Draining the Network, and Only One Has Driven a Contraction of This Kind Before Luxor's Hashrate Index attributed the decline to three overlapping causes: worsening mining economics (falling Bitcoin prices and compressed hashprice), the AI infrastructure buildout pulling capital and power away from mining, and a long tail of smaller drags including Texas 4CP curtailment costs and approximately 7 EH/s knocked offline by the conflict in Iran. The April 2024 halving cut the block reward from 6.25 to 3.125 Bitcoin. At Bitcoin's October 2025 all-time high near $126,000, a single block was worth approximately $393,750. As of August 1, Bitcoin traded near $63,100 — down approximately 47% from that peak — meaning a block now yields roughly $197,000. That is a per-block revenue decline of more than 50% in less than a year, with the halving's supply cut baked on top. Hashprice — the expected daily revenue per petahash per second of computing power — fell to an all-time spot low of $27.66 as of late June, within one cent of February's prior low, according to Hashrate Index. The math for older hardware tells the story clearly: an Antminer S19-generation machine running at 100 terahashes per second earns roughly $3.19 per day at current hashprice and consumes more in electricity than that at even $0.05 per kilowatt-hour, putting a large segment of the older fleet below breakeven. CoinShares estimated in March 2026 that 15% to 20% of the global mining fleet was already operating at a loss. Transaction fees, which once provided a meaningful secondary revenue stream during the Ordinals inscription boom of 2023 and early 2024, have normalized back to roughly 1% of total miner revenue — far below the 7% they briefly reached — removing a supplemental buffer at exactly the moment miners need one most. The last time that happened was in mid-2021, when China's government forced roughly half of the world's mining operations offline in a matter of weeks.

The machines are shutting down because the same power infrastructure that runs a Bitcoin miner is worth more to artificial intelligence data centers — and the AI market is willing to pay three to 25 times more per megawatt than Bitcoin mining currently offers.
And it raises a question prior contractions never required asking: will the hashrate come back at all?
Bitcoin's Self-Regulating Security Mechanism Designed for a Different Problem To understand why this moment matters, it helps to understand what mining difficulty actually measures.

Bitcoin uses a cryptographic process called proof-of-work: miners compete to find a hash value — the output of the SHA-256 algorithm applied to a block of transaction data — that falls below a numerical target.

The only way to find a qualifying hash is brute force: modern application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) miners attempt trillions of hash calculations per second, each one a lottery ticket, searching for the rare output that satisfies the network's current requirements.
The Bitcoin Foundation's 2026 explainer on mining mechanics covers the underlying proof-of-work process in depth.
At current difficulty of 126.23 trillion, only approximately one in 70 trillion random hash attempts produces a qualifying result.

The network collectively performs roughly 868 quintillion such calculations every second — that is 868 exahashes per second — with the reward going to whichever miner finds a valid hash first, approximately once every ten minutes.
Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism exists to keep that 10-minute cadence stable regardless of how much computing power joins or leaves the network.
If the previous 2,016 blocks arrived faster than the 10-minute average implies, difficulty rises.
The formula is simple: new target equals old target multiplied by the ratio of actual epoch time to the ideal 20,160-minute epoch.
The adjustment is capped at four times in either direction to prevent wild swings.

It assumes that economic incentives will always bring hashrate back when it leaves — that when difficulty falls, surviving miners find more blocks and earn more per unit of computing power, making the network more attractive to capital until equilibrium is restored.

Within months, displaced miners had relocated to the United States, Kazakhstan, and other regions, and difficulty was climbing to new all-time highs.
The current contraction has reproduced the year-over-year reading without any policy catalyst.

Bitcoin's difficulty stands at 126.23 trillion as of the July 25 adjustment, roughly 1.1% below the 127.62 trillion it recorded one year earlier — only the second sub-zero year-over-year reading in the network's history, confirmed by Luxor's Hashrate Index on July 28, 2026.
The decline from the November 2025 all-time high of 155.97 trillion is 19.1% — the third-deepest drawdown since dedicated ASIC hardware became the standard mining tool.
Only the aftermath of the China ban and a 2018 bear market produced steeper declines.
Bitcoin Magazine Pro's data shows the downward hashrate trend has now extended approximately 287 consecutive days.

The seven-day average hashrate stood near 868 exahashes per second (EH/s) by late July, down from more than one zettahash per second at the network's late-2025 peak — a decline of roughly 12% from the all-time high.

The April 2024 halving cut the block reward from 6.25 to 3.125 Bitcoin.
At Bitcoin's October 2025 all-time high near $126,000, a single block was worth approximately $393,750.
As of August 1, Bitcoin traded near $63,100 — down approximately 47% from that peak — meaning a block now yields roughly $197,000.
That is a per-block revenue decline of more than 50% in less than a year, with the halving's supply cut baked on top.

extraction.body: Bitcoin mining difficulty has stayed below its 156 trillion peak for over a year, the longest such stretch yet, signaling deeper pressure on miners. Bitcoin mining difficulty has been stuck below its all-time high for more than a year. The metric sits just over 148 trillion as of November 8, 2026—about 5% below the 156 trillion peak it hit on October 29, 2025. That’s now the longest recordless stretch in Bitcoin’s history, surpassing a roughly 364-day run between August 2011 and July 2012. The question facing the industry: is this a temporary mining cycle, or has capital found better returns in AI data centers and high-performance computing? Bitcoin mining difficulty reached almost 156 trillion on October 29, 2025. It hasn’t reclaimed that level since. As of November 8, 2026, it stood at just over 148 trillion. The 5% gap matters less than the duration. Bitcoin has now blown past its previous record for the longest stretch without a new difficulty high, a period that began after the October 2025 peak. Difficulty adjusts as computing power enters or leaves the network, keeping block production close to 10 minutes. A lower reading after a previous peak means mining conditions haven’t returned to their earlier high-water mark. Saifedean Ammous, author of The Bitcoin Standard , says the current slowdown is now the longest in Bitcoin’s history. His reading: the industry faces structural pressure, not a single shock like those that drove earlier downturns. He points to Bitcoin’s halvings. The block subsidy drops 50% roughly every four years, so Bitcoin’s value must rise fast enough to offset the smaller reward. His estimate: mining economics need almost 19% annual appreciation over four years, before accounting for dollar devaluation and the opportunity cost of competing infrastructure businesses. Core Scientific offers a concrete example. The company recently announced plans to fully exit Bitcoin mining by the end of 2026 and enter 2027 as a dedicated AI and high-performance-computing colocation provider. It has already cut its mining fleet by almost half while redirecting electricity and data-center capacity toward infrastructure customers. Colocation revenue jumped 58% quarter over quarter to $215.4 million in the third quarter, compared with $15 million a year earlier. CryptoPotato detailed the difficulty record and the changing economics facing Bitcoin miners. Bitcoin’s previous longest recordless period ran from August 2011 to July 2012, lasting roughly 364 days. During that stretch, Bitcoin’s price collapsed by roughly 94% to 95%, providing a clear explanation for the deterioration in mining conditions. The 2021 episode stemmed from a clear regulatory event and a geographic migration. The current difficulty streak is being discussed alongside subsidy pressure, competition for power and the changing value of data-center capacity. The network previously moved in the opposite direction as Bitcoin’s price recovered and Ordinals activity increased. Miners deployed more machines, computing power rose and difficulty reached new highs. An earlier mining report linked the 2023 rise in difficulty to stronger Bitcoin prices and Ordinals-related demand for block space. It also described how new-generation machines were being installed as rack space became available. The earlier account also described the effect of rising difficulty on miners’ chances of earning block revenue. Every halving cuts the block subsidy in half. Miners must find ways to lower operating costs, improve machine efficiency or benefit from a higher Bitcoin price to preserve the economics of their facilities. Ammous’s estimate of almost 19% annual appreciation describes the pace of value growth he believes mining needs over four years. It’s an estimate about industry economics, not a Bitcoin price target. AI companies are competing for the same cheap electricity, data-center space and power infrastructure miners use. If AI colocation produces better returns, operators can redirect facilities and capital rather than add more Bitcoin mining machines. That outcome depends on how much capacity leaves mining, how much new capacity enters elsewhere and whether Bitcoin’s price provides enough incentive for operators to return to expansion. The current reading of just over 148 trillion sits about 5% below the record near 156 trillion. A gap that size wouldn’t by itself define a major industry break, but it has persisted for more than a year and exceeded the roughly 364-day record from 2011–2012. The combination of time and the absence of a new peak is the central signal. Miners haven’t returned the network to the computing-power conditions of the October 2025 high. Core Scientific’s colocation revenue reached $215.4 million in the third quarter after rising 58% from the previous quarter. The figure was $15 million a year earlier, showing why high-performance-computing customers can compete with Bitcoin mining for facility space and electricity. Those figures come from colocation, the business Core Scientific is building around AI and other computing customers. The company’s planned mining exit makes that shift one of the clearest company-level examples of the broader pressure Ammous describes. Core Scientific’s planned exit illustrates the competitive risk at the company level. Other operators may make different choices, but the availability of an alternative customer base changes how they value electricity and real estate. Bitcoin mining difficulty can remain below a prior high while the network continues operating and processing blocks. The metric describes the amount of computing competition at a point in time; it doesn’t by itself establish that Bitcoin is fundamentally weakening. Ammous offers a counterargument to the bearish interpretation. If mining becomes less attractive than holding BTC, capital that might have gone into machines, facilities and electricity could flow directly into the asset instead. Core Scientific plans to complete its Bitcoin mining exit by the end of 2026. It expects to enter 2027 as a dedicated AI and high-performance-computing colocation provider, making the end-of-year transition a key date for the company’s strategy. Bitcoin mining difficulty would need to reclaim the almost 156 trillion record set on October 29, 2025 to end the current recordless period. Until that happens, the network will continue extending the longest stretch in its history without a new difficulty high. Miners will continue weighing Bitcoin mining against AI colocation and other uses of electricity and data-center capacity. The main variables are Bitcoin’s price appreciation, the next subsidy reductions, equipment efficiency and the revenue available from non-mining infrastructure customers. The recordless streak is both a mining statistic and a sign of changing capital allocation. Whether it ends with a new expansion in hash rate or a longer shift toward AI will depend on the relative returns available to operators. Bitcoin mining difficulty reached almost 156 trillion on October 29, 2025. It has remained below that level through November 8, 2026. The metric stood at just over 148 trillion as of November 8, 2026. That is approximately 5% below the October 2025 peak. Core Scientific plans to fully exit Bitcoin mining by the end of 2026. It aims to enter 2027 as a dedicated AI and high-performance-computing colocation provider. Ammous estimated that mining economics require Bitcoin’s value to appreciate by almost 19% annually over four years. His estimate comes before accounting for dollar devaluation and the opportunity cost created by AI infrastructure. This article is for information only and is not financial advice.

That outcome depends on how much capacity leaves mining, how much new capacity enters elsewhere and whether Bitcoin’s price provides enough incentive for operators to return to expansion.

Those figures come from colocation, the business Core Scientific is building around AI and other computing customers. The company’s planned mining exit makes that shift one of the clearest company-level examples of the broader pressure Ammous describes.

The metric stands at 148.36 trillion hashes after the retarget of 29 October 2026, which lifted it 5.54% from 140.58 trillion.
The record remains 155.97 trillion, set at block 921,312 on 29 October 2025 at 10:14 UTC, according to mempool.space difficulty data.
That leaves the network 4.88% below its peak, and spot Bitcoin at $75,577, down 2.5% over seven days and 7.6% over 30.
A year without a record is not a malfunction.

On daily difficulty samples, the current 356-day run below the record is the longest in the network’s history, ahead of the 348 days between August 2011 and July 2012, the 236 days from May 2021 to January 2022, and the 225 days from October 2018 to May 2019.
Neither result depends on a new difficulty record; both depend on the price of Bitcoin, which has fallen 7.6% in 30 days.

Put that $700 million annualized colocation book against the $12.4 billion the entire network earns from issuance each year, and one company’s real-estate and power business is worth about 5.6% of everything Bitcoin mining produces.
A halving cuts the same hashprice by half unless price doubles, and it lands before the next difficulty record decision is settled in any meaningful sense.

Until then, the correct read is a network consolidating below its ceiling while its publicly traded operators shift revenue toward contracted colocation and away from a hashprice that no longer covers high-cost power.
For traders, miner balance sheets are a supply variable to watch rather than a signal to chase.
For anyone modelling hashprice, $33.4 per petahash per day is the number the whole industry is currently underwriting.
Bitcoin recalculates difficulty every 2,016 blocks, roughly two weeks of mining.
The mechanism is self-limiting, which is why the record has held through a year of infrastructure building.
With Bitcoin near $75,577 and hashrate averaging about 1.02 ZH/s, miners have little incentive to add capacity, so the retargets of the past year have not been enough to clear the October 2025 peak.

extraction.body: Bitcoin’s mining difficulty has not printed a new all-time high in 374 days. The metric stands at 148.36 trillion hashes after the retarget of 29 October 2026, which lifted it 5.54% from 140.58 trillion. The record remains 155.97 trillion, set at block 921,312 on 29 October 2025 at 10:14 UTC, according to mempool.space difficulty data. That leaves the network 4.88% below its peak, and spot Bitcoin at $75,577, down 2.5% over seven days and 7.6% over 30. A year without a record is not a malfunction. Difficulty rises only when the network finds blocks faster than the ten-minute target, and it falls or stalls when hashrate growth slows or capital leaves. What makes this stretch unusual is its length. On daily difficulty samples, the current 356-day run below the record is the longest in the network’s history, ahead of the 348 days between August 2011 and July 2012, the 236 days from May 2021 to January 2022, and the 225 days from October 2018 to May 2019. Bitcoin recalculates difficulty every 2,016 blocks, roughly two weeks of mining. The protocol compares the time taken for that batch against the 20,160 minutes implied by ten-minute blocks, then scales the target proportionally. If the batch arrived in nine minutes per block, difficulty climbs about 11%. If blocks slowed to twelve minutes, it drops. The mechanism is self-limiting, which is why the record has held through a year of infrastructure building. Difficulty can only break out when hashrate expands faster than price. Between the record on 29 October 2025 and the most recent retarget exactly one year later, difficulty moved from 155.97 trillion to 148.36 trillion. Two separate retargets in the interim, on 3 October 2026 and 19 September 2026, produced 132.72 trillion and 132.76 trillion, so the network spent the northern autumn recovering ground it had already covered. Hashrate tells a similar story. Current network hashrate sits near 1.02 zettahashes per second, with the 30-day peak at 1.22 ZH/s, based on blockchain.info’s hash-rate series. A rising hashrate that outruns price does not raise difficulty indefinitely. It raises the cost of production instead, until marginal operators switch off and the retarget resets the field. Difficulty matters to miners because it converts into revenue per unit of computing power. The arithmetic is simple enough to run directly. Bitcoin issues 3.125 $BTC per block and produces roughly 144 blocks a day, so 450 $BTC enters the market daily. At $75,577, that is about $34.0 million of gross issuance value per day, or $12.4 billion annualized, before transaction fees. Divide that by the network’s 1.02 ZH/s, which is 1.017 million petahashes, and the industry earns roughly $33.4 per petahash per second per day. That figure is the hashprice in everything but name. A month ago, with Bitcoin near $81,750 by CoinGecko’s 30-day change, the same hashrate would have produced about $36.2 per PH/s per day. Difficulty barely moved. Revenue per unit of power fell 7.6%. That gap explains why miners did not respond to flat difficulty by adding machines. Adding hashrate when price falls simply lowers the industry’s return per petahash and raises the next difficulty adjustment in someone else’s favour. The rational move is to hold steady, sell coins, or repurpose the power. Revenue per petahash only means something against the cost of running one. Take a current-generation machine rated at 20 joules per terahash. One petahash of that hardware draws 20 kilowatts, which is 480 kilowatt-hours a day. Against $33.4 of daily issuance revenue, the break-even power price works out to about 7.0 cents per kilowatt-hour, before fees, cooling, staff and hosting. That single number explains most of the sector’s behaviour this year. An operator paying 4 cents keeps roughly $14 per petahash per day of gross margin. An operator paying 7.5 cents is losing money on the same machine at the same difficulty. Neither result depends on a new difficulty record; both depend on the price of Bitcoin, which has fallen 7.6% in 30 days. The clearest evidence of that shift came on 5 November, when Core Scientific reported third-quarter results that barely resemble a mining company. Colocation revenue rose nearly 60% sequentially to $215.4 million. The company billed for 485 megawatts as of 30 September, representing more than $700 million in average annualized colocation GAAP revenue. Net income reached $1.2 billion, a figure the filed earnings release attributes to “a non-cash gain in the change in fair value of warrants,” not to mining. Adjusted EBITDA more than tripled sequentially to $133.6 million on a 57% margin, up from 25%. “Our execution at scale is translating into results, with a significant sequential increase in GAAP colocation revenue,” chief executive Adam Sullivan said in the release. “We are nearing full delivery under our first colocation agreement while construction under our second is underway across five campuses.” He added: “With revenue growing and substantial contracted capacity still to deliver, we have built a strong foundation for our next phase of growth.” Put that $700 million annualized colocation book against the $12.4 billion the entire network earns from issuance each year, and one company’s real-estate and power business is worth about 5.6% of everything Bitcoin mining produces. The warrants-driven net income is worth flagging separately. A $1.2 billion profit that depends on the mark on warrants is a balance-sheet event, and investors who read it as operating strength will misprice the quarter. This is the pattern BlockchainReporter documented when miners’ AI pivot decoupled their shares from Bitcoin, and again when AI contracts gave listed miners a valuation edge over pure-play operators. Flat difficulty does not hurt a company that is paid per megawatt of high-density colocation. It hurts the operator whose entire revenue line is the $33.4 per petahash. A new record requires hashrate to grow faster than the protocol can absorb, and the next decision point is close. The next retarget falls at block 975,744, with the chain at 974,990 at the time of writing, which places it around 12 November. Difficulty would need to climb 5.1% from 148.36 trillion to clear 155.97 trillion. The 29 October adjustment delivered 5.54%, so the arithmetic is not exotic; it is a question of whether the hashrate behind it exists. Two conditions could produce it. A price recovery would restore miner margins and pull curtailed capacity back online, since the same machines become profitable at $81,750 that sit idle at $75,577. Alternatively, new capacity could come from operators with lower power costs or stranded energy contracts, which raises network hashrate without needing a higher Bitcoin price. Neither is visible in current data: the 30-day hashrate peak of 1.22 ZH/s has already faded to an average near 1.02 ZH/s. The longer calendar matters too. The subsidy has been 3.125 $BTC per block since April 2024, and the next halving sits at block 1,050,000. With the chain at 974,990, that is 75,010 blocks away, or roughly 521 days at the current pace of 144 blocks a day. A halving cuts the same hashprice by half unless price doubles, and it lands before the next difficulty record decision is settled in any meaningful sense. The invalidation is explicit. If difficulty closes an epoch above 155.97 trillion, the 374-day gap ends and the record resets. Until then, the correct read is a network consolidating below its ceiling while its publicly traded operators shift revenue toward contracted colocation and away from a hashprice that no longer covers high-cost power. For traders, miner balance sheets are a supply variable to watch rather than a signal to chase. For anyone modelling hashprice, $33.4 per petahash per day is the number the whole industry is currently underwriting. 148.36 trillion, set at the retarget of 29 October 2026. That is 4.88% below the all-time high of 155.97 trillion recorded on 29 October 2025 at block 921,312. Difficulty only rises when blocks arrive faster than the ten-minute target. With Bitcoin near $75,577 and hashrate averaging about 1.02 ZH/s, miners have little incentive to add capacity, so the retargets of the past year have not been enough to clear the October 2025 peak. Hashprice is daily revenue per unit of computing power. At 450 $BTC of daily issuance and $75,577 per coin, the network earns about $34.0 million a day, or roughly $33.4 per petahash per second per day before fees. Falling hashprice squeezes miners even when difficulty is flat. The next retarget falls at block 975,744. With the chain at 974,990 at the time of writing, that places the adjustment around 12 November 2026. Clearing the record would require a 5.1% increase. A Bitcoin price recovery that restores miner margins, or new low-cost capacity coming online from operators with cheaper power. The 30-day hashrate peak of 1.22 ZH/s shows the capacity exists, but it has not been sustained. Data: mempool.space, CoinGecko, Blockchain.com difficulty and hash-rate series. Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism exists to keep that 10-minute cadence stable regardless of how much computing power joins or leaves the network.

The April 2024 halving cut the block reward from 6.25 to 3.125 Bitcoin.
As of August 1, Bitcoin traded near $63,100 — down approximately 47% from that peak — meaning a block now yields roughly $197,000.

Publicly traded miners sold more than 32,000 Bitcoin in the first quarter of 2026 alone — a single-quarter record that exceeded the full-year total for 2025 and surpassed the roughly 20,000 Bitcoin sold during the 2022 Terra Luna collapse.

Bitcoin uses a cryptographic process called proof-of-work: miners compete to find a hash value — the output of the SHA-256 algorithm applied to a block of transaction data — that falls below a numerical target.

extraction.body: Bitcoin's mining network has just crossed a threshold that has appeared only once before in the currency's entire history: network difficulty has fallen below where it stood a year ago, confirmed by Luxor's Hashrate Index on July 28, 2026. The machines are shutting down because the same power infrastructure that runs a Bitcoin miner is worth more to artificial intelligence data centers — and the AI market is willing to pay three to 25 times more per megawatt than Bitcoin mining currently offers. And it raises a question prior contractions never required asking: will the hashrate come back at all? Bitcoin's Self-Regulating Security Mechanism Designed for a Different Problem To understand why this moment matters, it helps to understand what mining difficulty actually measures. Bitcoin uses a cryptographic process called proof-of-work: miners compete to find a hash value — the output of the SHA-256 algorithm applied to a block of transaction data — that falls below a numerical target. The only way to find a qualifying hash is brute force: modern application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) miners attempt trillions of hash calculations per second, each one a lottery ticket, searching for the rare output that satisfies the network's current requirements. The Bitcoin Foundation's 2026 explainer on mining mechanics covers the underlying proof-of-work process in depth. At current difficulty of 126.23 trillion, only approximately one in 70 trillion random hash attempts produces a qualifying result. The network collectively performs roughly 868 quintillion such calculations every second — that is 868 exahashes per second — with the reward going to whichever miner finds a valid hash first, approximately once every ten minutes. Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism exists to keep that 10-minute cadence stable regardless of how much computing power joins or leaves the network. If the previous 2,016 blocks arrived faster than the 10-minute average implies, difficulty rises. The formula is simple: new target equals old target multiplied by the ratio of actual epoch time to the ideal 20,160-minute epoch. The adjustment is capped at four times in either direction to prevent wild swings. It assumes that economic incentives will always bring hashrate back when it leaves — that when difficulty falls, surviving miners find more blocks and earn more per unit of computing power, making the network more attractive to capital until equilibrium is restored. Only the Second Time in Bitcoin's History This Metric Has Gone Negative The 2021 China ban dropped difficulty by roughly 28% in its steepest single adjustment and pushed year-over-year difficulty growth negative. Within months, displaced miners had relocated to the United States, Kazakhstan, and other regions, and difficulty was climbing to new all-time highs. The current contraction has reproduced the year-over-year reading without any policy catalyst. Bitcoin's difficulty stands at 126.23 trillion as of the July 25 adjustment, roughly 1.1% below the 127.62 trillion it recorded one year earlier — only the second sub-zero year-over-year reading in the network's history, confirmed by Luxor's Hashrate Index on July 28, 2026. The decline from the November 2025 all-time high of 155.97 trillion is 19.1% — the third-deepest drawdown since dedicated ASIC hardware became the standard mining tool. Only the aftermath of the China ban and a 2018 bear market produced steeper declines. Bitcoin Magazine Pro's data shows the downward hashrate trend has now extended approximately 287 consecutive days. The seven-day average hashrate stood near 868 exahashes per second (EH/s) by late July, down from more than one zettahash per second at the network's late-2025 peak — a decline of roughly 12% from the all-time high. Three Forces Are Draining the Network, and Only One Has Driven a Contraction of This Kind Before Luxor's Hashrate Index attributed the decline to three overlapping causes: worsening mining economics (falling Bitcoin prices and compressed hashprice), the AI infrastructure buildout pulling capital and power away from mining, and a long tail of smaller drags including Texas 4CP curtailment costs and approximately 7 EH/s knocked offline by the conflict in Iran. The April 2024 halving cut the block reward from 6.25 to 3.125 Bitcoin. At Bitcoin's October 2025 all-time high near $126,000, a single block was worth approximately $393,750. As of August 1, Bitcoin traded near $63,100 — down approximately 47% from that peak — meaning a block now yields roughly $197,000. That is a per-block revenue decline of more than 50% in less than a year, with the halving's supply cut baked on top. Hashprice — the expected daily revenue per petahash per second of computing power — fell to an all-time spot low of $27.66 as of late June, within one cent of February's prior low, according to Hashrate Index. The math for older hardware tells the story clearly: an Antminer S19-generation machine running at 100 terahashes per second earns roughly $3.19 per day at current hashprice and consumes more in electricity than that at even $0.05 per kilowatt-hour, putting a large segment of the older fleet below breakeven. CoinShares estimated in March 2026 that 15% to 20% of the global mining fleet was already operating at a loss. Transaction fees, which once provided a meaningful secondary revenue stream during the Ordinals inscription boom of 2023 and early 2024, have normalized back to roughly 1% of total miner revenue — far below the 7% they briefly reached — removing a supplemental buffer at exactly the moment miners need one most. Publicly traded miners sold more than 32,000 Bitcoin in the first quarter of 2026 alone — a single-quarter record that exceeded the full-year total for 2025 and surpassed the roughly 20,000 Bitcoin sold during the 2022 Terra Luna collapse. Why the ASIC Hardware Constraint Makes This Conversion Permanent, Not Provisional One detail the pivot narrative frequently elides deserves technical clarity: Bitcoin ASICs cannot be repurposed for artificial intelligence workloads. Bitcoin ASICs perform only SHA-256 double-hashing — the specific cryptographic operation Bitcoin uses for proof-of-work. They cannot execute the matrix multiplication operations that underlie neural network inference and training.

extraction.body: Bitcoin mining difficulty has stayed below its 156 trillion peak for over a year, the longest such stretch yet, signaling deeper pressure on miners. Bitcoin mining difficulty has been stuck below its all-time high for more than a year. The metric sits just over 148 trillion as of November 8, 2026—about 5% below the 156 trillion peak it hit on October 29, 2025. That’s now the longest recordless stretch in Bitcoin’s history, surpassing a roughly 364-day run between August 2011 and July 2012. The question facing the industry: is this a temporary mining cycle, or has capital found better returns in AI data centers and high-performance computing? Bitcoin mining difficulty reached almost 156 trillion on October 29, 2025. It hasn’t reclaimed that level since. As of November 8, 2026, it stood at just over 148 trillion. The 5% gap matters less than the duration. Bitcoin has now blown past its previous record for the longest stretch without a new difficulty high, a period that began after the October 2025 peak. Difficulty adjusts as computing power enters or leaves the network, keeping block production close to 10 minutes. A lower reading after a previous peak means mining conditions haven’t returned to their earlier high-water mark. Saifedean Ammous, author of The Bitcoin Standard , says the current slowdown is now the longest in Bitcoin’s history. His reading: the industry faces structural pressure, not a single shock like those that drove earlier downturns. He points to Bitcoin’s halvings. The block subsidy drops 50% roughly every four years, so Bitcoin’s value must rise fast enough to offset the smaller reward. His estimate: mining economics need almost 19% annual appreciation over four years, before accounting for dollar devaluation and the opportunity cost of competing infrastructure businesses. Core Scientific offers a concrete example. The company recently announced plans to fully exit Bitcoin mining by the end of 2026 and enter 2027 as a dedicated AI and high-performance-computing colocation provider. It has already cut its mining fleet by almost half while redirecting electricity and data-center capacity toward infrastructure customers. Colocation revenue jumped 58% quarter over quarter to $215.4 million in the third quarter, compared with $15 million a year earlier. CryptoPotato detailed the difficulty record and the changing economics facing Bitcoin miners. Bitcoin’s previous longest recordless period ran from August 2011 to July 2012, lasting roughly 364 days. During that stretch, Bitcoin’s price collapsed by roughly 94% to 95%, providing a clear explanation for the deterioration in mining conditions. The 2021 episode stemmed from a clear regulatory event and a geographic migration. The current difficulty streak is being discussed alongside subsidy pressure, competition for power and the changing value of data-center capacity. The network previously moved in the opposite direction as Bitcoin’s price recovered and Ordinals activity increased. Miners deployed more machines, computing power rose and difficulty reached new highs. An earlier mining report linked the 2023 rise in difficulty to stronger Bitcoin prices and Ordinals-related demand for block space. It also described how new-generation machines were being installed as rack space became available. The earlier account also described the effect of rising difficulty on miners’ chances of earning block revenue. Every halving cuts the block subsidy in half. Miners must find ways to lower operating costs, improve machine efficiency or benefit from a higher Bitcoin price to preserve the economics of their facilities. Ammous’s estimate of almost 19% annual appreciation describes the pace of value growth he believes mining needs over four years. It’s an estimate about industry economics, not a Bitcoin price target. AI companies are competing for the same cheap electricity, data-center space and power infrastructure miners use. If AI colocation produces better returns, operators can redirect facilities and capital rather than add more Bitcoin mining machines. That outcome depends on how much capacity leaves mining, how much new capacity enters elsewhere and whether Bitcoin’s price provides enough incentive for operators to return to expansion. The current reading of just over 148 trillion sits about 5% below the record near 156 trillion. A gap that size wouldn’t by itself define a major industry break, but it has persisted for more than a year and exceeded the roughly 364-day record from 2011–2012. The combination of time and the absence of a new peak is the central signal. Miners haven’t returned the network to the computing-power conditions of the October 2025 high. Core Scientific’s colocation revenue reached $215.4 million in the third quarter after rising 58% from the previous quarter. The figure was $15 million a year earlier, showing why high-performance-computing customers can compete with Bitcoin mining for facility space and electricity. Those figures come from colocation, the business Core Scientific is building around AI and other computing customers. The company’s planned mining exit makes that shift one of the clearest company-level examples of the broader pressure Ammous describes. Core Scientific’s planned exit illustrates the competitive risk at the company level. Other operators may make different choices, but the availability of an alternative customer base changes how they value electricity and real estate. Bitcoin mining difficulty can remain below a prior high while the network continues operating and processing blocks. The metric describes the amount of computing competition at a point in time; it doesn’t by itself establish that Bitcoin is fundamentally weakening. Ammous offers a counterargument to the bearish interpretation. If mining becomes less attractive than holding BTC, capital that might have gone into machines, facilities and electricity could flow directly into the asset instead. Core Scientific plans to complete its Bitcoin mining exit by the end of 2026. It expects to enter 2027 as a dedicated AI and high-performance-computing colocation provider, making the end-of-year transition a key date for the company’s strategy. Bitcoin mining difficulty would need to reclaim the almost 156 trillion record set on October 29, 2025 to end the current recordless period. Until that happens, the network will continue extending the longest stretch in its history without a new difficulty high. Miners will continue weighing Bitcoin mining against AI colocation and other uses of electricity and data-center capacity. The main variables are Bitcoin’s price appreciation, the next subsidy reductions, equipment efficiency and the revenue available from non-mining infrastructure customers. The recordless streak is both a mining statistic and a sign of changing capital allocation. Whether it ends with a new expansion in hash rate or a longer shift toward AI will depend on the relative returns available to operators. The metric stood at just over 148 trillion as of November 8, 2026. That is approximately 5% below the October 2025 peak. Core Scientific plans to fully exit Bitcoin mining by the end of 2026. It aims to enter 2027 as a dedicated AI and high-performance-computing colocation provider. Ammous estimated that mining economics require Bitcoin’s value to appreciate by almost 19% annually over four years. His estimate comes before accounting for dollar devaluation and the opportunity cost created by AI infrastructure. This article is for information only and is not financial advice.

The 2021 episode stemmed from a clear regulatory event and a geographic migration. The current difficulty streak is being discussed alongside subsidy pressure, competition for power and the changing value of data-center capacity.

The network previously moved in the opposite direction as Bitcoin’s price recovered and Ordinals activity increased. Miners deployed more machines, computing power rose and difficulty reached new highs.

An earlier mining report linked the 2023 rise in difficulty to stronger Bitcoin prices and Ordinals-related demand for block space. It also described how new-generation machines were being installed as rack space became available.
The earlier account also described the effect of rising difficulty on miners’ chances of earning block revenue.

Every halving cuts the block subsidy in half. Miners must find ways to lower operating costs, improve machine efficiency or benefit from a higher Bitcoin price to preserve the economics of their facilities.
Ammous’s estimate of almost 19% annual appreciation describes the pace of value growth he believes mining needs over four years. It’s an estimate about industry economics, not a Bitcoin price target.

AI companies are competing for the same cheap electricity, data-center space and power infrastructure miners use. If AI colocation produces better returns, operators can redirect facilities and capital rather than add more Bitcoin mining machines.
That outcome depends on how much capacity leaves mining, how much new capacity enters elsewhere and whether Bitcoin’s price provides enough incentive for operators to return to expansion.

The current reading of just over 148 trillion sits about 5% below the record near 156 trillion. A gap that size wouldn’t by itself define a major industry break, but it has persisted for more than a year and exceeded the roughly 364-day record from 2011–2012.
The combination of time and the absence of a new peak is the central signal. Miners haven’t returned the network to the computing-power conditions of the October 2025 high.

Core Scientific’s colocation revenue reached $215.4 million in the third quarter after rising 58% from the previous quarter. The figure was $15 million a year earlier, showing why high-performance-computing customers can compete with Bitcoin mining for facility space and electricity.

Those figures come from colocation, the business Core Scientific is building around AI and other computing customers. The company’s planned mining exit makes that shift one of the clearest company-level examples of the broader pressure Ammous describes.

Core Scientific’s planned exit illustrates the competitive risk at the company level. Other operators may make different choices, but the availability of an alternative customer base changes how they value electricity and real estate.

Bitcoin mining difficulty can remain below a prior high while the network continues operating and processing blocks. The metric describes the amount of computing competition at a point in time; it doesn’t by itself establish that Bitcoin is fundamentally weakening.

Ammous offers a counterargument to the bearish interpretation. If mining becomes less attractive than holding BTC, capital that might have gone into machines, facilities and electricity could flow directly into the asset instead.

Core Scientific plans to complete its Bitcoin mining exit by the end of 2026. It expects to enter 2027 as a dedicated AI and high-performance-computing colocation provider, making the end-of-year transition a key date for the company’s strategy.

Bitcoin mining difficulty would need to reclaim the almost 156 trillion record set on October 29, 2025 to end the current recordless period. Until that happens, the network will continue extending the longest stretch in its history without a new difficulty high.

Miners will continue weighing Bitcoin mining against AI colocation and other uses of electricity and data-center capacity. The main variables are Bitcoin’s price appreciation, the next subsidy reductions, equipment efficiency and the revenue available from non-mining infrastructure customers.

The recordless streak is both a mining statistic and a sign of changing capital allocation. Whether it ends with a new expansion in hash rate or a longer shift toward AI will depend on the relative returns available to operators.
Bitcoin mining difficulty reached almost 156 trillion on October 29, 2025. It has remained below that level through November 8, 2026.
The metric stood at just over 148 trillion as of November 8, 2026. That is approximately 5% below the October 2025 peak.
Core Scientific plans to fully exit Bitcoin mining by the end of 2026. It aims to enter 2027 as a dedicated AI and high-performance-computing colocation provider.

Ammous estimated that mining economics require Bitcoin’s value to appreciate by almost 19% annually over four years. His estimate comes before accounting for dollar devaluation and the opportunity cost created by AI infrastructure.

The project is organized by the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) and the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA).

The path to a quantum secure future requires more than strong cryptography; it requires cryptographic agility, the ability to adapt to evolving algorithms, standards, and regulatory requirements, without redesigning the systems from ground up.
It also reinforces the role of SIM and eSIM technologies beyond subscriber authentication, positioning them as trusted platforms for quantum-safe telecom, IoT, government and defense applications.
Within this architecture, the Quantum-Resistant SIM acts as a hardware root of trust for secure communications, generating and protecting sensitive credentials and cryptographic operations.
The project demonstrates how secure element technologies, already widely used in telecom environments, can evolve to support future quantum safe requirements.

They serve as dedicated cryptographic modules for connected devices, enabling secure key management and cryptographic services for government, defense and other critical infrastructure applications requiring the highest levels of security and resilience.

The implementation is designed to support both international NIST standardized and Korea-specific PQC algorithms. Subject to final validation, the project is expected to deliver the first implementation of KpqC 1 algorithms on a smart-card platform in Korea, demonstrating a practical path to adding quantum-safe and crypto-agility capabilities at the secure-element level while limiting extensive changes at device level. extraction.body: Quantum computing’s threat to today’s cryptography has been evident for some time. More than half of surveyed experts expect a cryptographically relevant quantum computer within 15 years, and as many as 49% say within 10. The timeline that matters more, however, is the one set by regulators. The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations began September 11, 2026, with full requirements following in December 2027. NSA’s CNSA 2.0 requirements for new national security system acquisitions begin in January 2027. Most compliance planning has centered on software that encrypts data in transit and at rest. That overlooks a system’s first line of defense: the hardware root of trust (HRoT) that authenticates firmware and anchors trust for everything above it. Traditional HRoT options are fixed-function, with device IDs and firmware signatures locked in at design time. That stability is what makes them trustworthy, but it also locks in algorithm choices. When those algorithms age out, designers must replace the component or layer software on top. Because software updates are far easier than hardware changes, many systems pair modern software with legacy hardware. That works only as long as the underlying algorithms hold. Quantum computing ends that arrangement. NIST has finalized ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), and specifies LMS and XMSS (SP 800-208) for firmware signing. Yet most traditional HRoT options, including MCUs and secure-boot SoCs, rely solely on RSA and ECC, which a sufficiently powerful quantum computer can break. No software layer can fix a foundation that cannot be trusted. Decision-makers are left in a difficult position. Existing devices are no longer adequate, and quantum capabilities will keep changing quickly and unpredictably. They need an approach that addresses today’s threats while remaining adaptable to tomorrow’s requirements. The answer is cryptographically agile, hardware-level protection. Crypto-agility, the ability to update cryptographic algorithms in the field without replacing hardware, offers a path to protection without sending systems back to square one. Crypto-agile PQC systems counter the perception that an effective HRoT must be completely static. They preserve the fixed security elements that matter while adding flexibility where it is needed, through a combination of features: Adaptable hardware such as Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) makes crypto-agility accessible in a unified hardware package. A single FPGA can serve as both the HRoT and the system control layer, handling boot, power sequencing, and monitoring in one place, while reconfigurable logic allows security functions to be updated after deployment. Low-power, always-on operation, deterministic low-latency response, parallel processing for multiple simultaneous key operations, and high I/O capacity add to their value in secure-by-design systems, with or without PQC considerations. Specialized FPGAs like the Lattice Mach™-N2 family are built for PQC-ready operation . Mach-N2 offers logic densities of up to 220k cells and boots in under 30 milliseconds, closing the firmware-boot gap that leaves systems exposed. It supports a full CNSA 2.0-compliant PQC suite (ML-DSA, LMS, and XMSS for authentication, ML-KEM for key exchange) alongside AES-256-GCM, ECC521, and RSA4096 for backward compatibility. Field-updatable algorithms let designers and operators adapt as requirements change, and PUF-derived device identity with DICE and SPDM support extends trust across the platform and supply chain. The root of trust is only one layer. Protecting platform firmware across its lifecycle also requires detection, recovery, and attestation, and these capabilities need to be post-quantum ready as well. Platform Firmware Resilience (PFR) aligned to NIST SP 800-193 provides protection, detection, and recovery, while SPDM 1.4 attestation extends trust across the devices in a system. Solutions such as the Lattice Sentry™ solution stack pair PQC-enabled PFR and attestation with a crypto-agile hardware root of trust, giving teams a practical path to PQC-ready operation. PQC preparedness will take years and will evolve as attackers and protections adapt to one another. The hardware designers choose today must meet requirements that have not yet been written. The only certainty is that the unknown is coming, so the right foundation is one built to change as quickly as the quantum landscape.

The project is organized by the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) and the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA). As part of the initiative, with KT playing a leading role, IST is implementing NIST-standardized and Korean PQC algorithms on the Quantum-Resistant SIM equipped smart-card platform to support the protection of defense communications systems against emerging cryptographic threats. Bringing post-quantum cryptography to SIM and eSIM deployments Post-quantum algorithms place significantly higher demands on processing power and memory than many classical cryptographic schemes. IST is addressing these constraints through the PQC dedicated SIM and eSIM, enabling demanding cryptographic operations to be handled efficiently within a secure, tamper-resistant environment. The implementation is designed to support both international NIST standardized and Korea-specific PQC algorithms. Subject to final validation, the project is expected to deliver the first implementation of KpqC 1 algorithms on a smart-card platform in Korea, demonstrating a practical path to adding quantum-safe and crypto-agility capabilities at the secure-element level while limiting extensive changes at device level. Supporting quantum-safe defense communications KT’s broader pilot, conducted for the Ministry of National Defense and the Army Information and Communication School, is designed to apply and verify PQC across critical defense infrastructures, including smart-unit platforms and user PCs, CCTV and video storage systems, drones and ground control systems, and 5G network environments. The aim is to assess performance and applicability in demanding operational conditions. Within this architecture, the Quantum-Resistant SIM acts as a hardware root of trust for secure communications, generating and protecting sensitive credentials and cryptographic operations. The project demonstrates how secure element technologies, already widely used in telecom environments, can evolve to support future quantum safe requirements. They serve as dedicated cryptographic modules for connected devices, enabling secure key management and cryptographic services for government, defense and other critical infrastructure applications requiring the highest levels of security and resilience. South Korea is accelerating its transition toward post-quantum security across critical sectors. The pilot builds on IST’s broader post-quantum roadmap as part of IDEMIA SPHERE cybersecurity suite, and its expertise in cryptography for secure connectivity and cybersecurity, to deliver a scalable foundation for quantum-resilient security services. extraction.body: Quantum computing’s threat to today’s cryptography has been evident for some time. More than half of surveyed experts expect a cryptographically relevant quantum computer within 15 years, and as many as 49% say within 10. The timeline that matters more, however, is the one set by regulators. The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations began September 11, 2026, with full requirements following in December 2027. NSA’s CNSA 2.0 requirements for new national security system acquisitions begin in January 2027. Most compliance planning has centered on software that encrypts data in transit and at rest. That overlooks a system’s first line of defense: the hardware root of trust (HRoT) that authenticates firmware and anchors trust for everything above it. Traditional HRoT options are fixed-function, with device IDs and firmware signatures locked in at design time. That stability is what makes them trustworthy, but it also locks in algorithm choices. When those algorithms age out, designers must replace the component or layer software on top. Because software updates are far easier than hardware changes, many systems pair modern software with legacy hardware. That works only as long as the underlying algorithms hold. Quantum computing ends that arrangement. NIST has finalized ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), and specifies LMS and XMSS (SP 800-208) for firmware signing. Yet most traditional HRoT options, including MCUs and secure-boot SoCs, rely solely on RSA and ECC, which a sufficiently powerful quantum computer can break. No software layer can fix a foundation that cannot be trusted. Decision-makers are left in a difficult position. Existing devices are no longer adequate, and quantum capabilities will keep changing quickly and unpredictably. They need an approach that addresses today’s threats while remaining adaptable to tomorrow’s requirements. The answer is cryptographically agile, hardware-level protection. Crypto-agility, the ability to update cryptographic algorithms in the field without replacing hardware, offers a path to protection without sending systems back to square one. Crypto-agile PQC systems counter the perception that an effective HRoT must be completely static. They preserve the fixed security elements that matter while adding flexibility where it is needed, through a combination of features: Adaptable hardware such as Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) makes crypto-agility accessible in a unified hardware package. A single FPGA can serve as both the HRoT and the system control layer, handling boot, power sequencing, and monitoring in one place, while reconfigurable logic allows security functions to be updated after deployment. Low-power, always-on operation, deterministic low-latency response, parallel processing for multiple simultaneous key operations, and high I/O capacity add to their value in secure-by-design systems, with or without PQC considerations. Specialized FPGAs like the Lattice Mach™-N2 family are built for PQC-ready operation . Mach-N2 offers logic densities of up to 220k cells and boots in under 30 milliseconds, closing the firmware-boot gap that leaves systems exposed. It supports a full CNSA 2.0-compliant PQC suite (ML-DSA, LMS, and XMSS for authentication, ML-KEM for key exchange) alongside AES-256-GCM, ECC521, and RSA4096 for backward compatibility. Field-updatable algorithms let designers and operators adapt as requirements change, and PUF-derived device identity with DICE and SPDM support extends trust across the platform and supply chain. The root of trust is only one layer. Protecting platform firmware across its lifecycle also requires detection, recovery, and attestation, and these capabilities need to be post-quantum ready as well. Platform Firmware Resilience (PFR) aligned to NIST SP 800-193 provides protection, detection, and recovery, while SPDM 1.4 attestation extends trust across the devices in a system. Solutions such as the Lattice Sentry™ solution stack pair PQC-enabled PFR and attestation with a crypto-agile hardware root of trust, giving teams a practical path to PQC-ready operation. PQC preparedness will take years and will evolve as attackers and protections adapt to one another. The hardware designers choose today must meet requirements that have not yet been written. The only certainty is that the unknown is coming, so the right foundation is one built to change as quickly as the quantum landscape.

Artificial intelligence (AI) has been a gold mine for companies selling chips and building data centers . But without software, those AI chips don't really have anything to do. That's why I think software stocks are as important as chipmakers and hyperscalers when you consider how to invest in the AI build-out. The more companies depend on AI, the more important those software services become. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » Two companies that stand to benefit are Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) and CrowdStrike (NASDAQ: CRWD). They approach AI from different directions, but both are already seeing growing demand for their products. With $5,000 to invest, I'd consider splitting my money equally between these two outstanding software stocks. You likely already use Microsoft software, though you may not realize it. Microsoft makes some of the most popular software programs, such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook. All of them are available in the company's popular Microsoft 365 suite. In addition, its Azure cloud platform supplies the infrastructure needed to develop and run AI applications. Azure AI Foundry provides tools for developers to build those applications, while GitHub Copilot helps them write code. The strategy is paying off. In Microsoft's fiscal first quarter of 2027, which ended Sept. 30, Azure and other cloud services revenue increased 48% year over year to $33.16 billion. Microsoft has also incorporated Copilot in its 365 software suite of office tools. During the quarter, Microsoft reported that daily Copilot users increased nearly 50% sequentially and more than fivefold year over year. The number of customers with more than 50,000 Copilot seats also increased more than eightfold year over year. That's particularly encouraging because it demonstrates that businesses are willing to pay for AI capabilities within software they already use. Microsoft reported $677 billion in commercial remaining performance obligations, representing contracted revenue that hasn't yet been recognized. That figure increased 73% year over year, although commitments from OpenAI contributed substantially to the growth. If there's a downside to Microsoft stock now, however, it's in spending. Microsoft is dropping billions of dollars every quarter to satisfy AI demand. Capital expenditures reached $45.2 billion in the quarter, and management expects spending to increase to $50 billion in Q2. Those investments are putting pressure on margins, and there's no guarantee they'll produce the returns investors expect. Still, Microsoft generated $18.6 billion in quarterly free cash flow despite its spending. That gives the company considerable financial flexibility as it expands its AI business. While AI offers businesses new opportunities to develop new products and work more efficiently, it also creates new opportunities for cybercriminals. And unfortunately, there are always bad actors looking for an opportunity to break the rules and make a quick buck. Companies that deploy AI agents capable of accessing sensitive information and performing tasks without constant human supervision are susceptible to cyberattacks, and CrowdStrike addresses these risks through its Falcon cybersecurity platform. During the company's fiscal second-quarter earnings call, CEO George Kurtz discussed the emerging market for AI detection and response (AIDR). He suggested that protecting AI agents could eventually become a larger business than traditional endpoint detection and response. That's an ambitious prediction, but CrowdStrike's existing business is already producing impressive results. In the quarter ended July 31, revenue increased 26% year over year to $1.47 billion. Annual recurring revenue (ARR) reached $5.84 billion, up 25%, while net new ARR jumped 51% to a record $333 million. And there's evidence that customers are expanding their relationships with CrowdStrike. The company reported that ARR from accounts adopting its Falcon Flex subscription model exceeded $2.29 billion, up 101% from the previous year. Falcon Flex allows customers to adopt additional security products under a flexible purchasing arrangement. So, CrowdStrike doesn't have to rely exclusively on finding new customers. It can generate additional revenue by selling more services to businesses already using its platform.
