extraction.body: The Pentagon said it has delivered more than 25,000 unmanned and counter-drone systems to U.S. Central Command in 2026, backed by about $782 million in investment. More than 24,000 were counter-drone systems, fielded through Joint Interagency Task Force 401 to protect forward-deployed forces from drone attacks. The deliveries also included more than 1,300 one-way attack drones for precision strikes at longer ranges. U.S. Central Command received more than 100 uncrewed surface and underwater vessels to expand its maritime reconnaissance and strike capabilities. The Pentagon said it is expanding production on commercial lines and using modular software to get new equipment to troops faster. The aim is to give commanders lower-cost systems they can use in large numbers, reducing the need to expend munitions that cost millions of dollars apiece. “The thousands of systems operating across CENTCOM this year are just the beginning,” said Owen West, chief executive of Project Agincourt and the Pentagon’s direct reporting portfolio manager for unmanned systems. “We will out-innovate, out-build, and out-adapt any adversary on the battlefield.” The Pentagon plans to keep supplying Central Command while expanding deliveries to U.S. forces in the Pacific and Europe and across the wider joint force. The effort also lays the groundwork for Autonomous Warfare Command, a planned four-star combatant command due to be established by Oct. 1, 2027. France has finalised an order with Naval Group and MBDA to increase the Aster air defence missile capacity of its FDI frigates from 16 to 32 per ship. AIRO Group Holdings said a U.S. government customer ordered two types of drones from the company, the RQ-35 Heidrun and RQ-70 Dainn, in its first U.S. drone sale. RTX is adding production capacity for Tomahawk, AMRAAM, SM-6 and SM-3 IB missiles under four multiyear Pentagon contracts worth about $70 billion combined. The Department of the Air Force has assigned senior leaders to 15 mission areas to move what it calls “super intelligence” from testing into operational use. Canada is considering a firm order for eight Type 212CD submarines from German shipbuilder TKMS, with options for another four, CBC News reported. Rheinmetall expects Germany’s parliament to approve the Arminius Boxer armoured vehicle contract in the first quarter of 2027, with a detailed price audit likely to push the decision past year-end. Japan and the United States wrapped up Keen Sword 27 on Oct. 29 after 11 days of training with forces from seven other countries. British F-35 jets flying from HMS Prince of Wales intercepted a Russian Tu-95 Bear long-range bomber during a major NATO exercise off Norway, the Royal Navy said. Britain’s Titania military satellite is in orbit, giving the armed forces another way to observe military activity on Earth, the Ministry of Defence said. The 46,000-square-foot building will be the first at Dyess dedicated solely to the new bomber, with secure workspaces and communications networks for planning and preparing strike missions. extraction.body: Aircraft armed with advanced laser-guided rocket systems took out a little under half of the one-way attack drones the Houthis launched against military and commercial vessels during the U.S. military campaign that unfolded between March and May in and around the Red Sea, Gen. Erik Kurilla told lawmakers Tuesday. At a House Armed Services Committee posture hearing, the U.S. Central Command commander shared new details about that operation and said it underscores the military’s intensifying need for more and better counter-drone technologies and software. “We absolutely need to be putting more work into directed energy [and] high-powered microwaves, I think, are some of the innovations that have come out of this since Operation Rough Rider. About 40% of the drones shot down were shot down by something called Advanced Precision Weapon Kill System , a laser-guided 2.75-inch rocket fired off our F-16s or F-15s. That’s a $25,000 munition going against a roughly $50,000 or $100,000 drone — that is an Iranian-provided drone,” Kurilla said. Iran-backed Houthi fighters based in Yemen kicked off their attacks against vessels traversing crucial international shipping routes near the Red Sea in 2023. They indicated the disruption was meant as a form of protest of America’s support for Israel’s military actions in Gaza. Early into his second administration, President Donald Trump initiated Operation Rough Rider to dismantle Houthi infrastructure and leadership in the region. Trump announced an end to the operation in early May, following an agreement between America and the Houthis — brokered in part through the Omani government — to suspend the strikes. Operation Rough Rider cost the U.S. an estimated $1 billion , lawmakers pointed out at the posture hearing. It also resulted in the loss of multiple high-dollar military drones and fighter aircraft. “The president gave us a very specific mission, which was to get the Houthis to quit shooting at American ships. Six months ago on 12 November 2024, was the last time a destroyer went through the Bab-el-Mandeb. It was attacked 17 times with anti-ship ballistic missiles and anti-ship cruise missiles and [unmanned aerial vehicles or UAVs]. In the last week, we put four destroyers back through the Bab-el-Mandeb,” Kurilla said. After the conclusion of Rough Rider, however, Centcom is “still defending Israel with” its Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system against ongoing assaults from the Houthis, which remain under the foreign terrorist organization designation by the U.S. In the operation’s aftermath though, one major lesson the command learned, as Kurilla put it, is that “software is a weapon” that is rapidly changing the character of warfare. “Our ability to do Combined Joint All-Domain Command and Control , the things that we are doing with software — it’s amazing. We have advanced that. We have engineers every day making improvements on our ability to do that. It’s a warfighting headquarters,” Kurilla said. Software is also driving significant transformations in ballistic missile defense on the contemporary battlefield, the commander noted. “The same thing, I would tell you, as it comes to counter-UAS as well. We are making changes to the Navy’s software on the SPY radars based on what we’re seeing,” Kurilla told the committee. When asked by lawmakers to recommend the top weapons capabilities he views they should most quickly invest in, the commander repeatedly pointed to counter-drone systems, calling them the “number one” in-demand tool at this time. “We’re only going to see the systems get smaller, more lethal. [On] the electromagnetic spectrum, we try and jam that. That’s why Ukraine and Russia went to fiber optics — going out to 40 kilometers with fiber optic drones — you can’t jam that. So those are the things I would ask for right now, the counter-UAS [and detection capabilities]. I think we need to put aerial [Inverse Synthetic Aperture Radars or ISAR] for low-radar cross section to be able to pick up, elevate it, and then [use] ballistic missile defense,” Kurilla said.

So those are the things I would ask for right now, the counter-UAS [and detection capabilities]. I think we need to put aerial [Inverse Synthetic Aperture Radars or ISAR] for low-radar cross section to be able to pick up, elevate it, and then [use] ballistic missile defense,” Kurilla said.

Bryan Cercy, an innovation officer at CENTCOM, told C4ISRNET the innovation team will choose sensors this summer to participate in a U.S.-based exercise in October focused on spotting UAS threats. CENTCOM’s innovation team traveled to the Middle East to observe operators and hear first hand about the challenges they face in conducting their missions. CENTCOM also leveraged its technology residency program, which temporarily embeds private sector experts within the command to help solve technical challenges. It sent its resident at the time to observe operators tracking UAS threats and better understand their capability needs. Air Force Col. Nate Huston, CENTCOM’s director of innovation and capability integration, said in the same interview that part of the intent behind technology sprints like this is to demonstrate a process for identifying innovative solutions to problems in the field and validating whether there’s a capability that can address it. “What we want to say is like, ‘Hey, we started at this point, we got these disparate folks together, we showed that this could be integrated,’” he said. “The other part of this is . . . we fully understand some integration will not work exactly right, and we’ll learn from that.” Courtney Albon is C4ISRNET’s space and emerging technology reporter. extraction.body: The Pentagon said it has delivered more than 25,000 unmanned and counter-drone systems to U.S. Central Command in 2026, backed by about $782 million in investment. More than 24,000 were counter-drone systems, fielded through Joint Interagency Task Force 401 to protect forward-deployed forces from drone attacks. The deliveries also included more than 1,300 one-way attack drones for precision strikes at longer ranges. U.S. Central Command received more than 100 uncrewed surface and underwater vessels to expand its maritime reconnaissance and strike capabilities. The Pentagon said it is expanding production on commercial lines and using modular software to get new equipment to troops faster. The aim is to give commanders lower-cost systems they can use in large numbers, reducing the need to expend munitions that cost millions of dollars apiece. “The thousands of systems operating across CENTCOM this year are just the beginning,” said Owen West, chief executive of Project Agincourt and the Pentagon’s direct reporting portfolio manager for unmanned systems. “We will out-innovate, out-build, and out-adapt any adversary on the battlefield.” The Pentagon plans to keep supplying Central Command while expanding deliveries to U.S. forces in the Pacific and Europe and across the wider joint force. The effort also lays the groundwork for Autonomous Warfare Command, a planned four-star combatant command due to be established by Oct. 1, 2027. France has finalised an order with Naval Group and MBDA to increase the Aster air defence missile capacity of its FDI frigates from 16 to 32 per ship. AIRO Group Holdings said a U.S. government customer ordered two types of drones from the company, the RQ-35 Heidrun and RQ-70 Dainn, in its first U.S. drone sale. RTX is adding production capacity for Tomahawk, AMRAAM, SM-6 and SM-3 IB missiles under four multiyear Pentagon contracts worth about $70 billion combined. The Department of the Air Force has assigned senior leaders to 15 mission areas to move what it calls “super intelligence” from testing into operational use. Canada is considering a firm order for eight Type 212CD submarines from German shipbuilder TKMS, with options for another four, CBC News reported. Rheinmetall expects Germany’s parliament to approve the Arminius Boxer armoured vehicle contract in the first quarter of 2027, with a detailed price audit likely to push the decision past year-end. Japan and the United States wrapped up Keen Sword 27 on Oct. 29 after 11 days of training with forces from seven other countries. British F-35 jets flying from HMS Prince of Wales intercepted a Russian Tu-95 Bear long-range bomber during a major NATO exercise off Norway, the Royal Navy said. Britain’s Titania military satellite is in orbit, giving the armed forces another way to observe military activity on Earth, the Ministry of Defence said. The 46,000-square-foot building will be the first at Dyess dedicated solely to the new bomber, with secure workspaces and communications networks for planning and preparing strike missions. extraction.body: The 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 has already made plenty of noise with its new engine lineup. After getting a closer look at the Denali Ultimate, though, I think the conversation is going to turn to what GMC has done inside the truck. There is a lot going on here, from the materials and seats to the screens, storage and lighting. This was a walk-around of a preproduction truck, not a road test. Some functions were turned off during the demonstration, so I’m treating this as a look at the design and features rather than a verdict on how the finished truck drives or how every system works in daily use. For the broader lineup announcement, see our earlier 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 coverage . The Denali Ultimate’s grille makes a statement before you open a door. GMC showed a dark GMC badge with illumination. The grille finish prompted a little back-and-forth during the walk-around because I’m going to miss saying “Vader Chrome.” That name was fun. There are useful details beyond the grille. The engine-displacement badges move to the hood, and GMC’s team explained that the familiar external antennas have been removed as part of the new design. The Denali Ultimate shown also had 22-inch diamond-cut aluminum wheels and articulating assist steps. Its lighting includes welcome and farewell animations, which add another bit of theater when you approach or leave the truck. Inside, GMC showed an open-pore forged birch wood treatment on the console and instrument panel. The team explained that the wood is chopped and pressed to create the pattern. It has a different look from a conventional glossy wood insert, and it gives the Denali Ultimate something distinctive to put alongside its stitching, piping and topographic details. The Denali Ultimate comes with 14-way power front seats with heating, ventilation and massage. I also spent some time checking the seats. My first impression was that they felt more comfortable, especially in the area I pointed out during the demonstration. That is encouraging, but a few minutes in a parked truck is different from a long day behind the wheel. I still want that seat time before making a bigger claim about comfort. In the rear, GMC confirmed heated outboard seats rather than ventilated ones. GM also got rid of those funky storage compartments built into the rear seatbacks. The flat floor and underseat storage remain useful features for the gloves, towing equipment and other things that tend to live in a truck cab. The ambient lighting demonstration was a good example of how much customization GMC is building into this interior. The team described 143 color combinations, with separate upper and lower zones. I can already see owners sharing their favorite combinations online, especially when they can match a school or team’s colors. The cabin also needs to work as a place to charge devices and get things done. During the walk-around, GMC pointed out six USB connections across the front and rear of the cabin, along with a 120-volt outlet. The available MultiPro center console and articulating screen with hidden storage are part of the larger interior redesign GMC highlighted at the event. The follow-up screen demonstration showed a new user interface with customizable information and quick-access controls. One practical example was switching between two connected phones, which could be useful if you carry separate work and personal devices. Another was a garage-door control that can appear based on your location. Those are the kinds of features I want to try repeatedly in a production truck to see whether they make things easier. There is also an 11.5-inch passenger display, alongside the 16.3-inch center screen and 12.2-inch driver display GMC demonstrated. The passenger screen has a privacy filter, and the team walked through options for streaming, connecting a device through HDMI and choosing where the audio plays. I want to see how useful that setup is with someone riding along. GMC also confirms that wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto remain part of the new infotainment system. One change that will get truck owners talking is the digital oil-level reading for the next-generation V8s. GMC showed it in the vehicle-status app, where the display reports the oil level alongside information such as battery voltage. That is a feature I want to try myself when checking a production truck. The Sierra’s new interior gives us plenty to explore, but the real test will come with everyday use. I want to see how quickly the controls become familiar, how the screens behave in different lighting and whether the seats stay comfortable after several hours. I’m also interested in spending more time with the truck’s towing features, including available Super Cruise with trailering capability. GMC lists the Denali Ultimate’s starting price at $87,895, including the $2,795 destination freight charge. The new 6.6-liter V8 is standard, with 481 horsepower and 501 pound-feet of torque; the 3.0-liter Duramax diesel is available. GMC says the first 2027 Sierra models will reach U.S. dealers before the end of 2026. For now, the Denali Ultimate makes a strong first impression as a cabin GMC has put considerable thought into. The combination of new materials, storage ideas and configurable technology gives buyers more to consider than a new grille or a larger display alone. We’ll need a proper drive to find out how well it all comes together. Tim Esterdahl is an award-winning automotive journalist who has covered the industry since 2011, specializing in pickup trucks, SUVs, towing and vehicle reliability. His work has appeared on CBS Sunday Morning, NewsNation, MotorTrend and The Boston Globe, and he has tested hundreds of new vehicles across North America. The follow-up screen demonstration showed a new user interface with customizable information and quick-access controls. One practical example was switching between two connected phones, which could be useful if you carry separate work and personal devices. Another was a garage-door control that can appear based on your location. Those are the kinds of features I want to try repeatedly in a production truck to see whether they make things easier.

There is also an 11.5-inch passenger display, alongside the 16.3-inch center screen and 12.2-inch driver display GMC demonstrated. The passenger screen has a privacy filter, and the team walked through options for streaming, connecting a device through HDMI and choosing where the audio plays. I want to see how useful that setup is with someone riding along. GMC also confirms that wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto remain part of the new infotainment system.

One change that will get truck owners talking is the digital oil-level reading for the next-generation V8s. GMC showed it in the vehicle-status app, where the display reports the oil level alongside information such as battery voltage. That is a feature I want to try myself when checking a production truck.

The Sierra’s new interior gives us plenty to explore, but the real test will come with everyday use. I want to see how quickly the controls become familiar, how the screens behave in different lighting and whether the seats stay comfortable after several hours. I’m also interested in spending more time with the truck’s towing features, including available Super Cruise with trailering capability.

GMC lists the Denali Ultimate’s starting price at $87,895, including the $2,795 destination freight charge. The new 6.6-liter V8 is standard, with 481 horsepower and 501 pound-feet of torque; the 3.0-liter Duramax diesel is available. GMC says the first 2027 Sierra models will reach U.S. dealers before the end of 2026.

For now, the Denali Ultimate makes a strong first impression as a cabin GMC has put considerable thought into. The combination of new materials, storage ideas and configurable technology gives buyers more to consider than a new grille or a larger display alone. We’ll need a proper drive to find out how well it all comes together.

sources.title: The 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and GMC Sierra 1500 Get Worse Fuel Economy Numbers - MotorTrend
passages: The 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and GMC Sierra 1500 are getting major updates, including new small-block V-8 engines, updated transmissions, and refreshed exterior and interior designs.
Those changes bring revised EPA fuel economy ratings, and the numbers point to a small efficiency hit for most configurations compared with the 2026 trucks.
The EPA has released ratings for the 5.7-liter V-8, 6.6-liter V-8, and 3.0-liter turbodiesel available in both trucks; final fuel economy figures for the base 2.7-liter turbo-four are still pending.
According to data from GM Authority , nearly every listed powertrain and trim combination returns lower ratings for 2027.
The exception is the GMC Sierra AT4X equipped with the turbodiesel.
The amount of the change varies by engine, drivetrain, and trim.
In several configurations, the difference is only 1 or 2 mpg, while certain four-wheel-drive diesel versions have larger drops.
Choosing a different drivetrain or trim can therefore affect the comparison as much as the engine itself.
It gains 1 mpg in city driving and 2 mpg on both the highway and combined cycle.
The V-8 changes help explain some of the decline.
Both engines have larger displacements and more horsepower and torque, which in some cases can also mean more fuel consumption.
Miguel Cortina is Mexico Editor at MotorTrend , covering the auto industry in the U.S. and south of the border.
He joined MotorTrend in January 2015 and is an avid automotive enthusiast who enjoys playing golf, surfing, and running in his free time.

sources.title: Preview: 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 Comes With Luxury, Power, and Off-Road Capabilities - Consumer Reports
passages: Like the Chevrolet Silverado 1500 , the GMC Sierra 1500 received an evolutionary redesign for the 2027 model year.
The off-road trims can handle tougher conditions, and luxury editions get luxury amenities that rival those of high-end SUVs.
GMC says the turbocharged four-cylinder has been upgraded, now producing 350 hp. (The previous version of that 2.7-liter engine produces 310 hp.)
The most extroverted trim is the Sierra 1500 AT4X.

It enhances the truck’s off-road capability with 35-inch Goodyear Mud Terrain (MT) tires, a 2-inch suspension lift, off-road shocks, front and rear electronically locked differentials to optimize traction, and a distinctive front fascia.
Like the previous model, the AT4X will again be sold with the AEV Edition package, which further fortifies the truck.
Think of the Pro as the work-centered entry point, with the Elevation scaling the trim walk with more creature comforts.
The turbo four has been changed, and the V8s are next-generation small blocks.
The outgoing Sierra 1500 is a competitive option within the full-sized truck class, and we expect the new version to be as well.
Bartlett is the managing editor for the autos team at Consumer Reports.

The off-road trims can handle tougher conditions, and luxury editions get luxury amenities that rival those of high-end SUVs. The four available engines are a turbocharged four-cylinder, two new V8s, and a turbodiesel six-cylinder. The turbo four has been changed, and the V8s are next-generation small blocks. Trim options for the Sierra 1500 are the Pro, Elevation, AT4, AT4X, Denali, and Denali Ultimate. Think of the Pro as the work-centered entry point, with the Elevation scaling the trim walk with more creature comforts. Each trim separates into the off-road-focused AT4 and more capable AT4X, while the Denali and Denali Ultimate chart a luxury and tech-focused path. What it competes with: Chevrolet Silverado 1500 , Ford F-150 , Ram 1500 , Toyota Tundra Powertrains: • 350-hp, 2.7-liter turbocharged four-cylinder • 402-hp, 5.7-liter V8 • 481-hp, 6.6-liter V8 • 305-hp, 3.0-liter turbocharged diesel six-cylinder engine Each with a 10-speed automatic transmission; rear- or four-wheel drive Price: $48,500-$85,100 for crew cab 4WD Destination: $2,795 On sale: Late 2026 Final assembly point: Fort Wayne, Ind. The outgoing Sierra 1500 is a competitive option within the full-sized truck class, and we expect the new version to be as well. But like other full-sized pickups, the current Sierra 1500 has below-average reliability. Even though the 2027 Sierra 1500 has all-new sheet metal, it’s so similar to the 2026 body that you might need to look for the trapezoidal grille and more complicated headlamps to identify one. Trim-specific details distinguish various versions of the Sierra, as seen in the lower front design, wheels, and exhaust outlets. GMC says there are available welcome and farewell light animations, addressing a need you probably didn’t know existed. Trucks … with animations. The Sierra 1500 will once again be available as a regular cab/long bed, extended cab/standard bed, crew cab/standard bed, and crew cab/long bed. The most extroverted trim is the Sierra 1500 AT4X. It enhances the truck’s off-road capability with 35-inch Goodyear Mud Terrain (MT) tires, a 2-inch suspension lift, off-road shocks, front and rear electronically locked differentials to optimize traction, and a distinctive front fascia. Like the previous model, the AT4X will again be sold with the AEV Edition package, which further fortifies the truck. The redesigned cabin is simpler than the outgoing model, with screens spread across the dashboard. All combined, GMC says there’s more than 60 inches of total screen. The digital real estate includes a 12.2-inch instrument display, 16.3-inch infotainment screen, and 11.5-inch front passenger screen. Plus, there’s an available 15-inch color head-up display and an 8.5-inch rearview mirror display, which can show behind the vehicle when the view is being obstructed by passengers and head restraints. Different trims come with specific materials, including leather and real wood, along with stitching and accents. The AT4X has a flat-bottom steering wheel, increased seat bolsters, perforated upholstery, stainless steel speaker grilles, and abundant stitching. Adding to the luxury experience is an available panoramic roof (standard on AT4X) and a new MultiPro center console that slides and folds, allowing for different configurations between the driver and front passenger, including transforming into a flat table well-suited to placing a laptop or having a picnic. The 2027 GMC Sierra 1500’s powertrains only look like carryovers from last year. GMC says the turbocharged four-cylinder has been upgraded, now producing 350 hp. (The previous version of that 2.7-liter engine produces 310 hp.) The 3.0-liter turbodiesel six-cylinder engine may be changed only slightly. The previous truck produced 310 hp, and it achieved 23 mpg overall in our tests. The new diesel makes 305 hp. The 5.7-liter and 6.6-liter V8s are next-generation small blocks, producing 402 and 481 hp, respectively. This time around, all four engines will be matched with a 10-speed automatic transmission. There has been no mention of a hybrid to rival Ford and Toyota’s truck offerings. The 2027 Sierra 1500 comes standard with forward collision warning, automatic emergency braking with bicyclist and pedestrian detection, adaptive cruise control, blind spot warning, rear cross traffic warning, and front and rear parking collision warning.. GM’s Super Cruise active driving assistance system will be available and feature hands-free driving while towing. The system will come with a free three-year OnStar trial to support Super Cruise functionality. Jeff S. Bartlett is the managing editor for the autos team at Consumer Reports. coreStoryFacts.text: The 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 has already made plenty of noise with its new engine lineup.
After getting a closer look at the Denali Ultimate, though, I think the conversation is going to turn to what GMC has done inside the truck.
There is a lot going on here, from the materials and seats to the screens, storage and lighting.
This was a walk-around of a preproduction truck, not a road test.
The new 6.6-liter V8 is standard, with 481 horsepower and 501 pound-feet of torque; the 3.0-liter Duramax diesel is available.
GMC says the first 2027 Sierra models will reach U.S. dealers before the end of 2026.
Inside, GMC showed an open-pore forged birch wood treatment on the console and instrument panel.
The team explained that the wood is chopped and pressed to create the pattern.
© 2026 Pickup Truck +SUV Talk (PUTT). All rights reserved.
The combination of new materials, storage ideas and configurable technology gives buyers more to consider than a new grille or a larger display alone.
We’ll need a proper drive to find out how well it all comes together.
Tim Esterdahl is an award-winning automotive journalist who has covered the industry since 2011, specializing in pickup trucks, SUVs, towing and vehicle reliability.
One change that will get truck owners talking is the digital oil-level reading for the next-generation V8s.
The 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and GMC Sierra 1500 are getting major updates, including new small-block V-8 engines, updated transmissions, and refreshed exterior and interior designs.
Those changes bring revised EPA fuel economy ratings, and the numbers point to a small efficiency hit for most configurations compared with the 2026 trucks.
The EPA has released ratings for the 5.7-liter V-8, 6.6-liter V-8, and 3.0-liter turbodiesel available in both trucks; final fuel economy figures for the base 2.7-liter turbo-four are still pending.
According to data from GM Authority , nearly every listed powertrain and trim combination returns lower ratings for 2027.
The exception is the GMC Sierra AT4X equipped with the turbodiesel.
The amount of the change varies by engine, drivetrain, and trim.
In several configurations, the difference is only 1 or 2 mpg, while certain four-wheel-drive diesel versions have larger drops.
Choosing a different drivetrain or trim can therefore affect the comparison as much as the engine itself.
It gains 1 mpg in city driving and 2 mpg on both the highway and combined cycle.
The V-8 changes help explain some of the decline.
Both engines have larger displacements and more horsepower and torque, which in some cases can also mean more fuel consumption.

sources.title: The 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and GMC Sierra 1500 Get Worse Fuel Economy Numbers - MotorTrend
passages: The 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and GMC Sierra 1500 are getting major updates, including new small-block V-8 engines, updated transmissions, and refreshed exterior and interior designs.
Those changes bring revised EPA fuel economy ratings, and the numbers point to a small efficiency hit for most configurations compared with the 2026 trucks.
The EPA has released ratings for the 5.7-liter V-8, 6.6-liter V-8, and 3.0-liter turbodiesel available in both trucks; final fuel economy figures for the base 2.7-liter turbo-four are still pending.
According to data from GM Authority , nearly every listed powertrain and trim combination returns lower ratings for 2027.
The exception is the GMC Sierra AT4X equipped with the turbodiesel.
The amount of the change varies by engine, drivetrain, and trim.
In several configurations, the difference is only 1 or 2 mpg, while certain four-wheel-drive diesel versions have larger drops.
Choosing a different drivetrain or trim can therefore affect the comparison as much as the engine itself.
It gains 1 mpg in city driving and 2 mpg on both the highway and combined cycle.
The V-8 changes help explain some of the decline.
Both engines have larger displacements and more horsepower and torque, which in some cases can also mean more fuel consumption.
Miguel Cortina is Mexico Editor at MotorTrend , covering the auto industry in the U.S. and south of the border.
He joined MotorTrend in January 2015 and is an avid automotive enthusiast who enjoys playing golf, surfing, and running in his free time.

sources.title: Preview: 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 Comes With Luxury, Power, and Off-Road Capabilities - Consumer Reports
passages: Like the Chevrolet Silverado 1500 , the GMC Sierra 1500 received an evolutionary redesign for the 2027 model year.
The off-road trims can handle tougher conditions, and luxury editions get luxury amenities that rival those of high-end SUVs.
GMC says the turbocharged four-cylinder has been upgraded, now producing 350 hp. (The previous version of that 2.7-liter engine produces 310 hp.)
The most extroverted trim is the Sierra 1500 AT4X.

It enhances the truck’s off-road capability with 35-inch Goodyear Mud Terrain (MT) tires, a 2-inch suspension lift, off-road shocks, front and rear electronically locked differentials to optimize traction, and a distinctive front fascia.
Like the previous model, the AT4X will again be sold with the AEV Edition package, which further fortifies the truck.
Think of the Pro as the work-centered entry point, with the Elevation scaling the trim walk with more creature comforts.
The turbo four has been changed, and the V8s are next-generation small blocks.
The outgoing Sierra 1500 is a competitive option within the full-sized truck class, and we expect the new version to be as well.
Bartlett is the managing editor for the autos team at Consumer Reports.
Consumer Reports is an independent, nonprofit member organization that works side by side with consumers for truth, transparency, and fairness in the marketplace.

GMC latest version of its full-sized pickup is set to compete with the Ford F-150, Ram 1500, and Toyota Tundra Like the Chevrolet Silverado 1500 , the GMC Sierra 1500 received an evolutionary redesign for the 2027 model year. The changes exemplify how pickup trucks, like the Ford F-150 and Ram 1500 the Sierra competes with, keep getting more upscale. The off-road trims can handle tougher conditions, and luxury editions get luxury amenities that rival those of high-end SUVs. The 2027 Sierra 1500’s exterior is new compared to last year, and the interior will have a new screen-intensive layout. The four available engines are a turbocharged four-cylinder, two new V8s, and a turbodiesel six-cylinder. The turbo four has been changed, and the V8s are next-generation small blocks. Trim options for the Sierra 1500 are the Pro, Elevation, AT4, AT4X, Denali, and Denali Ultimate. Think of the Pro as the work-centered entry point, with the Elevation scaling the trim walk with more creature comforts. Each trim separates into the off-road-focused AT4 and more capable AT4X, while the Denali and Denali Ultimate chart a luxury and tech-focused path. What it competes with: Chevrolet Silverado 1500 , Ford F-150 , Ram 1500 , Toyota Tundra Powertrains: • 350-hp, 2.7-liter turbocharged four-cylinder • 402-hp, 5.7-liter V8 • 481-hp, 6.6-liter V8 • 305-hp, 3.0-liter turbocharged diesel six-cylinder engine Each with a 10-speed automatic transmission; rear- or four-wheel drive Price: $48,500-$85,100 for crew cab 4WD Destination: $2,795 On sale: Late 2026 Final assembly point: Fort Wayne, Ind. The outgoing Sierra 1500 is a competitive option within the full-sized truck class, and we expect the new version to be as well. But like other full-sized pickups, the current Sierra 1500 has below-average reliability. Even though the 2027 Sierra 1500 has all-new sheet metal, it’s so similar to the 2026 body that you might need to look for the trapezoidal grille and more complicated headlamps to identify one. Trim-specific details distinguish various versions of the Sierra, as seen in the lower front design, wheels, and exhaust outlets. GMC says there are available welcome and farewell light animations, addressing a need you probably didn’t know existed. Trucks … with animations. The Sierra 1500 will once again be available as a regular cab/long bed, extended cab/standard bed, crew cab/standard bed, and crew cab/long bed. The most extroverted trim is the Sierra 1500 AT4X. It enhances the truck’s off-road capability with 35-inch Goodyear Mud Terrain (MT) tires, a 2-inch suspension lift, off-road shocks, front and rear electronically locked differentials to optimize traction, and a distinctive front fascia. Like the previous model, the AT4X will again be sold with the AEV Edition package, which further fortifies the truck. The redesigned cabin is simpler than the outgoing model, with screens spread across the dashboard. All combined, GMC says there’s more than 60 inches of total screen. The digital real estate includes a 12.2-inch instrument display, 16.3-inch infotainment screen, and 11.5-inch front passenger screen. Plus, there’s an available 15-inch color head-up display and an 8.5-inch rearview mirror display, which can show behind the vehicle when the view is being obstructed by passengers and head restraints. Different trims come with specific materials, including leather and real wood, along with stitching and accents. The AT4X has a flat-bottom steering wheel, increased seat bolsters, perforated upholstery, stainless steel speaker grilles, and abundant stitching. Adding to the luxury experience is an available panoramic roof (standard on AT4X) and a new MultiPro center console that slides and folds, allowing for different configurations between the driver and front passenger, including transforming into a flat table well-suited to placing a laptop or having a picnic. The 2027 GMC Sierra 1500’s powertrains only look like carryovers from last year. GMC says the turbocharged four-cylinder has been upgraded, now producing 350 hp. (The previous version of that 2.7-liter engine produces 310 hp.) The 3.0-liter turbodiesel six-cylinder engine may be changed only slightly. The previous truck produced 310 hp, and it achieved 23 mpg overall in our tests. The new diesel makes 305 hp. The 5.7-liter and 6.6-liter V8s are next-generation small blocks, producing 402 and 481 hp, respectively. This time around, all four engines will be matched with a 10-speed automatic transmission. There has been no mention of a hybrid to rival Ford and Toyota’s truck offerings. The 2027 Sierra 1500 comes standard with forward collision warning, automatic emergency braking with bicyclist and pedestrian detection, adaptive cruise control, blind spot warning, rear cross traffic warning, and front and rear parking collision warning.. GM’s Super Cruise active driving assistance system will be available and feature hands-free driving while towing. The system will come with a free three-year OnStar trial to support Super Cruise functionality. Jeff S. Bartlett is the managing editor for the autos team at Consumer Reports. He has been with CR since 2005. Previously, Jeff served as the online editorial director of Motor Trend for 11 years. Throughout his career, Jeff has driven thousands of cars, many on racetracks around the globe. Follow him on X: @JeffSBartlett We respect your privacy . The Sierra 1500 will once again be available as a regular cab/long bed, extended cab/standard bed, crew cab/standard bed, and crew cab/long bed.

The most extroverted trim is the Sierra 1500 AT4X. It enhances the truck’s off-road capability with 35-inch Goodyear Mud Terrain (MT) tires, a 2-inch suspension lift, off-road shocks, front and rear electronically locked differentials to optimize traction, and a distinctive front fascia. Like the previous model, the AT4X will again be sold with the AEV Edition package, which further fortifies the truck.

The redesigned cabin is simpler than the outgoing model, with screens spread across the dashboard. All combined, GMC says there’s more than 60 inches of total screen. The digital real estate includes a 12.2-inch instrument display, 16.3-inch infotainment screen, and 11.5-inch front passenger screen. Plus, there’s an available 15-inch color head-up display and an 8.5-inch rearview mirror display, which can show behind the vehicle when the view is being obstructed by passengers and head restraints.

Different trims come with specific materials, including leather and real wood, along with stitching and accents. The AT4X has a flat-bottom steering wheel, increased seat bolsters, perforated upholstery, stainless steel speaker grilles, and abundant stitching.

Adding to the luxury experience is an available panoramic roof (standard on AT4X) and a new MultiPro center console that slides and folds, allowing for different configurations between the driver and front passenger, including transforming into a flat table well-suited to placing a laptop or having a picnic.

The 2027 GMC Sierra 1500’s powertrains only look like carryovers from last year. GMC says the turbocharged four-cylinder has been upgraded, now producing 350 hp. (The previous version of that 2.7-liter engine produces 310 hp.)
The 3.0-liter turbodiesel six-cylinder engine may be changed only slightly. The previous truck produced 310 hp, and it achieved 23 mpg overall in our tests. The new diesel makes 305 hp.
The 5.7-liter and 6.6-liter V8s are next-generation small blocks, producing 402 and 481 hp, respectively.
This time around, all four engines will be matched with a 10-speed automatic transmission. There has been no mention of a hybrid to rival Ford and Toyota’s truck offerings.

The 2027 Sierra 1500 comes standard with forward collision warning, automatic emergency braking with bicyclist and pedestrian detection, adaptive cruise control, blind spot warning, rear cross traffic warning, and front and rear parking collision warning..

GM’s Super Cruise active driving assistance system will be available and feature hands-free driving while towing. The system will come with a free three-year OnStar trial to support Super Cruise functionality.

passages: The 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 will go on sale later this year, and we now know how much the four-wheel-drive crew-cab models will cost.The Sierra 1500 Pro’s starting price rises $1955 to $51,295, while the mid-tier Elevation now opens at $59,995.The off-road-ready AT4 and AT4X’s prices are up by $2700 and $3100, respectively; the Denali now starts at $76,795 (up $4105), but the Denali Ultimate is only $205 more than before.CLARIFICATION 9/22/26, 4:45 p.m.: This story has been updated to clarify pricing details about the Elevation and Denali Ultimate trim levels.GMC pulled the covers off the new next-generation Sierra 1500 earlier this summer, but we’ve been patiently waiting for more information about its specs and pricing.

extraction.body: The 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 will go on sale later this year, and we now know how much the four-wheel-drive crew-cab models will cost.The Sierra 1500 Pro’s starting price rises $1955 to $51,295, while the mid-tier Elevation now opens at $59,995.The off-road-ready AT4 and AT4X’s prices are up by $2700 and $3100, respectively; the Denali now starts at $76,795 (up $4105), but the Denali Ultimate is only $205 more than before.CLARIFICATION 9/22/26, 4:45 p.m.: This story has been updated to clarify pricing details about the Elevation and Denali Ultimate trim levels.GMC pulled the covers off the new next-generation Sierra 1500 earlier this summer, but we’ve been patiently waiting for more information about its specs and pricing. Now, GMC has released prices for its new Sierra 1500, though only for the four-wheel-drive crew-cab models, almost all of which have risen by a few thousand dollars.For 2027, the Sierra 1500 lineup still kicks off with the entry-level Pro, which now starts at $51,295. That’s a $1955 increase compared with last year’s four-wheel-drive crew-cab version. GMC purists might be sad to learn that the long-running SLE and SLT models have been dropped. That makes the familiar Elevation trim level the new middle ground; it initially starts at $59,995 for 2027. That’s $3600 more than the least expensive Elevation from the 2026 model year, but that truck had the 3VL equipment package, which a GMC spokesperson told Car and Driver will eventually rejoin the lineup and lower its entry price.Both trucks get the updated 350-hp 2.7-liter turbo four standard, but they can be optioned with the Duramax diesel 3.0-liter straight-six (still with 495 pound-feet of torque) or the new 402-hp 5.7-liter V-8. A 10-speed automatic is the only transmission available on all of GMC’s half-ton trucks.Meanwhile, the AT4 and AT4X remain the most off-road-focused Sierra 1500 models and were only ever offered with a crew cab and four-wheel drive. Along with a two-inch lift, they both have knobby all-terrain tires measuring 34 inches tall on the AT4 and 35 inches tall on the AT4X. The latter also debuts Mutlimatic jounce control dampers as well as a plethora of Denali-like luxury features. The AT4 comes standard with the 5.7-liter V-8, but the diesel engine is available too. The AT4X defaults with the diesel, but it can be equipped with the 481-hp 6.6-liter V-8.The new Sierra 1500 Denali starts at $76,795, which represents a $4105 spike versus its predecessor. It comes standard with the 5.7-liter V-8, but the 6.6-liter version and the Duramax diesel are both optional. Every Denali also features a specially tuned suspension as well as an interior that’s covered in upscale materials. The Technology package includes an 11.5-inch touchscreen display that’s built into the dashboard facing the front-seat passenger.Now starting at $87,895, the top-of-the-line Denali Ultimate’s price has only increased by $205. Last year, choosing the Duramax option lowered the truck’s price by $1500, so we expect the newest version to receive a similar discount.The 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 will reach dealerships before the year ends. extraction.body: Investing.com -- OpenAI will continue to invest in artificial intelligence infrastructure despite voter opposition to data centers in Tuesday's midterm elections, CFO Sarah Friar said Friday. Still guessing which stocks will beat the market? Our AI portfolio updates monthly and is outperforming the S&P 500 by 118%. See this month's list » "When I think about the midterms, I need to keep thinking about how do we keep investing to meet that customer demand," Friar told CNBC's Sara Eisen at the Citi TMT Leadership Summit in Pebble Beach, California. "It starts early with having built relationships with all of the hyperscalers, and it will continue to mean that we raise capital." Voters rejected data center development across the country on Tuesday. Out of 41 local ballot measures across 10 states, voters backed restrictions or rejected pro-development measures in all but one, according to an analysis by Ballotpedia and additional results gathered by CNBC on Wednesday. Americans grew worried about potential environmental harm, higher utility bills and job loss. The Nasdaq on Thursday posted its steepest drop in 19 months, led by declines in chipmaker and neocloud company shares tied to AI buildout. The stocks recovered partially on Friday. Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks » Friar said the election results did not dramatically change anything for OpenAI. The company published a policy blueprint and commitments on Thursday that it pledged to apply to company-owned and operated data centers in the future. "If the midterm means more focus on data centers and communities, we're going to keep doing the work to get into those communities and to build trust with them," Friar said. OpenAI filed its prospectus confidentially with the Securities and Exchange Commission in June. Friar said Friday the company would continue to look into a 2027 debut. Anthropic, OpenAI's main rival, aims to list on the Nasdaq in mid-November. Anthropic's revenue in the first nine months of the year rose roughly 1,200% to $33.2 billion, according to its prospectus. The company entered into purchase commitments and lease agreements with an aggregate committed spend of about $895.4 billion, substantially all related to compute and infrastructure. OpenAI is in talks to raise funding at a $1.25 billion pre-money valuation, Friar said Friday. She said "a good CFO always raises money when she can" and that the round is ongoing. "The demand for AI is real," Friar said. "I don't think anyone's arguing with that, or if they are, I think it's a losing argument." sources.title: After the midterms, things are looking rocky for Elon Musk and data centers
passages: On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry.

Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.”

Anthony: One thing I want to emphasize is that they’re calling it this [their] “compute campus policy.” And part of what that’s doing, beyond laying out these policy changes, is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, because they have become such a toxic phrase.

Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center.

Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center.

extraction.body: Democrats’ historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could also have a dramatic effect on the tech industry. In dozens of local ballot measures, voters rejected data centers . And even when they weren’t voting on the issue directly, they were electing politicians — like Texas’ new governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned on the promise of restricting data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry. Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.” And Kirsten said that while data centers probably weren’t the main cause of the “blue wave,” they’ve become an “an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about” getting their projects approved. And now, “we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, ‘Actually, we can change our policies.’” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity. Sean O’Kane: First off, let’s talk about the fact that one of the biggest data center builders was also the largest donor to the Republican Party. Elon Musk seems to have gotten basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars — maybe even more, by the time we see the final count — and in fact is now sitting there with all of his businesses in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn for the first time in a very long time, if ever. That, I think, is the biggest thing hanging above a lot of this discussion. But, there were also a bunch of ballot measures up around the country that would have paved the way for data centers to get built faster. Almost all of them got shot down, or voted against. [Actually, many of the ballot measures would have imposed restrictions or moratoriums on data centers, and almost all of those measures passed.] With [Democrats] in power, there is a consensus view, at least in the tech world, that this is going to mean we have a lot of roadblocks ahead for data centers, especially in places like Texas, where [you have] folks like the governor-elect [Gina] Hinojosa, who has spoken pretty openly about this being a campaign promise and something that she wants to focus on once she takes power, now that she’s beaten Greg Abbott. It’s the thing that I think the tech world is maybe a little too focused on. I’m curious what you guys think about that. Anthony Ha: I don’t necessarily think that they’re too focused on it, but I understand why it would feel a little bit disproportionate — the data center ballot measures, certainly there were a number of them, but it wasn’t something that was on the ballot everywhere. And in different races, the dynamic might have been a bit different, but there was this undercurrent and sense that it seems to be an issue that reaches across the country, that is bipartisan in a lot of ways, but that the Democrats seem to have been more effective at harnessing that energy. And of course, there’s all kinds of reasons why the Democrats did so well on Tuesday, but it does seem like anti-AI and especially anti-data center sentiment was a big part of it. That seems like a pretty potent political force. The next two years, [and] potentially beyond that, are going to be more difficult for tech companies in general, and hyperscalers, data center companies in particular. I also imagine that they have to be a little bit worried about: Is this going to continue to be an issue, not just with the people who got elected this year, but potentially in 2028 and beyond? Kirsten Korosec: Absolutely. I don’t think that the data center issue is what brought everyone to the polls and led to the quote-unquote “blue wave.” However, I will say that data centers have been an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about getting these data centers [approved] — very secretive, oftentimes requiring NDAs of a elected officials or appointed officials, not sharing information about the scale of a project in very environmentally sensitive areas, including in the Southwest, where there’s very much a water scarcity issue. So I think that a lot of folks — Republicans, independents, and Democrats — all saw this as wrong. They were motivated by it, but I don’t think it was a singular issue. Now, here’s the interesting thing. There was a lot of waving of hands about how [AI companies] can’t possibly operate under any other circumstances. And we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, “Actually, we can change our policies.” They just released what they call a compute campus policy blueprint . And guess what? They’re not going to require NDAs anymore. They’re going to share their plans and supposedly operate in less secrecy. I think what this shows is that when you put up either a regulatory certainty in the marketplace, or at least signals of going in that direction, then corporations will respond. If you don’t do that, they will not necessarily do the thing that we hope that they will do. Anthony: One thing I want to emphasize is that they’re calling it this [their] “compute campus policy.” And part of what that’s doing, beyond laying out these policy changes, is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, because they have become such a toxic phrase. So they’re not data centers anymore, they are compute campuses, and I’m curious, whether either of you think that’ll take. Sean: I mean, this is ridiculous. Come on. It’s not going to change anything. It’s going to cause them more effort. For a company that likes to say that it’s no longer focused on side quests, OpenAI still loves to go in different directions a lot. And this is just the latest kind of thing where it’s just like: Why are you spending time on this at all? It doesn’t really seem like it’s going to move the needle. Kirsten: I have a great idea for OpenAI. Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center. Anthony: And if these are just lovely compute campuses, they should just build their own offices there or work next door, see how that works out for them. Something else that I’m wondering about is, to what extent the election is maybe the second part of a one-two punch. [We’ve just seen] a big shift in how Wall Street is reacting to a lot of these hyperscalers and AI companies and this sense that [investors] are not excited about the idea that they should be spending all this money building new data centers, spending all this money on compute. And so there’s a financial incentive not to build all these data centers. I’m very curious how that’s going to play out. [From a regulatory standpoint,] it’s probably going to be harder to build data centers. Wall Street is probably not going to reward you for building data centers. But at the same time, to get to the scale that they want to get to, they are probably going to need to build data centers somewhere. Sean O’Kane: First off, let’s talk about the fact that one of the biggest data center builders was also the largest donor to the Republican Party. Elon Musk seems to have gotten basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars — maybe even more, by the time we see the final count — and in fact is now sitting there with all of his businesses in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn for the first time in a very long time, if ever.

That, I think, is the biggest thing hanging above a lot of this discussion. But, there were also a bunch of ballot measures up around the country that would have paved the way for data centers to get built faster. Almost all of them got shot down, or voted against. [Actually, many of the ballot measures would have imposed restrictions or moratoriums on data centers, and almost all of those measures passed.]

With [Democrats] in power, there is a consensus view, at least in the tech world, that this is going to mean we have a lot of roadblocks ahead for data centers, especially in places like Texas, where [you have] folks like the governor-elect [Gina] Hinojosa, who has spoken pretty openly about this being a campaign promise and something that she wants to focus on once she takes power, now that she’s beaten Greg Abbott.
It’s the thing that I think the tech world is maybe a little too focused on. I’m curious what you guys think about that.

Anthony Ha: I don’t necessarily think that they’re too focused on it, but I understand why it would feel a little bit disproportionate — the data center ballot measures, certainly there were a number of them, but it wasn’t something that was on the ballot everywhere.

And in different races, the dynamic might have been a bit different, but there was this undercurrent and sense that it seems to be an issue that reaches across the country, that is bipartisan in a lot of ways, but that the Democrats seem to have been more effective at harnessing that energy. And of course, there’s all kinds of reasons why the Democrats did so well on Tuesday, but it does seem like anti-AI and especially anti-data center sentiment was a big part of it. That seems like a pretty potent political force.

The next two years, [and] potentially beyond that, are going to be more difficult for tech companies in general, and hyperscalers, data center companies in particular. I also imagine that they have to be a little bit worried about: Is this going to continue to be an issue, not just with the people who got elected this year, but potentially in 2028 and beyond?

I don’t think that the data center issue is what brought everyone to the polls and led to the quote-unquote “blue wave.” However, I will say that data centers have been an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about getting these data centers [approved] — very secretive, oftentimes requiring NDAs of a elected officials or appointed officials, not sharing information about the scale of a project in very environmentally sensitive areas, including in the Southwest, where there’s very much a water scarcity issue.
So I think that a lot of folks — Republicans, independents, and Democrats — all saw this as wrong. They were motivated by it, but I don’t think it was a singular issue.

Now, here’s the interesting thing. There was a lot of waving of hands about how [AI companies] can’t possibly operate under any other circumstances. And we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, “Actually, we can change our policies.” They just released what they call a compute campus policy blueprint . And guess what? They’re not going to require NDAs anymore. They’re going to share their plans and supposedly operate in less secrecy.

I think what this shows is that when you put up either a regulatory certainty in the marketplace, or at least signals of going in that direction, then corporations will respond. If you don’t do that, they will not necessarily do the thing that we hope that they will do.

Anthony: One thing I want to emphasize is that they’re calling it this [their] “compute campus policy.” And part of what that’s doing, beyond laying out these policy changes, is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, because they have become such a toxic phrase. So they’re not data centers anymore, they are compute campuses, and I’m curious, whether either of you think that’ll take.

Sean: I mean, this is ridiculous. Come on. It’s not going to change anything. It’s going to cause them more effort. For a company that likes to say that it’s no longer focused on side quests, OpenAI still loves to go in different directions a lot. And this is just the latest kind of thing where it’s just like: Why are you spending time on this at all? It doesn’t really seem like it’s going to move the needle.

Kirsten: I have a great idea for OpenAI. Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center.
Anthony: And if these are just lovely compute campuses, they should just build their own offices there or work next door, see how that works out for them.

Something else that I’m wondering about is, to what extent the election is maybe the second part of a one-two punch. [We’ve just seen] a big shift in how Wall Street is reacting to a lot of these hyperscalers and AI companies and this sense that [investors] are not excited about the idea that they should be spending all this money building new data centers, spending all this money on compute. And so there’s a financial incentive not to build all these data centers.

I’m very curious how that’s going to play out. [From a regulatory standpoint,] it’s probably going to be harder to build data centers. Wall Street is probably not going to reward you for building data centers. But at the same time, to get to the scale that they want to get to, they are probably going to need to build data centers somewhere.

passages: Democrats’ historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could also have a dramatic effect on the tech industry.

In dozens of local ballot measures, voters rejected data centers . And even when they weren’t voting on the issue directly, they were electing politicians — like Texas’ new governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned on the promise of restricting data centers.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry. Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.”

And Kirsten said that while data centers probably weren’t the main cause of the “blue wave,” they’ve become an “an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about” getting their projects approved. And now, “we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, ‘Actually, we can change our policies.’”
Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity.

Sean O’Kane: First off, let’s talk about the fact that one of the biggest data center builders was also the largest donor to the Republican Party. Elon Musk seems to have gotten basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars — maybe even more, by the time we see the final count — and in fact is now sitting there with all of his businesses in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn for the first time in a very long time, if ever.

That, I think, is the biggest thing hanging above a lot of this discussion. But, there were also a bunch of ballot measures up around the country that would have paved the way for data centers to get built faster. Almost all of them got shot down, or voted against. [Actually, many of the ballot measures would have imposed restrictions or moratoriums on data centers, and almost all of those measures passed.]

With [Democrats] in power, there is a consensus view, at least in the tech world, that this is going to mean we have a lot of roadblocks ahead for data centers, especially in places like Texas, where [you have] folks like the governor-elect [Gina] Hinojosa, who has spoken pretty openly about this being a campaign promise and something that she wants to focus on once she takes power, now that she’s beaten Greg Abbott.
It’s the thing that I think the tech world is maybe a little too focused on. I’m curious what you guys think about that.

Anthony Ha: I don’t necessarily think that they’re too focused on it, but I understand why it would feel a little bit disproportionate — the data center ballot measures, certainly there were a number of them, but it wasn’t something that was on the ballot everywhere.

And in different races, the dynamic might have been a bit different, but there was this undercurrent and sense that it seems to be an issue that reaches across the country, that is bipartisan in a lot of ways, but that the Democrats seem to have been more effective at harnessing that energy. And of course, there’s all kinds of reasons why the Democrats did so well on Tuesday, but it does seem like anti-AI and especially anti-data center sentiment was a big part of it. That seems like a pretty potent political force.

The next two years, [and] potentially beyond that, are going to be more difficult for tech companies in general, and hyperscalers, data center companies in particular. I also imagine that they have to be a little bit worried about: Is this going to continue to be an issue, not just with the people who got elected this year, but potentially in 2028 and beyond?

Kirsten Korosec: Absolutely. I don’t think that the data center issue is what brought everyone to the polls and led to the quote-unquote “blue wave.” However, I will say that data centers have been an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about getting these data centers [approved] — very secretive, oftentimes requiring NDAs of a elected officials or appointed officials, not sharing information about the scale of a project in very environmentally sensitive areas, including in the Southwest, where there’s very much a water scarcity issue.
So I think that a lot of folks — Republicans, independents, and Democrats — all saw this as wrong. They were motivated by it, but I don’t think it was a singular issue.

Now, here’s the interesting thing. There was a lot of waving of hands about how [AI companies] can’t possibly operate under any other circumstances. And we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, “Actually, we can change our policies.” They just released what they call a compute campus policy blueprint . And guess what? They’re not going to require NDAs anymore. They’re going to share their plans and supposedly operate in less secrecy.

I think what this shows is that when you put up either a regulatory certainty in the marketplace, or at least signals of going in that direction, then corporations will respond. If you don’t do that, they will not necessarily do the thing that we hope that they will do.

Anthony: One thing I want to emphasize is that they’re calling it this [their] “compute campus policy.” And part of what that’s doing, beyond laying out these policy changes, is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, because they have become such a toxic phrase. So they’re not data centers anymore, they are compute campuses, and I’m curious, whether either of you think that’ll take.

Sean: I mean, this is ridiculous. Come on. It’s not going to change anything. It’s going to cause them more effort. For a company that likes to say that it’s no longer focused on side quests, OpenAI still loves to go in different directions a lot. And this is just the latest kind of thing where it’s just like: Why are you spending time on this at all? It doesn’t really seem like it’s going to move the needle.

Kirsten: I have a great idea for OpenAI. Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center.
Anthony: And if these are just lovely compute campuses, they should just build their own offices there or work next door, see how that works out for them.

Something else that I’m wondering about is, to what extent the election is maybe the second part of a one-two punch. [We’ve just seen] a big shift in how Wall Street is reacting to a lot of these hyperscalers and AI companies and this sense that [investors] are not excited about the idea that they should be spending all this money building new data centers, spending all this money on compute. And so there’s a financial incentive not to build all these data centers.

I’m very curious how that’s going to play out. [From a regulatory standpoint,] it’s probably going to be harder to build data centers. Wall Street is probably not going to reward you for building data centers. But at the same time, to get to the scale that they want to get to, they are probably going to need to build data centers somewhere.

While the debate over the future of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending continues to rage on Wall Street, many corporations aren't just saying they will spend more on AI; they are backing up their words with action. So far this earnings season, we have seen that many leaders in the field are still pouring fortunes into hopes of capitalizing on what they see as a transformative opportunity. This provides strong evidence that the ongoing AI revolution isn't over yet, and there is still time to invest in stocks that could ride this tailwind over the long run. Here are four great examples to consider: Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD), and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO). Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Nvidia's indispensable role in the industry has made it one of the biggest winners of the AI revolution so far. In my view, that's likely to remain the case over the long run. Despite increased competition in the GPU ( graphics processing unit ) market, the company has maintained a runaway lead. This has a lot to do with the company's wide moat, thanks to its CUDA ecosystem, which creates high switching costs. Demand for GPUs may not be quite as impressive moving forward as it has been in recent years, but Nvidia has expanded beyond its core market. The company's existing relationships with many corporations that continue to rely on its GPUs can enable it to offer these clients other hardware and services that complement -- and work best with -- its GPUs for training, deploying, and running AI models. That puts Nvidia in a good position to ride the AI tailwind. Microsoft is proving the doubters wrong. Some investors feared that AI would make its services obsolete, since the technology has reduced software development costs. But Microsoft has adapted. Its cloud business is booming, in part thanks to its library of AI services. It has also integrated AI across its productivity suite. Meanwhile, the company boasts a massive and rapidly growing cloud backlog. These are all signs that Microsoft may continue cashing in on AI, at least over the next few years. And beyond that, the company's ability to deliver consistent revenue and earnings, strong cash position, and innovative capabilities grant it the opportunity to tap into an AI market that could continue to expand over the long run. Advanced Micro Devices has also benefited from an increased demand for GPUs, although it has played second fiddle to Nvidia in that market. However, the company is now seeing soaring demand for CPUs (central processing units). Recent financial results have been excellent, particularly for the company's data center segment. The advent of AI agents -- which run on CPUs -- could be a powerful long-term tailwind. In fact, it has even surprised management. AMD has increased its 2030 total addressable opportunity guidance several times over the past year. The company could face more competition, but it also benefits from a competitive edge. It boasts significant technological expertise in this industry -- where it has been a leader for decades -- deep relationships with corporations, and high switching costs. All good reasons why AMD's outlook appears attractive. Broadcom could become increasingly important in the AI industry. The company designs custom AI chips, which are seeing rising demand as corporations seek to diversify away from Nvidia by buying custom chips that aren't as versatile but are often cheaper and much more power-efficient than GPUs. That doesn't mean the GPU market will shrink substantially, but as AI infrastructure scales, an increasingly large share could shift toward custom AI chips, and Broadcom will cash in on this. The company is a leader in this niche and has relationships with major AI companies, including Meta Platforms (NASDAQ:META), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL), and Anthropic, the corporation behind Claude, which is expected to go public soon. Broadcom's AI semiconductor business has lower margins than its infrastructure software segment, but over the long run, the lower gross margins will be worth it, as Broadcom's total revenue and earnings growth maintain a solid pace thanks to the continued rise in AI infrastructure spending. The stock could beat the market along the way. While the debate over the future of artificial intelligence (AI) infrastructure spending continues to rage on Wall Street, many corporations aren't just saying they will spend more on AI; they are backing up their words with action. So far this earnings season, we have seen that many leaders in the field are still pouring fortunes into hopes of capitalizing on what they see as a transformative opportunity. This provides strong evidence that the ongoing AI revolution isn't over yet, and there is still time to invest in stocks that could ride this tailwind over the long run. Here are four great examples to consider: Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Advanced Micro Devices (NASDAQ:AMD), and Broadcom (NASDAQ:AVGO).

Nvidia's indispensable role in the industry has made it one of the biggest winners of the AI revolution so far. In my view, that's likely to remain the case over the long run. Despite increased competition in the GPU ( graphics processing unit ) market, the company has maintained a runaway lead.

This has a lot to do with the company's wide moat, thanks to its CUDA ecosystem, which creates high switching costs. Demand for GPUs may not be quite as impressive moving forward as it has been in recent years, but Nvidia has expanded beyond its core market.

The company's existing relationships with many corporations that continue to rely on its GPUs can enable it to offer these clients other hardware and services that complement -- and work best with -- its GPUs for training, deploying, and running AI models. That puts Nvidia in a good position to ride the AI tailwind.

Its cloud business is booming, in part thanks to its library of AI services. It has also integrated AI across its productivity suite.

Meanwhile, the company boasts a massive and rapidly growing cloud backlog. These are all signs that Microsoft may continue cashing in on AI, at least over the next few years. And beyond that, the company's ability to deliver consistent revenue and earnings, strong cash position, and innovative capabilities grant it the opportunity to tap into an AI market that could continue to expand over the long run.

The advent of AI agents -- which run on CPUs -- could be a powerful long-term tailwind.

The company could face more competition, but it also benefits from a competitive edge. It boasts significant technological expertise in this industry -- where it has been a leader for decades -- deep relationships with corporations, and high switching costs. passages: Bitcoin’s mining difficulty has not printed a new all-time high in 374 days.
The metric stands at 148.36 trillion hashes after the retarget of 29 October 2026, which lifted it 5.54% from 140.58 trillion.
The record remains 155.97 trillion, set at block 921,312 on 29 October 2025 at 10:14 UTC, according to mempool.space difficulty data.
That leaves the network 4.88% below its peak, and spot Bitcoin at $75,577, down 2.5% over seven days and 7.6% over 30.
A year without a record is not a malfunction.

On daily difficulty samples, the current 356-day run below the record is the longest in the network’s history, ahead of the 348 days between August 2011 and July 2012, the 236 days from May 2021 to January 2022, and the 225 days from October 2018 to May 2019.
Neither result depends on a new difficulty record; both depend on the price of Bitcoin, which has fallen 7.6% in 30 days.

Put that $700 million annualized colocation book against the $12.4 billion the entire network earns from issuance each year, and one company’s real-estate and power business is worth about 5.6% of everything Bitcoin mining produces.
A halving cuts the same hashprice by half unless price doubles, and it lands before the next difficulty record decision is settled in any meaningful sense.

Until then, the correct read is a network consolidating below its ceiling while its publicly traded operators shift revenue toward contracted colocation and away from a hashprice that no longer covers high-cost power.
For traders, miner balance sheets are a supply variable to watch rather than a signal to chase.
For anyone modelling hashprice, $33.4 per petahash per day is the number the whole industry is currently underwriting.
Bitcoin recalculates difficulty every 2,016 blocks, roughly two weeks of mining.
The mechanism is self-limiting, which is why the record has held through a year of infrastructure building.
With Bitcoin near $75,577 and hashrate averaging about 1.02 ZH/s, miners have little incentive to add capacity, so the retargets of the past year have not been enough to clear the October 2025 peak.
