extraction.body: Bitcoin’s mining difficulty has not printed a new all-time high in 374 days. The metric stands at 148.36 trillion hashes after the retarget of 29 October 2026, which lifted it 5.54% from 140.58 trillion. The record remains 155.97 trillion, set at block 921,312 on 29 October 2025 at 10:14 UTC, according to mempool.space difficulty data. That leaves the network 4.88% below its peak, and spot Bitcoin at $75,577, down 2.5% over seven days and 7.6% over 30. A year without a record is not a malfunction. Difficulty rises only when the network finds blocks faster than the ten-minute target, and it falls or stalls when hashrate growth slows or capital leaves. What makes this stretch unusual is its length. On daily difficulty samples, the current 356-day run below the record is the longest in the network’s history, ahead of the 348 days between August 2011 and July 2012, the 236 days from May 2021 to January 2022, and the 225 days from October 2018 to May 2019. Bitcoin recalculates difficulty every 2,016 blocks, roughly two weeks of mining. The protocol compares the time taken for that batch against the 20,160 minutes implied by ten-minute blocks, then scales the target proportionally. If the batch arrived in nine minutes per block, difficulty climbs about 11%. If blocks slowed to twelve minutes, it drops. The mechanism is self-limiting, which is why the record has held through a year of infrastructure building. Difficulty can only break out when hashrate expands faster than price. Between the record on 29 October 2025 and the most recent retarget exactly one year later, difficulty moved from 155.97 trillion to 148.36 trillion. Two separate retargets in the interim, on 3 October 2026 and 19 September 2026, produced 132.72 trillion and 132.76 trillion, so the network spent the northern autumn recovering ground it had already covered. Hashrate tells a similar story. Current network hashrate sits near 1.02 zettahashes per second, with the 30-day peak at 1.22 ZH/s, based on blockchain.info’s hash-rate series. A rising hashrate that outruns price does not raise difficulty indefinitely. It raises the cost of production instead, until marginal operators switch off and the retarget resets the field. Difficulty matters to miners because it converts into revenue per unit of computing power. The arithmetic is simple enough to run directly. Bitcoin issues 3.125 $BTC per block and produces roughly 144 blocks a day, so 450 $BTC enters the market daily. At $75,577, that is about $34.0 million of gross issuance value per day, or $12.4 billion annualized, before transaction fees. Divide that by the network’s 1.02 ZH/s, which is 1.017 million petahashes, and the industry earns roughly $33.4 per petahash per second per day. That figure is the hashprice in everything but name. A month ago, with Bitcoin near $81,750 by CoinGecko’s 30-day change, the same hashrate would have produced about $36.2 per PH/s per day. Difficulty barely moved. Revenue per unit of power fell 7.6%. That gap explains why miners did not respond to flat difficulty by adding machines. Adding hashrate when price falls simply lowers the industry’s return per petahash and raises the next difficulty adjustment in someone else’s favour. The rational move is to hold steady, sell coins, or repurpose the power. Revenue per petahash only means something against the cost of running one. Take a current-generation machine rated at 20 joules per terahash. One petahash of that hardware draws 20 kilowatts, which is 480 kilowatt-hours a day. Against $33.4 of daily issuance revenue, the break-even power price works out to about 7.0 cents per kilowatt-hour, before fees, cooling, staff and hosting. That single number explains most of the sector’s behaviour this year. An operator paying 4 cents keeps roughly $14 per petahash per day of gross margin. An operator paying 7.5 cents is losing money on the same machine at the same difficulty. Neither result depends on a new difficulty record; both depend on the price of Bitcoin, which has fallen 7.6% in 30 days. The clearest evidence of that shift came on 5 November, when Core Scientific reported third-quarter results that barely resemble a mining company. Colocation revenue rose nearly 60% sequentially to $215.4 million. The company billed for 485 megawatts as of 30 September, representing more than $700 million in average annualized colocation GAAP revenue. Net income reached $1.2 billion, a figure the filed earnings release attributes to “a non-cash gain in the change in fair value of warrants,” not to mining. Adjusted EBITDA more than tripled sequentially to $133.6 million on a 57% margin, up from 25%. “Our execution at scale is translating into results, with a significant sequential increase in GAAP colocation revenue,” chief executive Adam Sullivan said in the release. “We are nearing full delivery under our first colocation agreement while construction under our second is underway across five campuses.” He added: “With revenue growing and substantial contracted capacity still to deliver, we have built a strong foundation for our next phase of growth.” Put that $700 million annualized colocation book against the $12.4 billion the entire network earns from issuance each year, and one company’s real-estate and power business is worth about 5.6% of everything Bitcoin mining produces. The warrants-driven net income is worth flagging separately. A $1.2 billion profit that depends on the mark on warrants is a balance-sheet event, and investors who read it as operating strength will misprice the quarter. This is the pattern BlockchainReporter documented when miners’ AI pivot decoupled their shares from Bitcoin, and again when AI contracts gave listed miners a valuation edge over pure-play operators. Flat difficulty does not hurt a company that is paid per megawatt of high-density colocation. It hurts the operator whose entire revenue line is the $33.4 per petahash. A new record requires hashrate to grow faster than the protocol can absorb, and the next decision point is close. The next retarget falls at block 975,744, with the chain at 974,990 at the time of writing, which places it around 12 November. Difficulty would need to climb 5.1% from 148.36 trillion to clear 155.97 trillion. The 29 October adjustment delivered 5.54%, so the arithmetic is not exotic; it is a question of whether the hashrate behind it exists. Two conditions could produce it. A price recovery would restore miner margins and pull curtailed capacity back online, since the same machines become profitable at $81,750 that sit idle at $75,577. Alternatively, new capacity could come from operators with lower power costs or stranded energy contracts, which raises network hashrate without needing a higher Bitcoin price. Neither is visible in current data: the 30-day hashrate peak of 1.22 ZH/s has already faded to an average near 1.02 ZH/s. The longer calendar matters too. The subsidy has been 3.125 $BTC per block since April 2024, and the next halving sits at block 1,050,000. With the chain at 974,990, that is 75,010 blocks away, or roughly 521 days at the current pace of 144 blocks a day. A halving cuts the same hashprice by half unless price doubles, and it lands before the next difficulty record decision is settled in any meaningful sense. The invalidation is explicit. If difficulty closes an epoch above 155.97 trillion, the 374-day gap ends and the record resets. Until then, the correct read is a network consolidating below its ceiling while its publicly traded operators shift revenue toward contracted colocation and away from a hashprice that no longer covers high-cost power. For traders, miner balance sheets are a supply variable to watch rather than a signal to chase. The metric stands at 148.36 trillion hashes after the retarget of 29 October 2026, which lifted it 5.54% from 140.58 trillion. The record remains 155.97 trillion, set at block 921,312 on 29 October 2025 at 10:14 UTC, according to mempool.space difficulty data. That leaves the network 4.88% below its peak, and spot Bitcoin at $75,577, down 2.5% over seven days and 7.6% over 30.

A year without a record is not a malfunction. Difficulty rises only when the network finds blocks faster than the ten-minute target, and it falls or stalls when hashrate growth slows or capital leaves. What makes this stretch unusual is its length. On daily difficulty samples, the current 356-day run below the record is the longest in the network’s history, ahead of the 348 days between August 2011 and July 2012, the 236 days from May 2021 to January 2022, and the 225 days from October 2018 to May 2019.

Bitcoin recalculates difficulty every 2,016 blocks, roughly two weeks of mining. The protocol compares the time taken for that batch against the 20,160 minutes implied by ten-minute blocks, then scales the target proportionally. If the batch arrived in nine minutes per block, difficulty climbs about 11%. If blocks slowed to twelve minutes, it drops.

The mechanism is self-limiting, which is why the record has held through a year of infrastructure building. Difficulty can only break out when hashrate expands faster than price. Between the record on 29 October 2025 and the most recent retarget exactly one year later, difficulty moved from 155.97 trillion to 148.36 trillion. Two separate retargets in the interim, on 3 October 2026 and 19 September 2026, produced 132.72 trillion and 132.76 trillion, so the network spent the northern autumn recovering ground it had already covered.

Hashrate tells a similar story. Current network hashrate sits near 1.02 zettahashes per second, with the 30-day peak at 1.22 ZH/s, based on blockchain.info’s hash-rate series. A rising hashrate that outruns price does not raise difficulty indefinitely. It raises the cost of production instead, until marginal operators switch off and the retarget resets the field.

Difficulty matters to miners because it converts into revenue per unit of computing power. The arithmetic is simple enough to run directly. Bitcoin issues 3.125 $BTC per block and produces roughly 144 blocks a day, so 450 $BTC enters the market daily. At $75,577, that is about $34.0 million of gross issuance value per day, or $12.4 billion annualized, before transaction fees.

Divide that by the network’s 1.02 ZH/s, which is 1.017 million petahashes, and the industry earns roughly $33.4 per petahash per second per day. That figure is the hashprice in everything but name. A month ago, with Bitcoin near $81,750 by CoinGecko’s 30-day change, the same hashrate would have produced about $36.2 per PH/s per day. Difficulty barely moved. Revenue per unit of power fell 7.6%.

That gap explains why miners did not respond to flat difficulty by adding machines. Adding hashrate when price falls simply lowers the industry’s return per petahash and raises the next difficulty adjustment in someone else’s favour. The rational move is to hold steady, sell coins, or repurpose the power.

Revenue per petahash only means something against the cost of running one. Take a current-generation machine rated at 20 joules per terahash. One petahash of that hardware draws 20 kilowatts, which is 480 kilowatt-hours a day. Against $33.4 of daily issuance revenue, the break-even power price works out to about 7.0 cents per kilowatt-hour, before fees, cooling, staff and hosting.

That single number explains most of the sector’s behaviour this year. An operator paying 4 cents keeps roughly $14 per petahash per day of gross margin. An operator paying 7.5 cents is losing money on the same machine at the same difficulty. Neither result depends on a new difficulty record; both depend on the price of Bitcoin, which has fallen 7.6% in 30 days.

The clearest evidence of that shift came on 5 November, when Core Scientific reported third-quarter results that barely resemble a mining company. Colocation revenue rose nearly 60% sequentially to $215.4 million. The company billed for 485 megawatts as of 30 September, representing more than $700 million in average annualized colocation GAAP revenue. Net income reached $1.2 billion, a figure the filed earnings release attributes to “a non-cash gain in the change in fair value of warrants,” not to mining. Adjusted EBITDA more than tripled sequentially to $133.6 million on a 57% margin, up from 25%.

“Our execution at scale is translating into results, with a significant sequential increase in GAAP colocation revenue,” chief executive Adam Sullivan said in the release. “We are nearing full delivery under our first colocation agreement while construction under our second is underway across five campuses.” He added: “With revenue growing and substantial contracted capacity still to deliver, we have built a strong foundation for our next phase of growth.”

Put that $700 million annualized colocation book against the $12.4 billion the entire network earns from issuance each year, and one company’s real-estate and power business is worth about 5.6% of everything Bitcoin mining produces. The warrants-driven net income is worth flagging separately. A $1.2 billion profit that depends on the mark on warrants is a balance-sheet event, and investors who read it as operating strength will misprice the quarter.

This is the pattern BlockchainReporter documented when miners’ AI pivot decoupled their shares from Bitcoin, and again when AI contracts gave listed miners a valuation edge over pure-play operators. Flat difficulty does not hurt a company that is paid per megawatt of high-density colocation. It hurts the operator whose entire revenue line is the $33.4 per petahash.

A new record requires hashrate to grow faster than the protocol can absorb, and the next decision point is close. The next retarget falls at block 975,744, with the chain at 974,990 at the time of writing, which places it around 12 November. Difficulty would need to climb 5.1% from 148.36 trillion to clear 155.97 trillion. The 29 October adjustment delivered 5.54%, so the arithmetic is not exotic; it is a question of whether the hashrate behind it exists.

Two conditions could produce it. A price recovery would restore miner margins and pull curtailed capacity back online, since the same machines become profitable at $81,750 that sit idle at $75,577. Alternatively, new capacity could come from operators with lower power costs or stranded energy contracts, which raises network hashrate without needing a higher Bitcoin price. Neither is visible in current data: the 30-day hashrate peak of 1.22 ZH/s has already faded to an average near 1.02 ZH/s.

The longer calendar matters too. The subsidy has been 3.125 $BTC per block since April 2024, and the next halving sits at block 1,050,000. With the chain at 974,990, that is 75,010 blocks away, or roughly 521 days at the current pace of 144 blocks a day. A halving cuts the same hashprice by half unless price doubles, and it lands before the next difficulty record decision is settled in any meaningful sense.

The invalidation is explicit. If difficulty closes an epoch above 155.97 trillion, the 374-day gap ends and the record resets. Until then, the correct read is a network consolidating below its ceiling while its publicly traded operators shift revenue toward contracted colocation and away from a hashprice that no longer covers high-cost power. sources.title: Bitcoin’s Second-Ever Negative Difficulty Reading: AI Capital Does What China’s Mining Ban Did
passages: Only the Second Time in Bitcoin's History This Metric Has Gone Negative The 2021 China ban dropped difficulty by roughly 28% in its steepest single adjustment and pushed year-over-year difficulty growth negative.

Bitcoin's mining network has just crossed a threshold that has appeared only once before in the currency's entire history: network difficulty has fallen below where it stood a year ago, confirmed by Luxor's Hashrate Index on July 28, 2026.
The last time that happened was in mid-2021, when China's government forced roughly half of the world's mining operations offline in a matter of weeks.
Bitcoin's Self-Regulating Security Mechanism Designed for a Different Problem To understand why this moment matters, it helps to understand what mining difficulty actually measures.
Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism exists to keep that 10-minute cadence stable regardless of how much computing power joins or leaves the network.

The machines are shutting down because the same power infrastructure that runs a Bitcoin miner is worth more to artificial intelligence data centers — and the AI market is willing to pay three to 25 times more per megawatt than Bitcoin mining currently offers.
The April 2024 halving cut the block reward from 6.25 to 3.125 Bitcoin.
As of August 1, Bitcoin traded near $63,100 — down approximately 47% from that peak — meaning a block now yields roughly $197,000.

Publicly traded miners sold more than 32,000 Bitcoin in the first quarter of 2026 alone — a single-quarter record that exceeded the full-year total for 2025 and surpassed the roughly 20,000 Bitcoin sold during the 2022 Terra Luna collapse.

Bitcoin uses a cryptographic process called proof-of-work: miners compete to find a hash value — the output of the SHA-256 algorithm applied to a block of transaction data — that falls below a numerical target.

The machines are shutting down because the same power infrastructure that runs a Bitcoin miner is worth more to artificial intelligence data centers — and the AI market is willing to pay three to 25 times more per megawatt than Bitcoin mining currently offers. And it raises a question prior contractions never required asking: will the hashrate come back at all? Bitcoin's Self-Regulating Security Mechanism Designed for a Different Problem To understand why this moment matters, it helps to understand what mining difficulty actually measures. Bitcoin uses a cryptographic process called proof-of-work: miners compete to find a hash value — the output of the SHA-256 algorithm applied to a block of transaction data — that falls below a numerical target. The only way to find a qualifying hash is brute force: modern application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) miners attempt trillions of hash calculations per second, each one a lottery ticket, searching for the rare output that satisfies the network's current requirements. The Bitcoin Foundation's 2026 explainer on mining mechanics covers the underlying proof-of-work process in depth. At current difficulty of 126.23 trillion, only approximately one in 70 trillion random hash attempts produces a qualifying result. The network collectively performs roughly 868 quintillion such calculations every second — that is 868 exahashes per second — with the reward going to whichever miner finds a valid hash first, approximately once every ten minutes. Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism exists to keep that 10-minute cadence stable regardless of how much computing power joins or leaves the network. If the previous 2,016 blocks arrived faster than the 10-minute average implies, difficulty rises. The formula is simple: new target equals old target multiplied by the ratio of actual epoch time to the ideal 20,160-minute epoch. The adjustment is capped at four times in either direction to prevent wild swings. It assumes that economic incentives will always bring hashrate back when it leaves — that when difficulty falls, surviving miners find more blocks and earn more per unit of computing power, making the network more attractive to capital until equilibrium is restored. Only the Second Time in Bitcoin's History This Metric Has Gone Negative The 2021 China ban dropped difficulty by roughly 28% in its steepest single adjustment and pushed year-over-year difficulty growth negative. Within months, displaced miners had relocated to the United States, Kazakhstan, and other regions, and difficulty was climbing to new all-time highs. The current contraction has reproduced the year-over-year reading without any policy catalyst. Bitcoin's difficulty stands at 126.23 trillion as of the July 25 adjustment, roughly 1.1% below the 127.62 trillion it recorded one year earlier — only the second sub-zero year-over-year reading in the network's history, confirmed by Luxor's Hashrate Index on July 28, 2026. The decline from the November 2025 all-time high of 155.97 trillion is 19.1% — the third-deepest drawdown since dedicated ASIC hardware became the standard mining tool. Only the aftermath of the China ban and a 2018 bear market produced steeper declines. Bitcoin Magazine Pro's data shows the downward hashrate trend has now extended approximately 287 consecutive days. The seven-day average hashrate stood near 868 exahashes per second (EH/s) by late July, down from more than one zettahash per second at the network's late-2025 peak — a decline of roughly 12% from the all-time high. Three Forces Are Draining the Network, and Only One Has Driven a Contraction of This Kind Before Luxor's Hashrate Index attributed the decline to three overlapping causes: worsening mining economics (falling Bitcoin prices and compressed hashprice), the AI infrastructure buildout pulling capital and power away from mining, and a long tail of smaller drags including Texas 4CP curtailment costs and approximately 7 EH/s knocked offline by the conflict in Iran. The April 2024 halving cut the block reward from 6.25 to 3.125 Bitcoin. At Bitcoin's October 2025 all-time high near $126,000, a single block was worth approximately $393,750. As of August 1, Bitcoin traded near $63,100 — down approximately 47% from that peak — meaning a block now yields roughly $197,000. That is a per-block revenue decline of more than 50% in less than a year, with the halving's supply cut baked on top. Hashprice — the expected daily revenue per petahash per second of computing power — fell to an all-time spot low of $27.66 as of late June, within one cent of February's prior low, according to Hashrate Index. The math for older hardware tells the story clearly: an Antminer S19-generation machine running at 100 terahashes per second earns roughly $3.19 per day at current hashprice and consumes more in electricity than that at even $0.05 per kilowatt-hour, putting a large segment of the older fleet below breakeven. CoinShares estimated in March 2026 that 15% to 20% of the global mining fleet was already operating at a loss. Transaction fees, which once provided a meaningful secondary revenue stream during the Ordinals inscription boom of 2023 and early 2024, have normalized back to roughly 1% of total miner revenue — far below the 7% they briefly reached — removing a supplemental buffer at exactly the moment miners need one most. Publicly traded miners sold more than 32,000 Bitcoin in the first quarter of 2026 alone — a single-quarter record that exceeded the full-year total for 2025 and surpassed the roughly 20,000 Bitcoin sold during the 2022 Terra Luna collapse. Why the ASIC Hardware Constraint Makes This Conversion Permanent, Not Provisional One detail the pivot narrative frequently elides deserves technical clarity: Bitcoin ASICs cannot be repurposed for artificial intelligence workloads. Bitcoin ASICs perform only SHA-256 double-hashing — the specific cryptographic operation Bitcoin uses for proof-of-work. They cannot execute the matrix multiplication operations that underlie neural network inference and training.

extraction.body: Bitcoin mining difficulty has stayed below its 156 trillion peak for over a year, the longest such stretch yet, signaling deeper pressure on miners. Bitcoin mining difficulty has been stuck below its all-time high for more than a year. The metric sits just over 148 trillion as of November 8, 2026—about 5% below the 156 trillion peak it hit on October 29, 2025. That’s now the longest recordless stretch in Bitcoin’s history, surpassing a roughly 364-day run between August 2011 and July 2012. The question facing the industry: is this a temporary mining cycle, or has capital found better returns in AI data centers and high-performance computing? Bitcoin mining difficulty reached almost 156 trillion on October 29, 2025. It hasn’t reclaimed that level since. As of November 8, 2026, it stood at just over 148 trillion. The 5% gap matters less than the duration. Bitcoin has now blown past its previous record for the longest stretch without a new difficulty high, a period that began after the October 2025 peak. Difficulty adjusts as computing power enters or leaves the network, keeping block production close to 10 minutes. A lower reading after a previous peak means mining conditions haven’t returned to their earlier high-water mark. Saifedean Ammous, author of The Bitcoin Standard , says the current slowdown is now the longest in Bitcoin’s history. His reading: the industry faces structural pressure, not a single shock like those that drove earlier downturns. He points to Bitcoin’s halvings. The block subsidy drops 50% roughly every four years, so Bitcoin’s value must rise fast enough to offset the smaller reward. coreStoryFacts.text: Bitcoin’s mining difficulty has not printed a new all-time high in 374 days.
The metric stands at 148.36 trillion hashes after the retarget of 29 October 2026, which lifted it 5.54% from 140.58 trillion.
The record remains 155.97 trillion, set at block 921,312 on 29 October 2025 at 10:14 UTC, according to mempool.space difficulty data.
That leaves the network 4.88% below its peak, and spot Bitcoin at $75,577, down 2.5% over seven days and 7.6% over 30.
A year without a record is not a malfunction.

On daily difficulty samples, the current 356-day run below the record is the longest in the network’s history, ahead of the 348 days between August 2011 and July 2012, the 236 days from May 2021 to January 2022, and the 225 days from October 2018 to May 2019.
Neither result depends on a new difficulty record; both depend on the price of Bitcoin, which has fallen 7.6% in 30 days.

Put that $700 million annualized colocation book against the $12.4 billion the entire network earns from issuance each year, and one company’s real-estate and power business is worth about 5.6% of everything Bitcoin mining produces.
A halving cuts the same hashprice by half unless price doubles, and it lands before the next difficulty record decision is settled in any meaningful sense.

Until then, the correct read is a network consolidating below its ceiling while its publicly traded operators shift revenue toward contracted colocation and away from a hashprice that no longer covers high-cost power.
For traders, miner balance sheets are a supply variable to watch rather than a signal to chase.
For anyone modelling hashprice, $33.4 per petahash per day is the number the whole industry is currently underwriting.
Bitcoin recalculates difficulty every 2,016 blocks, roughly two weeks of mining.
The mechanism is self-limiting, which is why the record has held through a year of infrastructure building.
With Bitcoin near $75,577 and hashrate averaging about 1.02 ZH/s, miners have little incentive to add capacity, so the retargets of the past year have not been enough to clear the October 2025 peak.

Only the Second Time in Bitcoin's History This Metric Has Gone Negative The 2021 China ban dropped difficulty by roughly 28% in its steepest single adjustment and pushed year-over-year difficulty growth negative.

Bitcoin's mining network has just crossed a threshold that has appeared only once before in the currency's entire history: network difficulty has fallen below where it stood a year ago, confirmed by Luxor's Hashrate Index on July 28, 2026.
The last time that happened was in mid-2021, when China's government forced roughly half of the world's mining operations offline in a matter of weeks.
Bitcoin's Self-Regulating Security Mechanism Designed for a Different Problem To understand why this moment matters, it helps to understand what mining difficulty actually measures.
Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism exists to keep that 10-minute cadence stable regardless of how much computing power joins or leaves the network.

The machines are shutting down because the same power infrastructure that runs a Bitcoin miner is worth more to artificial intelligence data centers — and the AI market is willing to pay three to 25 times more per megawatt than Bitcoin mining currently offers.
The April 2024 halving cut the block reward from 6.25 to 3.125 Bitcoin.
As of August 1, Bitcoin traded near $63,100 — down approximately 47% from that peak — meaning a block now yields roughly $197,000.

Publicly traded miners sold more than 32,000 Bitcoin in the first quarter of 2026 alone — a single-quarter record that exceeded the full-year total for 2025 and surpassed the roughly 20,000 Bitcoin sold during the 2022 Terra Luna collapse.

The last time that happened was in mid-2021, when China's government forced roughly half of the world's mining operations offline in a matter of weeks. The machines are shutting down because the same power infrastructure that runs a Bitcoin miner is worth more to artificial intelligence data centers — and the AI market is willing to pay three to 25 times more per megawatt than Bitcoin mining currently offers. And it raises a question prior contractions never required asking: will the hashrate come back at all? Bitcoin's Self-Regulating Security Mechanism Designed for a Different Problem To understand why this moment matters, it helps to understand what mining difficulty actually measures. Bitcoin uses a cryptographic process called proof-of-work: miners compete to find a hash value — the output of the SHA-256 algorithm applied to a block of transaction data — that falls below a numerical target. The only way to find a qualifying hash is brute force: modern application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC) miners attempt trillions of hash calculations per second, each one a lottery ticket, searching for the rare output that satisfies the network's current requirements. The Bitcoin Foundation's 2026 explainer on mining mechanics covers the underlying proof-of-work process in depth. At current difficulty of 126.23 trillion, only approximately one in 70 trillion random hash attempts produces a qualifying result. The network collectively performs roughly 868 quintillion such calculations every second — that is 868 exahashes per second — with the reward going to whichever miner finds a valid hash first, approximately once every ten minutes. Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism exists to keep that 10-minute cadence stable regardless of how much computing power joins or leaves the network. If the previous 2,016 blocks arrived faster than the 10-minute average implies, difficulty rises. The formula is simple: new target equals old target multiplied by the ratio of actual epoch time to the ideal 20,160-minute epoch. The adjustment is capped at four times in either direction to prevent wild swings. It assumes that economic incentives will always bring hashrate back when it leaves — that when difficulty falls, surviving miners find more blocks and earn more per unit of computing power, making the network more attractive to capital until equilibrium is restored. Only the Second Time in Bitcoin's History This Metric Has Gone Negative The 2021 China ban dropped difficulty by roughly 28% in its steepest single adjustment and pushed year-over-year difficulty growth negative. Within months, displaced miners had relocated to the United States, Kazakhstan, and other regions, and difficulty was climbing to new all-time highs. The current contraction has reproduced the year-over-year reading without any policy catalyst. Bitcoin's difficulty stands at 126.23 trillion as of the July 25 adjustment, roughly 1.1% below the 127.62 trillion it recorded one year earlier — only the second sub-zero year-over-year reading in the network's history, confirmed by Luxor's Hashrate Index on July 28, 2026. The decline from the November 2025 all-time high of 155.97 trillion is 19.1% — the third-deepest drawdown since dedicated ASIC hardware became the standard mining tool. Only the aftermath of the China ban and a 2018 bear market produced steeper declines. Bitcoin Magazine Pro's data shows the downward hashrate trend has now extended approximately 287 consecutive days. The seven-day average hashrate stood near 868 exahashes per second (EH/s) by late July, down from more than one zettahash per second at the network's late-2025 peak — a decline of roughly 12% from the all-time high. Three Forces Are Draining the Network, and Only One Has Driven a Contraction of This Kind Before Luxor's Hashrate Index attributed the decline to three overlapping causes: worsening mining economics (falling Bitcoin prices and compressed hashprice), the AI infrastructure buildout pulling capital and power away from mining, and a long tail of smaller drags including Texas 4CP curtailment costs and approximately 7 EH/s knocked offline by the conflict in Iran. extraction.body: Bitcoin mining difficulty has stayed below its 156 trillion peak for over a year, the longest such stretch yet, signaling deeper pressure on miners. Bitcoin mining difficulty has been stuck below its all-time high for more than a year. The metric sits just over 148 trillion as of November 8, 2026—about 5% below the 156 trillion peak it hit on October 29, 2025. That’s now the longest recordless stretch in Bitcoin’s history, surpassing a roughly 364-day run between August 2011 and July 2012. The question facing the industry: is this a temporary mining cycle, or has capital found better returns in AI data centers and high-performance computing? Bitcoin mining difficulty reached almost 156 trillion on October 29, 2025. It hasn’t reclaimed that level since. As of November 8, 2026, it stood at just over 148 trillion. The 5% gap matters less than the duration. Bitcoin has now blown past its previous record for the longest stretch without a new difficulty high, a period that began after the October 2025 peak. Difficulty adjusts as computing power enters or leaves the network, keeping block production close to 10 minutes. A lower reading after a previous peak means mining conditions haven’t returned to their earlier high-water mark. Saifedean Ammous, author of The Bitcoin Standard , says the current slowdown is now the longest in Bitcoin’s history. His reading: the industry faces structural pressure, not a single shock like those that drove earlier downturns. He points to Bitcoin’s halvings. The block subsidy drops 50% roughly every four years, so Bitcoin’s value must rise fast enough to offset the smaller reward. His estimate: mining economics need almost 19% annual appreciation over four years, before accounting for dollar devaluation and the opportunity cost of competing infrastructure businesses. Core Scientific offers a concrete example. The company recently announced plans to fully exit Bitcoin mining by the end of 2026 and enter 2027 as a dedicated AI and high-performance-computing colocation provider. It has already cut its mining fleet by almost half while redirecting electricity and data-center capacity toward infrastructure customers. Colocation revenue jumped 58% quarter over quarter to $215.4 million in the third quarter, compared with $15 million a year earlier. CryptoPotato detailed the difficulty record and the changing economics facing Bitcoin miners. Bitcoin’s previous longest recordless period ran from August 2011 to July 2012, lasting roughly 364 days. During that stretch, Bitcoin’s price collapsed by roughly 94% to 95%, providing a clear explanation for the deterioration in mining conditions. The 2021 episode stemmed from a clear regulatory event and a geographic migration. The current difficulty streak is being discussed alongside subsidy pressure, competition for power and the changing value of data-center capacity. The network previously moved in the opposite direction as Bitcoin’s price recovered and Ordinals activity increased. Miners deployed more machines, computing power rose and difficulty reached new highs. An earlier mining report linked the 2023 rise in difficulty to stronger Bitcoin prices and Ordinals-related demand for block space. It also described how new-generation machines were being installed as rack space became available. The earlier account also described the effect of rising difficulty on miners’ chances of earning block revenue. Every halving cuts the block subsidy in half. Miners must find ways to lower operating costs, improve machine efficiency or benefit from a higher Bitcoin price to preserve the economics of their facilities. Ammous’s estimate of almost 19% annual appreciation describes the pace of value growth he believes mining needs over four years. It’s an estimate about industry economics, not a Bitcoin price target. AI companies are competing for the same cheap electricity, data-center space and power infrastructure miners use. If AI colocation produces better returns, operators can redirect facilities and capital rather than add more Bitcoin mining machines. That outcome depends on how much capacity leaves mining, how much new capacity enters elsewhere and whether Bitcoin’s price provides enough incentive for operators to return to expansion. The current reading of just over 148 trillion sits about 5% below the record near 156 trillion. A gap that size wouldn’t by itself define a major industry break, but it has persisted for more than a year and exceeded the roughly 364-day record from 2011–2012. The combination of time and the absence of a new peak is the central signal. Miners haven’t returned the network to the computing-power conditions of the October 2025 high. Core Scientific’s colocation revenue reached $215.4 million in the third quarter after rising 58% from the previous quarter. The figure was $15 million a year earlier, showing why high-performance-computing customers can compete with Bitcoin mining for facility space and electricity. Those figures come from colocation, the business Core Scientific is building around AI and other computing customers. The company’s planned mining exit makes that shift one of the clearest company-level examples of the broader pressure Ammous describes. Core Scientific’s planned exit illustrates the competitive risk at the company level. Other operators may make different choices, but the availability of an alternative customer base changes how they value electricity and real estate. Bitcoin mining difficulty can remain below a prior high while the network continues operating and processing blocks. The metric describes the amount of computing competition at a point in time; it doesn’t by itself establish that Bitcoin is fundamentally weakening. Ammous offers a counterargument to the bearish interpretation. If mining becomes less attractive than holding BTC, capital that might have gone into machines, facilities and electricity could flow directly into the asset instead. Core Scientific plans to complete its Bitcoin mining exit by the end of 2026. It expects to enter 2027 as a dedicated AI and high-performance-computing colocation provider, making the end-of-year transition a key date for the company’s strategy. Bitcoin mining difficulty would need to reclaim the almost 156 trillion record set on October 29, 2025 to end the current recordless period. Until that happens, the network will continue extending the longest stretch in its history without a new difficulty high. Miners will continue weighing Bitcoin mining against AI colocation and other uses of electricity and data-center capacity. The main variables are Bitcoin’s price appreciation, the next subsidy reductions, equipment efficiency and the revenue available from non-mining infrastructure customers. The recordless streak is both a mining statistic and a sign of changing capital allocation. Whether it ends with a new expansion in hash rate or a longer shift toward AI will depend on the relative returns available to operators. Bitcoin mining difficulty reached almost 156 trillion on October 29, 2025. It has remained below that level through November 8, 2026. The metric stood at just over 148 trillion as of November 8, 2026. That is approximately 5% below the October 2025 peak. Core Scientific plans to fully exit Bitcoin mining by the end of 2026. It aims to enter 2027 as a dedicated AI and high-performance-computing colocation provider. Ammous estimated that mining economics require Bitcoin’s value to appreciate by almost 19% annually over four years. His estimate comes before accounting for dollar devaluation and the opportunity cost created by AI infrastructure. This article is for information only and is not financial advice.

facts.text: Bitcoin’s mining difficulty has not printed a new all-time high in 374 days.
The metric stands at 148.36 trillion hashes after the retarget of 29 October 2026, which lifted it 5.54% from 140.58 trillion.
The record remains 155.97 trillion, set at block 921,312 on 29 October 2025 at 10:14 UTC, according to mempool.space difficulty data.
That leaves the network 4.88% below its peak, and spot Bitcoin at $75,577, down 2.5% over seven days and 7.6% over 30.
A year without a record is not a malfunction.

On daily difficulty samples, the current 356-day run below the record is the longest in the network’s history, ahead of the 348 days between August 2011 and July 2012, the 236 days from May 2021 to January 2022, and the 225 days from October 2018 to May 2019.
Neither result depends on a new difficulty record; both depend on the price of Bitcoin, which has fallen 7.6% in 30 days.

Put that $700 million annualized colocation book against the $12.4 billion the entire network earns from issuance each year, and one company’s real-estate and power business is worth about 5.6% of everything Bitcoin mining produces.
A halving cuts the same hashprice by half unless price doubles, and it lands before the next difficulty record decision is settled in any meaningful sense.

Until then, the correct read is a network consolidating below its ceiling while its publicly traded operators shift revenue toward contracted colocation and away from a hashprice that no longer covers high-cost power.
For traders, miner balance sheets are a supply variable to watch rather than a signal to chase.
For anyone modelling hashprice, $33.4 per petahash per day is the number the whole industry is currently underwriting.
Bitcoin recalculates difficulty every 2,016 blocks, roughly two weeks of mining.
The mechanism is self-limiting, which is why the record has held through a year of infrastructure building.
With Bitcoin near $75,577 and hashrate averaging about 1.02 ZH/s, miners have little incentive to add capacity, so the retargets of the past year have not been enough to clear the October 2025 peak.

The last time that happened was in mid-2021, when China's government forced roughly half of the world's mining operations offline in a matter of weeks.
Bitcoin's Self-Regulating Security Mechanism Designed for a Different Problem To understand why this moment matters, it helps to understand what mining difficulty actually measures.
Bitcoin's difficulty adjustment mechanism exists to keep that 10-minute cadence stable regardless of how much computing power joins or leaves the network.

The machines are shutting down because the same power infrastructure that runs a Bitcoin miner is worth more to artificial intelligence data centers — and the AI market is willing to pay three to 25 times more per megawatt than Bitcoin mining currently offers.
The April 2024 halving cut the block reward from 6.25 to 3.125 Bitcoin.
As of August 1, Bitcoin traded near $63,100 — down approximately 47% from that peak — meaning a block now yields roughly $197,000.

Publicly traded miners sold more than 32,000 Bitcoin in the first quarter of 2026 alone — a single-quarter record that exceeded the full-year total for 2025 and surpassed the roughly 20,000 Bitcoin sold during the 2022 Terra Luna collapse.

Bitcoin uses a cryptographic process called proof-of-work: miners compete to find a hash value — the output of the SHA-256 algorithm applied to a block of transaction data — that falls below a numerical target.
Bitcoin mining difficulty has been stuck below its all-time high for more than a year.
Core Scientific plans to complete its Bitcoin mining exit by the end of 2026.
Bitcoin has now blown past its previous record for the longest stretch without a new difficulty high, a period that began after the October 2025 peak.
The current reading of just over 148 trillion sits about 5% below the record near 156 trillion.
During that stretch, Bitcoin’s price collapsed by roughly 94% to 95%, providing a clear explanation for the deterioration in mining conditions.
An earlier mining report linked the 2023 rise in difficulty to stronger Bitcoin prices and Ordinals-related demand for block space.
If AI colocation produces better returns, operators can redirect facilities and capital rather than add more Bitcoin mining machines.
CryptoPotato detailed the difficulty record and the changing economics facing Bitcoin miners.
Ammous estimated that mining economics require Bitcoin’s value to appreciate by almost 19% annually over four years.

The project is organized by the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) and the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA).

The path to a quantum secure future requires more than strong cryptography; it requires cryptographic agility, the ability to adapt to evolving algorithms, standards, and regulatory requirements, without redesigning the systems from ground up.
It also reinforces the role of SIM and eSIM technologies beyond subscriber authentication, positioning them as trusted platforms for quantum-safe telecom, IoT, government and defense applications.
Within this architecture, the Quantum-Resistant SIM acts as a hardware root of trust for secure communications, generating and protecting sensitive credentials and cryptographic operations.
The project demonstrates how secure element technologies, already widely used in telecom environments, can evolve to support future quantum safe requirements.

They serve as dedicated cryptographic modules for connected devices, enabling secure key management and cryptographic services for government, defense and other critical infrastructure applications requiring the highest levels of security and resilience.

extraction.body: Quantum computing’s threat to today’s cryptography has been evident for some time. More than half of surveyed experts expect a cryptographically relevant quantum computer within 15 years, and as many as 49% say within 10. The timeline that matters more, however, is the one set by regulators. The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations began September 11, 2026, with full requirements following in December 2027. NSA’s CNSA 2.0 requirements for new national security system acquisitions begin in January 2027. Most compliance planning has centered on software that encrypts data in transit and at rest. That overlooks a system’s first line of defense: the hardware root of trust (HRoT) that authenticates firmware and anchors trust for everything above it. Traditional HRoT options are fixed-function, with device IDs and firmware signatures locked in at design time. That stability is what makes them trustworthy, but it also locks in algorithm choices. When those algorithms age out, designers must replace the component or layer software on top. Because software updates are far easier than hardware changes, many systems pair modern software with legacy hardware. That works only as long as the underlying algorithms hold. Quantum computing ends that arrangement. NIST has finalized ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), and specifies LMS and XMSS (SP 800-208) for firmware signing. Yet most traditional HRoT options, including MCUs and secure-boot SoCs, rely solely on RSA and ECC, which a sufficiently powerful quantum computer can break. No software layer can fix a foundation that cannot be trusted. Decision-makers are left in a difficult position. Existing devices are no longer adequate, and quantum capabilities will keep changing quickly and unpredictably. They need an approach that addresses today’s threats while remaining adaptable to tomorrow’s requirements. The answer is cryptographically agile, hardware-level protection. Crypto-agility, the ability to update cryptographic algorithms in the field without replacing hardware, offers a path to protection without sending systems back to square one. Crypto-agile PQC systems counter the perception that an effective HRoT must be completely static. They preserve the fixed security elements that matter while adding flexibility where it is needed, through a combination of features: Adaptable hardware such as Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) makes crypto-agility accessible in a unified hardware package. A single FPGA can serve as both the HRoT and the system control layer, handling boot, power sequencing, and monitoring in one place, while reconfigurable logic allows security functions to be updated after deployment. Low-power, always-on operation, deterministic low-latency response, parallel processing for multiple simultaneous key operations, and high I/O capacity add to their value in secure-by-design systems, with or without PQC considerations. Specialized FPGAs like the Lattice Mach™-N2 family are built for PQC-ready operation . Mach-N2 offers logic densities of up to 220k cells and boots in under 30 milliseconds, closing the firmware-boot gap that leaves systems exposed. It supports a full CNSA 2.0-compliant PQC suite (ML-DSA, LMS, and XMSS for authentication, ML-KEM for key exchange) alongside AES-256-GCM, ECC521, and RSA4096 for backward compatibility. Field-updatable algorithms let designers and operators adapt as requirements change, and PUF-derived device identity with DICE and SPDM support extends trust across the platform and supply chain. The root of trust is only one layer. Protecting platform firmware across its lifecycle also requires detection, recovery, and attestation, and these capabilities need to be post-quantum ready as well. Platform Firmware Resilience (PFR) aligned to NIST SP 800-193 provides protection, detection, and recovery, while SPDM 1.4 attestation extends trust across the devices in a system. Solutions such as the Lattice Sentry™ solution stack pair PQC-enabled PFR and attestation with a crypto-agile hardware root of trust, giving teams a practical path to PQC-ready operation. PQC preparedness will take years and will evolve as attackers and protections adapt to one another. The hardware designers choose today must meet requirements that have not yet been written. The only certainty is that the unknown is coming, so the right foundation is one built to change as quickly as the quantum landscape.

The project is organized by the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT) and the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA). As part of the initiative, with KT playing a leading role, IST is implementing NIST-standardized and Korean PQC algorithms on the Quantum-Resistant SIM equipped smart-card platform to support the protection of defense communications systems against emerging cryptographic threats. Bringing post-quantum cryptography to SIM and eSIM deployments Post-quantum algorithms place significantly higher demands on processing power and memory than many classical cryptographic schemes. IST is addressing these constraints through the PQC dedicated SIM and eSIM, enabling demanding cryptographic operations to be handled efficiently within a secure, tamper-resistant environment. The implementation is designed to support both international NIST standardized and Korea-specific PQC algorithms. Subject to final validation, the project is expected to deliver the first implementation of KpqC 1 algorithms on a smart-card platform in Korea, demonstrating a practical path to adding quantum-safe and crypto-agility capabilities at the secure-element level while limiting extensive changes at device level. Supporting quantum-safe defense communications KT’s broader pilot, conducted for the Ministry of National Defense and the Army Information and Communication School, is designed to apply and verify PQC across critical defense infrastructures, including smart-unit platforms and user PCs, CCTV and video storage systems, drones and ground control systems, and 5G network environments. The aim is to assess performance and applicability in demanding operational conditions. Within this architecture, the Quantum-Resistant SIM acts as a hardware root of trust for secure communications, generating and protecting sensitive credentials and cryptographic operations. extraction.body: Quantum computing’s threat to today’s cryptography has been evident for some time. More than half of surveyed experts expect a cryptographically relevant quantum computer within 15 years, and as many as 49% say within 10. The timeline that matters more, however, is the one set by regulators. The EU Cyber Resilience Act’s reporting obligations began September 11, 2026, with full requirements following in December 2027. NSA’s CNSA 2.0 requirements for new national security system acquisitions begin in January 2027. Most compliance planning has centered on software that encrypts data in transit and at rest. That overlooks a system’s first line of defense: the hardware root of trust (HRoT) that authenticates firmware and anchors trust for everything above it. Traditional HRoT options are fixed-function, with device IDs and firmware signatures locked in at design time. That stability is what makes them trustworthy, but it also locks in algorithm choices. When those algorithms age out, designers must replace the component or layer software on top. Because software updates are far easier than hardware changes, many systems pair modern software with legacy hardware. That works only as long as the underlying algorithms hold. Quantum computing ends that arrangement. NIST has finalized ML-KEM (FIPS 203), ML-DSA (FIPS 204), and SLH-DSA (FIPS 205), and specifies LMS and XMSS (SP 800-208) for firmware signing. Yet most traditional HRoT options, including MCUs and secure-boot SoCs, rely solely on RSA and ECC, which a sufficiently powerful quantum computer can break. No software layer can fix a foundation that cannot be trusted. Decision-makers are left in a difficult position. Existing devices are no longer adequate, and quantum capabilities will keep changing quickly and unpredictably. They need an approach that addresses today’s threats while remaining adaptable to tomorrow’s requirements. The answer is cryptographically agile, hardware-level protection. Crypto-agility, the ability to update cryptographic algorithms in the field without replacing hardware, offers a path to protection without sending systems back to square one. Crypto-agile PQC systems counter the perception that an effective HRoT must be completely static. They preserve the fixed security elements that matter while adding flexibility where it is needed, through a combination of features: Adaptable hardware such as Field Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) makes crypto-agility accessible in a unified hardware package. A single FPGA can serve as both the HRoT and the system control layer, handling boot, power sequencing, and monitoring in one place, while reconfigurable logic allows security functions to be updated after deployment. Low-power, always-on operation, deterministic low-latency response, parallel processing for multiple simultaneous key operations, and high I/O capacity add to their value in secure-by-design systems, with or without PQC considerations. Specialized FPGAs like the Lattice Mach™-N2 family are built for PQC-ready operation . Mach-N2 offers logic densities of up to 220k cells and boots in under 30 milliseconds, closing the firmware-boot gap that leaves systems exposed. It supports a full CNSA 2.0-compliant PQC suite (ML-DSA, LMS, and XMSS for authentication, ML-KEM for key exchange) alongside AES-256-GCM, ECC521, and RSA4096 for backward compatibility. Field-updatable algorithms let designers and operators adapt as requirements change, and PUF-derived device identity with DICE and SPDM support extends trust across the platform and supply chain. The root of trust is only one layer. Protecting platform firmware across its lifecycle also requires detection, recovery, and attestation, and these capabilities need to be post-quantum ready as well. Platform Firmware Resilience (PFR) aligned to NIST SP 800-193 provides protection, detection, and recovery, while SPDM 1.4 attestation extends trust across the devices in a system. Solutions such as the Lattice Sentry™ solution stack pair PQC-enabled PFR and attestation with a crypto-agile hardware root of trust, giving teams a practical path to PQC-ready operation. PQC preparedness will take years and will evolve as attackers and protections adapt to one another. The hardware designers choose today must meet requirements that have not yet been written. The only certainty is that the unknown is coming, so the right foundation is one built to change as quickly as the quantum landscape.

extraction.body: MPs, local authorities, lawyers, schools and more are receiving floods of grievances, requests and legal challenges, often complex to read and respond to “I t started as a trickle in 2024 and now it’s an onslaught.” Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in a Labour MP’s office, is explaining the daily reality of dealing with surging volumes of artificial intelligence-generated correspondence. “Half the emails we receive are some form of AI,” she says, adding that this has made requests and complaints much more complex and time-consuming to read and deal with, despite her decade of experience in the role. “It is definitely more taxing.” At the start of this decade, applying for a job, writing a complaint or objecting to a local planning application typically required considerable effort: time to research a topic, fill in a form or write a formal-sounding email, with specialist knowledge often also required. The developers of AI tools promised huge productivity gains for employers and their staff: dull, routine tasks could be automated and carried out far more quickly, giving the human workforce more time for creative endeavours. There are signs of those gains in parts of the economy, with AI credited for some of this year’s better than expected UK GDP growth. However, UK businesses, local authorities, courts, schools and other public bodies are reporting being swamped by a flood of AI-generated complaints, letters and legal challenges that are massively increasing their workload , at a time of already stretched resources . This phenomenon has been called “AI clog” by commenters. With the concept of low-quality “AI slop” now mainstream, organisations are sounding the alarm that their operations are being gummed up by ever greater volumes of correspondence. These only take moments for users to create, but huge amounts of time for human employees to sift through and respond to. Bombarding public bodies with AI-generated requests has been labelled “agentic flooding” by researchers at the centre for digital governance at the Hertie School in Berlin, the Cooperative AI Foundation and GovAI. “Every sector is experiencing very similar issues,” says Deborah Evans, the chief executive of Lawyers in Local Government (LLG), an organisation that represents 5,600 lawyers working in local authorities. “Obviously AI is a wonderful tool that enables people to do things very, very quickly and it can make a complaint sound incredibly professional, very formal.” Local authorities are experiencing surging numbers of complaints, which can relate to issues from adult social care services to missed bin collections or objections to planning applications. “Local authorities have one pot of money and don’t get extra money because of more complaints,” Evans says. Local authorities believe the length of correspondence is an indication that it has been artificially generated, as does the inclusion of certain phrases or use of bullet points. “It’s a real problem,” says councillor Alessandro Georgiou, the leader of Enfield council. “More and more residents are using it to appeal decisions of the council, such as a significant uptick in parking appeals.” The information rights watchdog, the Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) , found that many public authorities received more requests in 2025. It noted that AI-generated requests can be “very long, repetitive and contain unrelated comments or misdirected demands”, have a greater scope, and be written in a way that makes it harder to identify what information is being requested. Before the widespread use of chatbots, the average length of complaints received by local authorities was about two pages. The majority are now 10 times longer, says Evans. “You get some huge ones. The worst one I’m aware of at the moment is about 200 pages long,” she says. Despite this, the ICO cautions that requests that appear to be drafted using AI and contain inaccuracies still need to be answered by humans. AI tools can often treat complaints as a legal claim, Evans says. “It will start referring to statute and pull out case law, but not necessarily tied to the jurisdictional boundaries in which you operate. It might find some great case law from Canada or somewhere. Before the widespread use of chatbots, the average length of complaints received by local authorities was about two pages.

“I t started as a trickle in 2024 and now it’s an onslaught.” Hollie Wickens, a senior caseworker in a Labour MP’s office, is explaining the daily reality of dealing with surging volumes of artificial intelligence-generated correspondence.
“You can tell by the wording [that the complaint is AI-generated] and it has a different tone.”

Put your iPad to good use with apps for journaling, discovering art and much more. Our favorite apps are elegant and well-designed, taking advantage of the entire iPad display.

extraction.body: Put your iPad to good use with apps for journaling, discovering art and much more. Your iPad should make every day easier. Whether you want to build new habits or improve your routines, we've rounded up apps that put the best iPads to work in your daily life. We found these by digging a bit deeper. These aren't first-party Apple apps or subscription-only Adobe staples. It's free to get started with each, though most charge for extra features, which we've noted where applicable. Our favorite apps are elegant and well-designed, taking advantage of the entire iPad display. They also keep AI to a bare minimum. There may be machine learning to help with search and transcriptions, but you won't find fake images or bogus text generators here. If you're a voracious consumer of media, you need Sofa to help keep track of it all. Start with books, TV shows and movies, then add whatever other categories you'd like. Sofa has a clean interface that grabs title images and info to give you an overview of everything you watch (or read). Sofa's tracking feature is especially useful for remembering which episodes you've seen. Mark them off as you watch them and add notes if you like, or rely on the included summaries. Sofa tracks two different series at once for free, while paid subscribers can track unlimited titles. Sofa's free tier offers all its best features without advertisements or pop-ups begging for more. If you want to fine-tune your media tracking with custom ratings that you create and smart lists that populate based on your filters, Sofa offers a subscription for $5.99 per month, $49.99 per year or $249.99 for a lifetime membership. Unless you're a professional TV critic, you'll likely be fine with the free features. Instead of Apple Notes or Google Keep, try Bear , an app for capturing thoughts. Bear has become a productivity favorite by keeping its interface deceptively simple; it's a large notepad app without a glut of buttons and menus. While it's powerful, you don't have to use advanced features you don't need. Bear is built around smooth Markdown styling and supports tags to organize your thoughts. For example, if you find yourself often complaining about your job, tag that post with #job . You can add links, tags or even to-do tasks that are easily searchable. If that sounds complicated, ignore what you don't need and you're left with an elegant, attractive note-taking and journaling app. Bear has a reasonably-priced subscription tier ($3/month or $30/year) that offers a few extra features if you're hardcore about your notes. With it, you can sync your Bear notes between devices, as well as publish your notes using HTML or ePub to use the app as a blogging tool. After a few minutes with Flipboard , you'll wonder why it isn't preloaded on every iPad. This decentralized social experience transforms the touchscreen into a magazine with a clean layout and large images. If you read a lot of news, Flipboard is the best way to stay current. The app starts by having you select from an endless list of topics to find stories. These can start as general as sports, music or science. Or by dialing down, you might find "UEFA Champions League," "blues music" or "sustainable design." If any sources arise that you don't want to see, block them. In general, the selection is great; you can follow individual authors and sites the same way you follow topics. The best part about Flipboard is that it's totally free: it doesn't make you cough up a fee for the best content, and you can sometimes find stories that are normally trapped behind a paywall. HappySpoon is an (artificially) intelligent meal planner that helps you create a menu for the week ahead following whatever ideas or guidelines you set. The app uses AI to understand plain-language requests that you make, like "I need to use up all my chicken breast, so make a bunch of different chicken recipes." Once you've created your menu, it even generates a handy shopping list sorted by grocery store aisle. I asked the app to generate "breakfasts that are simple and on-repeat, like a big batch of muffins or oatmeal to eat every day" and it did exactly that. It also understood the rule "no lunches" and left that spot blank on my weekly menu. HappySpoon automatically resizes your portions and recipes to match your eaters. You can specify adult-sized or kid-sized appetites, and it will conform: the grocery list populates with the right amounts. You don't need to use HappySpoon's AI features; in fact, they're only free for two weeks. That's enough time to get started and use the AI for help generating a variety of menus. There are plenty of other AI tools that can create recipes, but if you want to stick with HappySpoon, the fee is $5.99 per month or $49.99 per year. I found the AI tools useful at first, but after a couple of weeks, the extra AI benefits didn't seem necessary. Whatever you need to organize, MindNode is a perfect starting point. Whether it's a meeting agenda, a workout plan or your life's goals, MindNode offers a simple canvas to connect and organize thoughts. You'll find features to enhance, stylize and reorganize your finished maps. Start with the big idea in the center and then branch out. A map can grow large the more you dig in, but MindNode makes it easy to keep your idea maps looking neat. You also have the option to view your maps as a text outline instead. If this sort of mental organization appeals to you, the premium subscription may offer enough bonus features to make it worth the asking $2.99 per month or $24.99 per year. With the subscription, you get more editing tools, the ability to add photos and emoji to your nodes and some professional-strength features for teams working together. It also unlocks real-time collaboration with others so you see edits and additions as they happen. You can set each node as a task with a reminder and checklist. And Apple Intelligence will enhance the experience by offering new ideas, summarizing what it sees and similar. The AI extras aren't necessary, but are available with the premium plan. Journey is a place to store your memories, including journal entries, calendar appointments , major dates, photos, multimedia and maps of the places you've been. The more you use Journey, the more it rewards your dedication, with features that track your habits later on. The available templates are Journey's secret weapon. If you're planning a trip, for example, the travel planner template includes fields for details like your hotel address, flight information, car rental details and even a budget planner that tracks your anticipated versus actual spending. Templates include tons of other categories, from personal goal trackers to a 30-60-90 day plan for starting a new career. Once you've built a journaling habit, you're able to track your progress through Journey's graphs and statistics. If you tag each journal entry with a mood, you'll see how your feelings ebbed and flowed throughout your journaling experience. By paying $6.99 per month or $49.99 per year (or $199 for the app's lifetime), you get premium features that could be helpful if you share a journal with someone else. There's also a premium AI feature included, though thankfully it doesn't offer to write journal entries for you. Instead, you can ask "how many entries did I write last month?" or tell it to "summarize my summer vacation from 2026." Libby is your local library in app form , which should be enough to earn an immediate download. Did you know you can borrow ebooks from your library? Just register your library card with Libby — go get one if you don't have one! — and you're ready to download the glut of digital content you might not have even known your library offered. Day One will record an unlimited number of journal entries without paying a dime, but if you want to add unlimited photos and videos, or audio recordings, you'll need to pay a subscription fee. For $49.99/year you get all that, plus interesting integration with IFTTT (If This Then That) and other markup tools. Habitify can help you build habits without being intrusive or making you do so much work that the app becomes its own "habit" to maintain. You design a habit or goal, then Habitify monitors your progress in the background as much as it can. It's the rare app that you barely need to use to get value from. You tell Habitify what you want to do and on which days you'll repeat the habit, then give it a specific goal. Habitify integrates neatly with Siri, so you often won't need to open the app to log your habit since Siri will. Siri can even update you on your progress — just ask how you're doing with your goals and Habitify will feed Siri the answer. There is a paid option for $49.99 per year, which is useful if fitness is your goal since Apple Health and Google Health integrations sit behind that paywall. You can connect Habitify to your Apple Watch or Fitbit so it knows you kept up your routine. It works with Apple Health and Google Health to gather data, with your permission. The paid option can also monitor your screen time if limits are part of your habit goals. DailyArt is for art world enthusiasts who want to go beyond the most prolific canvases and dive deeper into the lives of the artists who created them. One recent offering was a gorgeous Autumn Landscape created in 1899 by the pseudonymous Hishida Shunsō. In addition to the image, the app offers a brief history of the work and artist, with an explanation of the style it exemplifies. You can select the artist name or other links to see more artwork, or wait until tomorrow to see what DailyArt serves up next.

There is a paid option for $49.99 per year, which is useful if fitness is your goal since Apple Health and Google Health integrations sit behind that paywall. You can connect Habitify to your Apple Watch or Fitbit so it knows you kept up your routine. It works with Apple Health and Google Health to gather data, with your permission. The paid option can also monitor your screen time if limits are part of your habit goals. DailyArt is for art world enthusiasts who want to go beyond the most prolific canvases and dive deeper into the lives of the artists who created them. One recent offering was a gorgeous Autumn Landscape created in 1899 by the pseudonymous Hishida Shunsō. Your iPad should make every day easier. Whether you want to build new habits or improve your routines, we've rounded up apps that put the best iPads to work in your daily life.

We found these by digging a bit deeper. These aren't first-party Apple apps or subscription-only Adobe staples. It's free to get started with each, though most charge for extra features, which we've noted where applicable.

Our favorite apps are elegant and well-designed, taking advantage of the entire iPad display. They also keep AI to a bare minimum. There may be machine learning to help with search and transcriptions, but you won't find fake images or bogus text generators here.

If you're a voracious consumer of media, you need Sofa to help keep track of it all. Start with books, TV shows and movies, then add whatever other categories you'd like. Sofa has a clean interface that grabs title images and info to give you an overview of everything you watch (or read).

Sofa's tracking feature is especially useful for remembering which episodes you've seen. Mark them off as you watch them and add notes if you like, or rely on the included summaries. Sofa tracks two different series at once for free, while paid subscribers can track unlimited titles.

Sofa's free tier offers all its best features without advertisements or pop-ups begging for more. If you want to fine-tune your media tracking with custom ratings that you create and smart lists that populate based on your filters, Sofa offers a subscription for $5.99 per month, $49.99 per year or $249.99 for a lifetime membership. Unless you're a professional TV critic, you'll likely be fine with the free features.

Instead of Apple Notes or Google Keep, try Bear , an app for capturing thoughts. Bear has become a productivity favorite by keeping its interface deceptively simple; it's a large notepad app without a glut of buttons and menus. While it's powerful, you don't have to use advanced features you don't need.

Bear is built around smooth Markdown styling and supports tags to organize your thoughts. For example, if you find yourself often complaining about your job, tag that post with #job . You can add links, tags or even to-do tasks that are easily searchable. If that sounds complicated, ignore what you don't need and you're left with an elegant, attractive note-taking and journaling app.

Bear has a reasonably-priced subscription tier ($3/month or $30/year) that offers a few extra features if you're hardcore about your notes. With it, you can sync your Bear notes between devices, as well as publish your notes using HTML or ePub to use the app as a blogging tool.

After a few minutes with Flipboard , you'll wonder why it isn't preloaded on every iPad. This decentralized social experience transforms the touchscreen into a magazine with a clean layout and large images. If you read a lot of news, Flipboard is the best way to stay current.

The app starts by having you select from an endless list of topics to find stories. These can start as general as sports, music or science. Or by dialing down, you might find "UEFA Champions League," "blues music" or "sustainable design."
If any sources arise that you don't want to see, block them. In general, the selection is great; you can follow individual authors and sites the same way you follow topics.
The best part about Flipboard is that it's totally free: it doesn't make you cough up a fee for the best content, and you can sometimes find stories that are normally trapped behind a paywall.

HappySpoon is an (artificially) intelligent meal planner that helps you create a menu for the week ahead following whatever ideas or guidelines you set. The app uses AI to understand plain-language requests that you make, like "I need to use up all my chicken breast, so make a bunch of different chicken recipes." Once you've created your menu, it even generates a handy shopping list sorted by grocery store aisle.

I asked the app to generate "breakfasts that are simple and on-repeat, like a big batch of muffins or oatmeal to eat every day" and it did exactly that. It also understood the rule "no lunches" and left that spot blank on my weekly menu.

HappySpoon automatically resizes your portions and recipes to match your eaters. You can specify adult-sized or kid-sized appetites, and it will conform: the grocery list populates with the right amounts.

You don't need to use HappySpoon's AI features; in fact, they're only free for two weeks. That's enough time to get started and use the AI for help generating a variety of menus. There are plenty of other AI tools that can create recipes, but if you want to stick with HappySpoon, the fee is $5.99 per month or $49.99 per year. I found the AI tools useful at first, but after a couple of weeks, the extra AI benefits didn't seem necessary.

Whatever you need to organize, MindNode is a perfect starting point. Whether it's a meeting agenda, a workout plan or your life's goals, MindNode offers a simple canvas to connect and organize thoughts. You'll find features to enhance, stylize and reorganize your finished maps.

Start with the big idea in the center and then branch out. A map can grow large the more you dig in, but MindNode makes it easy to keep your idea maps looking neat. You also have the option to view your maps as a text outline instead.
