candidates.title: The UV-tracking Gem made me rethink how sunlight affects my health, not just my appearance

integrityPreflight.title: The UV-tracking Gem made me rethink how sunlight affects my health, not just my appearance

sources.pageTitle: The UV-tracking Gem made me rethink how sunlight affects my health, not just my appearance | The Verge

sources.title: The UV-tracking Gem made me rethink how sunlight affects my health, not just my appearance

extraction.body: Around the same time, I received a notification from an app used by the $249 ($149 at the time of publication) UV-tracking necklace I’d been wearing, called Gem, from a company called The90. It warned that my UV exposure had climbed considerably. While UV exposure and overheating are different things, I’d mistakenly assumed the shade and the fan would adequately protect me from both. Having started going gray in my 20s, I’m keen on slowing down other visible signs of aging where I reasonably can. But between being Indian (I rarely get sunburned thanks in part to my skin’s higher melanin content, not that it eliminates the risk of sun damage or skin cancer) and living within walking distance of the beach in perpetually sunny LA, I hadn’t given much thought to how much UV exposure I was actually getting. The Gem has helped me better understand it by providing a range of estimates, some more useful than others. The included UV-detecting sensor measures UVA and UVB radiation separately, rather than simply displaying my area’s UV forecast. UVB is primarily responsible for sunburn and helps your skin produce vitamin D, while UVA contributes to premature aging, even when you aren’t visibly burning. While not required, you can create a skin profile so that it can estimate a range of metrics based on the sensor’s UVA and UVB readings. The profile is based upon factors like skin type, sensitivities, clothing, and sunscreen. That means its estimates aren’t based on UV exposure alone, though they’re still predictions rather than direct measurements of how your body is responding to sunlight. There’s a lot here, including your estimated vitamin D production, potential circadian light benefits, estimated nitric oxide-related benefits, cumulative UVA exposure, and recent accumulated UVA exposure. Alongside cumulative UVA exposure and weekly trends, its Skin Aging Zone assesses potential aging-related risk and offers personalized skincare advice. The Sun Score is a rating that incorporates various metrics to balance sunlight’s potential benefits against the risks of overexposure. The company encourages users to aim for a daily Sun Score of 90, though more sun isn’t necessarily better. Too little exposure means missing potential benefits, while excessive UV can damage your skin. Eventually, I discovered the app needs to remain running in the background (at least on iPhone; I haven’t tested on Android), as measurements aren’t stored on the sensor, and fully closing the app interrupts tracking. My experience at the outdoor party challenged my assumptions about how much protection I was getting from the shade. Just as surprising to me was learning how little UVB I accumulated during a typical week, despite living somewhere so sunny. I fell short of the app’s estimated sunlight-derived vitamin D target almost daily, prompting me to research how melanin, while offering some natural UV protection, impacts vitamin D production from sunlight. Until then, I’d mostly thought about sun exposure in terms of protecting my skin from damage. Seeing how little UVB I was accumulating made me consider what I might be missing out on, too. During one test, its estimate of how much additional sunlight I needed dropped from several hours to under an hour, then climbed past six hours just minutes later. The fluctuations appeared related to changing UVB intensity, though I couldn’t verify that. After my experience using it at the outdoor party in August, I’d expected it just would encourage me to spend less time in the sun each day. In reality, my exposure often falls at one of two extremes: either too little to meet the app’s estimated targets or enough to raise concerns about overexposure, even when I thought I was protected by the shade. I now try to be more mindful about my UV exposure, even when I’m not using the Gem. I try to limit time spent outdoors during peak UV hours, and I try to get some sunlight on days spent mostly indoors. I credit the Gem with helping me better understand how my time outside could affect my well-being in ways I’d never considered, though the usefulness of your findings may vary. At $249 outside of a deal, it’s expensive, though it’s nice that it doesn’t have a subscription. I personally can’t justify the price given how much time I spend indoors, but I see the appeal for people who spend considerable time outside, or those who want to be more mindful of sun protection. For the price, I wish the app’s guidance was clearer at times, and I wish it could track UV without the app being open in the background, but the Gem ultimately got me thinking less about how my body looks and more about how I’m treating it.

candidates.title: AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?

integrityPreflight.title: AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?

sources.pageTitle: How AI created a cybersecurity ‘dark age’ | The Verge

sources.title: AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?

extraction.body: Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era. Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s. That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. You had the script kiddies who could download tools to do things and then the next level up of the people who could write those tools and that was a more rarefied skill set. There were the vulnerability researchers and then there were the gods, and that god tier was in the hundreds of people and those are the people who could do the really, really good vulnerability research, who could write the really, really good shell code, who could reverse engineer patches from Microsoft or somebody like that. If you wanted to build an attack team, then you have a small R&D component and then you have a much larger operational component. What’s really concerning, and what you see with the ARTEX stuff, is you can now kind of let loose on the operational side. And that is what we’ve seen over the last decade is these mostly Russian ransomware actors nailing the mid-size companies that most people have never heard of that are actually really important, like some midsize industrial company that makes some widget that we all depend upon. It’s because a company like that’s got one security guy and a 10 person, 12 person IT team and they’re going up against a 20 person Russian ransomware team, they’re toast. Now two or three Russian kids can have a whole bank of Macs or, if they have the money, they can buy Nvidia H-100s and they can run a ton of agents who do this all day and that is what is changing.

sources.title: OpenAI reportedly raises an additional $11 billion at a $1.25 trillion valuation
passages: OpenAI has reportedly raised $11 billion so far in a new funding round that values the AI lab at $1.25 trillion.

The news comes only hours after Bloomberg also reported that potential buyers of shares in the IPO of OpenAI’s chief competitor, Anthropic, are eyeing a substantially lower valuation than Anthropic had targeted.
Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.
The current figures fall well short of that target.
Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.
TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.
OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans.
There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.

Bloomberg writes that some potential buyers believe Anthropic’s valuation could be as low as $1.1 trillion, compared with the $2 trillion that investors were said to be expecting roughly a month ago.
The current figures fall well short of that target.
Bloomberg reported on the new funding on Friday, citing sources familiar with the matter.
The round is expected to close in the coming weeks and could total about $20 billion, a source told Bloomberg.
TechCrunch has reached out to OpenAI for comment and will update this story if it responds.
OpenAI previously intimated that it would go public this year but subsequently delayed its plans.
There are expectations that the company will IPO next year at some point.

sources.title: Ramp data shows AI spending stalling just as Anthropic nears its IPO
passages: A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic.
According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September.
To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month.
Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference.
Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.
In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna.

Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million.
Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets.
As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed.
“Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch.

“That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.”
Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion.
The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies.
OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion.
Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things.
AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies.
“Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said.
Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns.
There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one.
Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights.
As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brrr. costs go ahhh.”

extraction.body: Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it. A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September. To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month. As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed. “Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.” Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “ AI-pilled ” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said. Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000. “If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Kharazian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.” “The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued. October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Kharazian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong. Kharazian (who has published a series of blogs called “ Cracks in the AI Thesis ”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace. “OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million. Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets. Kharazian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market. Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook. Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly. Kharazian says those dynamics don’t work in the AI world because there’s just too much competition. “Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said. He also pointed to the range of other open model companies from China and the United States, as well as a new company called Jev — a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs — that is increasingly among the top performers on Ramp. “For a lot of AI use cases, you just need a simple Yes/No,” Kharazian said. “So you take your already cheap models, you shift them over to Jev, and now your already cheap stuff gets even cheaper.” The ability to complete workloads at a much cheaper cost is another factor driving the spending slowdown. That’s partly due to the discounts from AI companies, but also because companies are just getting better at being thrifty. “As you get really advanced in using AI, you get better at figuring out how to control it,” Kharazian said. “You’re more likely to use defaults that prevent usage of very expensive models for long-running tasks. You’re more likely to impose some budgets on employees. You’re more likely to offload some of the spend from standard and light models to even cheaper light models via routers.” Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights. That’s great for the customers…but it’s not necessarily great for the model companies. And it does introduce new questions around their revenue trajectories.” Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion. The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies. OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion. Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns. There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one. Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things. AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies. The hope among investors is that there will be another revolution that will drive further spend. Some think personal agents will be the next coding agents. passages: Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it.

A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September. To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month.
As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed.

“Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.”

Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “ AI-pilled ” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said.
Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000.

“If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Kharazian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.”
“The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued.
October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Kharazian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong.

Kharazian (who has published a series of blogs called “ Cracks in the AI Thesis ”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace.

“OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million. Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets.
Kharazian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market.

Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook. Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly. Kharazian says those dynamics don’t work in the AI world because there’s just too much competition.

“Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said. He also pointed to the range of other open model companies from China and the United States, as well as a new company called Jev — a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs — that is increasingly among the top performers on Ramp.
“For a lot of AI use cases, you just need a simple Yes/No,” Kharazian said. “So you take your already cheap models, you shift them over to Jev, and now your already cheap stuff gets even cheaper.”

The ability to complete workloads at a much cheaper cost is another factor driving the spending slowdown. That’s partly due to the discounts from AI companies, but also because companies are just getting better at being thrifty.

“As you get really advanced in using AI, you get better at figuring out how to control it,” Kharazian said. “You’re more likely to use defaults that prevent usage of very expensive models for long-running tasks. You’re more likely to impose some budgets on employees. You’re more likely to offload some of the spend from standard and light models to even cheaper light models via routers.”
Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights. As he succinctly put it: “tokens go brrr. costs go ahhh.”
tokens go brrr costs go ahhh pic.twitter.com/1whCWCJCyM

“A lot of the assumptions that we had about the trajectory of AI spend are starting to break down,” Kharazian said. “You can use more AI, but use it for less. That’s great for the customers…but it’s not necessarily great for the model companies. And it does introduce new questions around their revenue trajectories.”

Bloomberg reported Friday that Anthropic’s potential valuation sank from the $2 trillion estimated in early October to just $1.2 to $1.3 trillion. The company is also reportedly expected to receive a high “junk” rating from credit agencies. OpenAI also lowered its proposed valuation to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion and slashed its latest fundraising goals by about $10 billion.
Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns. There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one.

Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things. AI coding emerged just a year and a half ago as the most commercially viable product that has led Anthropic and OpenAI to becoming trillion-dollar companies. The hope among investors is that there will be another revolution that will drive further spend.

Some think personal agents will be the next coding agents. OpenAI , SpaceXAI , and Meta have all released their own personal agents, alongside startups like Instinct . Kharazian is skeptical, though, that personal agents, which are “not as economically productive as coding,” will provide the boost the industry needs for nonstop growth.

“The projection is that there will be new products being introduced that will drive further growth,” Kharazian said. “But based on what we can observe today and the products available and what is commercially advanced, AI spend has started to slow down.”

extraction.body: Companies are using more AI than ever, but they’re not spending more on it. A new report from Ramp shows AI spending flatlined over late summer even as token volumes rose, a sign that price competition and savvier customers may be capping revenue for OpenAI and Anthropic. According to Ramp’s data, token spend only grew 1.5% across August and September. To compare, in July, it grew 42% from the previous month. As Anthropic gears up for its IPO , the data suggests investors might be wrong to assume AI companies will keep growing at breakneck speed. “Almost the entire spend on AI is from venture-backed, high-growth tech companies,” Ramp’s lead economist Ara Kharazian told TechCrunch. “That’s fine as long as AI spend continues to rise, but if it starts to slow down because of something in the market or some other factor, they will all start to slow down simultaneously, and that could lead to other cascading effects.” Kharazian said he’s already seeing evidence that the top 1% of firms — the most “ AI-pilled ” — have stuttered slightly in their spend in August and September, coming up just below the $10,000 per-employee they were hitting at their summer peaks. A slowdown among that cohort is “sufficient to slow down revenue entirely, despite the fact that we’re seeing rising volumes,” he said. Ramp data shows growth in spending among median and top 10%, but it’s not enough to make up the difference. Median firms spend $12-$15 per employee per month, and the top 10% spend $600-$1,000. “If you look at the use cases today, it’s not necessarily clear they will get up to that $10,000 per employee per month mark that the 1% is at,” Kharazian said. While there’s plenty of demand for AI coding agents in industries like software and finance, “it’s not necessarily true that a doctor’s office or a car dealership will need to spend that much on AI.” “The era of hypergrowth may be over, and now that we know there may not be as much juice to squeeze out of the top 1%,” he continued. October data did see a re-acceleration, with token spend up 8.9% from September 23 to October 23, but Kharazian said the headwinds on spend growth are strong. Kharazian (who has published a series of blogs called “ Cracks in the AI Thesis ”) said the slowdown isn’t due to a demand problem. Again, AI volumes are up. Instead he points to the competitive nature of the marketplace. “OpenAI and Anthropic price cuts have…just made it cheaper to use AI,” he said. In September, OpenAI cut API prices in half for GPT-6 Sol and GPT-6 Luna. Answering the price war, Anthropic has also made significant reductions to pricing for Fable 5.1 and Opus 5.5 — a decision that the company said in a recent filing slashed revenue growth by about $600 million. Both companies have also been offering enterprise discounts that are intended to lock-in spend, but in reality are hitting their revenue targets. Kharazian said this dynamic means it has very much become a buyer’s market. Subsidizing use of expensive technology in order to lock in customers has always been a part of the Big Tech playbook. Just recall how cheap it used to be to take an Uber or Lyft ride, and now that there are few other ride-hail players, the cost of going from A to B has risen significantly. Kharazian says those dynamics don’t work in the AI world because there’s just too much competition. “Meta and Nvidia are also introducing enterprise offerings with pretty cheap models or open source models,” Kharazian said. He also pointed to the range of other open model companies from China and the United States, as well as a new company called Jev — a lightweight tool for choosing between a few predetermined outputs — that is increasingly among the top performers on Ramp. “For a lot of AI use cases, you just need a simple Yes/No,” Kharazian said. “So you take your already cheap models, you shift them over to Jev, and now your already cheap stuff gets even cheaper.” The ability to complete workloads at a much cheaper cost is another factor driving the spending slowdown. That’s partly due to the discounts from AI companies, but also because companies are just getting better at being thrifty. “As you get really advanced in using AI, you get better at figuring out how to control it,” Kharazian said. “You’re more likely to use defaults that prevent usage of very expensive models for long-running tasks. You’re more likely to impose some budgets on employees. You’re more likely to offload some of the spend from standard and light models to even cheaper light models via routers.” Notion co-founder Akshay Kothari recently posted internal data that matched Ramp’s insights. Kharazian says Ramp’s dataset likely informs many investor concerns. There is, however, one potential brightside for spending trajectories, albeit a speculative one. Much of the thesis for hypergrowth spending is that AI will undoubtedly introduce new use cases that will accelerate things. The hosts are looking to increase their distance from the relegation zone, while the visitors from Seville aim to remain among the leading teams.

According to the standings after 10 rounds, as of October 29, Real Betis are fourth with 20 points, while Elche are fifteenth with 10. However, these are not necessarily the positions the teams will hold when they take the field: Elche still have a home match against Valencia CF, while Betis face Málaga CF. The results of the 11th round could change the pressure on both sides.
Ticket sales for the match began on October 21. Supporters planning to attend are advised to secure their tickets in good time, especially if they want seats in a particular section of the stands.

Betis have recorded six wins, two draws and two defeats in ten matches, scoring 16 goals and conceding 14. Fourth place confirms a strong start, but their defensive record shows that opponents can create opportunities against them. Manuel Pellegrini's team want to stay in contention for European qualification, and every point dropped against a side from the lower part of the table comes at a cost.

Elche have two wins, four draws and four defeats, with a goal difference of 14-17. Fifteenth place is far from comfortable, but recent results paint a different picture from the one seen in August. The hosts now have an opportunity to demonstrate that they can compete against a team near the top of the table. No one will decide their season with a single performance here, but it is essential for Elche to keep collecting points and for Betis to maintain their winning ambitions.

The team coached by Martín Anselmi failed to win any of their first six league matches. The turnaround began with an away victory against RCD Espanyol de Barcelona, followed by two goalless draws: against Celta at Martínez Valero and away to Villarreal CF. The highlight of that run was a 3-0 victory against Rayo Vallecano on October 24. Federico Redondo and Fer Niño converted penalties, while Germán Valera completed the scoring.

Two wins, two draws and one defeat during this period explain why the mood around the team has improved. Three consecutive clean sheets represent an important step forward after a difficult start, which included a heavy defeat against Barcelona. Nevertheless, more than defensive resilience will be required against Betis: the visitors have players capable of punishing an excessively defensive approach and taking control of possession.

Pellegrini's team defeated Real Madrid 1-0, Villarreal 2-1 and Getafe 1-0 during September. In October, they overcame CA Osasuna 5-2, lost 2-5 against FC Barcelona and then drew 0-0 with Celta. The contrast between scoring five goals against Osasuna and conceding five against Barcelona is particularly interesting. Betis can be extremely dangerous in attack, but they are not invulnerable when opponents move quickly into attacking positions.

The visitors also face a demanding schedule. After the match against Málaga CF comes a European encounter with Borussia Dortmund on November 4, followed by the trip to Elche. The selection of the starting lineup could depend on playing time and player recovery. However, it should not be assumed that potential rotation will result in a weakened Betis: Pellegrini has various options available in midfield and attack.

After ten rounds, Fer Niño is Elche's leading scorer with six goals. His finishing ability will be particularly important if the hosts create only a limited number of clear chances. Germán Valera has scored twice, while Federico Redondo was among the scorers in the convincing victory over Rayo. Tete Morente, with three assists, and Lucas Cepeda, with two, are also responsible for creating opportunities.

Víctor Chust has stood out for his high number of passes - 687 in ten rounds according to LaLiga statistics - highlighting his role in the initial buildup of play. Goalkeeper Matías Dituro is also involved in that process. Betis may try to press the home defenders high up the pitch, but such an approach carries the risk of leaving space behind the first line of pressure.

At the other end, Ez Abde leads Betis' scoring charts with three goals. Isco, Cucho Hernández and Rodrigo Riquelme have two each, while Antony is among the most active players in terms of shots on goal, having recorded 14. Particular attention should be paid to the attacking runs of Abde and Antony, as well as the passes from Isco and Pablo Fornals between opposition lines. Natan plays an important role in organizing the defensive line and initiating attacks.

After taking charge, Anselmi emphasized his desire for proactive play with the ball. The hosts will therefore have to decide how high up the pitch they want to build their attacks against an opponent that makes good use of recovered possession. Accurate passing from the back would allow Elche to escape pressure, but a mistake in that area would directly open a route toward their goalkeeper.

Betis, for example, used a 4-2-3-1 formation against Osasuna. Widely positioned wingers, an attacking midfielder operating between the lines and overlapping full-backs are elements Elche must prepare for, although the lineup and formation for this match have not yet been confirmed. If the hosts close down the middle, the visitors could look for passes toward the flanks and cutbacks. If Betis push both full-backs forward, Elche will have an opportunity to launch quick transitions.

The match could be decided precisely during these moments when possession changes hands. Elche need discipline after their own attacks, while Betis need to recover their defensive positions quickly. Set pieces and penalties cannot be overlooked either, as they have recently influenced the results of both teams.

For Elche, Marc Aguado missed the cup match against UD Pinatar following an injury sustained against Villarreal. His availability against Betis will depend on his recovery. The home coach will only be able to finalize his lineup after the upcoming training sessions and the match against Valencia.

Betis have confirmed that Cucho Hernández has a muscle injury in his left calf and have not announced an exact return date. Junior Firpo has also been unavailable due to a muscle injury. Facundo Bernal received a four-match suspension following his dismissal against Barcelona; according to the published schedule, the ban also includes the away match against Elche, unless a subsequent decision changes his eligibility.
For this reason, the final lists of available players, particularly after the league fixtures and Betis' trip to Dortmund, are more important than early projections of the starting elevens.

At Martínez Valero on August 18, 2025, the result was 1-1: Aitor Ruibal gave the visitors the lead before Germán Valera equalized. According to club information, more than 27,000 seats are occupied by season-ticket holders. The stadium also has three video scoreboards, and the stands are divided into clearly marked sections.

The large number of season-ticket holders means that seating choices are not unlimited. An allocation of 700 seats has been announced for Betis supporters, separate from the home sections. On matchday, green and white club merchandise is expected among supporters on both sides, particularly if the score remains close until the closing stages. Seats in certain stands may sell out earlier, so it is worth securing tickets in advance.

extraction.body: Aircraft armed with advanced laser-guided rocket systems took out a little under half of the one-way attack drones the Houthis launched against military and commercial vessels during the U.S. military campaign that unfolded between March and May in and around the Red Sea, Gen. Erik Kurilla told lawmakers Tuesday. At a House Armed Services Committee posture hearing, the U.S. Central Command commander shared new details about that operation and said it underscores the military’s intensifying need for more and better counter-drone technologies and software. “We absolutely need to be putting more work into directed energy [and] high-powered microwaves, I think, are some of the innovations that have come out of this since Operation Rough Rider. About 40% of the drones shot down were shot down by something called Advanced Precision Weapon Kill System , a laser-guided 2.75-inch rocket fired off our F-16s or F-15s. That’s a $25,000 munition going against a roughly $50,000 or $100,000 drone — that is an Iranian-provided drone,” Kurilla said. Iran-backed Houthi fighters based in Yemen kicked off their attacks against vessels traversing crucial international shipping routes near the Red Sea in 2023. They indicated the disruption was meant as a form of protest of America’s support for Israel’s military actions in Gaza. Early into his second administration, President Donald Trump initiated Operation Rough Rider to dismantle Houthi infrastructure and leadership in the region. Trump announced an end to the operation in early May, following an agreement between America and the Houthis — brokered in part through the Omani government — to suspend the strikes. Operation Rough Rider cost the U.S. an estimated $1 billion , lawmakers pointed out at the posture hearing. It also resulted in the loss of multiple high-dollar military drones and fighter aircraft. “The president gave us a very specific mission, which was to get the Houthis to quit shooting at American ships. Six months ago on 12 November 2024, was the last time a destroyer went through the Bab-el-Mandeb. It was attacked 17 times with anti-ship ballistic missiles and anti-ship cruise missiles and [unmanned aerial vehicles or UAVs]. In the last week, we put four destroyers back through the Bab-el-Mandeb,” Kurilla said. After the conclusion of Rough Rider, however, Centcom is “still defending Israel with” its Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system against ongoing assaults from the Houthis, which remain under the foreign terrorist organization designation by the U.S. In the operation’s aftermath though, one major lesson the command learned, as Kurilla put it, is that “software is a weapon” that is rapidly changing the character of warfare. “Our ability to do Combined Joint All-Domain Command and Control , the things that we are doing with software — it’s amazing. We have advanced that. We have engineers every day making improvements on our ability to do that. It’s a warfighting headquarters,” Kurilla said. Software is also driving significant transformations in ballistic missile defense on the contemporary battlefield, the commander noted. “The same thing, I would tell you, as it comes to counter-UAS as well. We are making changes to the Navy’s software on the SPY radars based on what we’re seeing,” Kurilla told the committee. When asked by lawmakers to recommend the top weapons capabilities he views they should most quickly invest in, the commander repeatedly pointed to counter-drone systems, calling them the “number one” in-demand tool at this time. “We’re only going to see the systems get smaller, more lethal. [On] the electromagnetic spectrum, we try and jam that. That’s why Ukraine and Russia went to fiber optics — going out to 40 kilometers with fiber optic drones — you can’t jam that. So those are the things I would ask for right now, the counter-UAS [and detection capabilities]. I think we need to put aerial [Inverse Synthetic Aperture Radars or ISAR] for low-radar cross section to be able to pick up, elevate it, and then [use] ballistic missile defense,” Kurilla said.

extraction.body: TAMPA, Fla. — U.S. Central Command is planning a set of exercises aimed at filling key gaps in its ability to detect and track drone threats in the Middle East. Amid a sharp increase in one-way drone attacks on U.S. and allied forces by Iraq, Syria and Houthi rebels, CENTCOM is working with the Pentagon’s chief digital and AI office to identify sensors that can detect adversary systems and be integrated into a command and control framework. Earlier this month, the command’s innovation team solicited proposals from industry for the effort, dubbed Desert Guardian. Army Maj. Bryan Cercy, an innovation officer at CENTCOM, told C4ISRNET the innovation team will choose sensors this summer to participate in a U.S.-based exercise in October focused on spotting UAS threats. Early next year, it will stage a second exercise — this one at a base in the Middle East — focused on integrating those sensors into a single interface used by operators in the field. “Our proof of concept is that there’s a world in which all of these different sensors are integrated together, and they provide the user, the operator one common picture of the threats to the base,” Cercy said June 25 during an interview at CENTCOM headquarters in Tampa, Fla. “Maybe we don’t accomplish everything, but we’re inching one step closer to make the operators, on a day-to-day basis, more effective.” The command’s innovation office regularly runs technology sprints to identify operator challenges and try to find solutions. The upcoming demonstrations are part of a series of sprints the team has been running this year focused on countering UAS threats . The effort began in March with several fact-finding missions. CENTCOM’s innovation team traveled to the Middle East to observe operators and hear first hand about the challenges they face in conducting their missions. CENTCOM also leveraged its technology residency program, which temporarily embeds private sector experts within the command to help solve technical challenges. It sent its resident at the time to observe operators tracking UAS threats and better understand their capability needs. As Rinderer compiled his findings, CENTCOM conducted its own market research to find out what other organizations were doing to meet counter UAS needs and whether there was a gap for the innovation team to focus on. “Counter UAS is a very broad problem that a lot of organizations across the department are trying to solve right now,” Cercy said. “We owe the due diligence to the warfighter to really see, is there already something out there that might close that gap, even just a little bit.” It became clear through this work, he said, that while base defense operators have access to many sensors, they lack an integrated picture of the threat. “You’ve got operators that are operating on different systems that are trying to protect against threats to the base, and sometimes those systems don’t necessarily talk to each other,” he said. “They’re not integrated, and so it’s a lot of swivel chair action that’s happening . . . between the different operators to make sure that they’re all detecting a threat.” Following the two exercises, if the team identifies a capability it thinks could benefit operators, it will work to find an acquisition pathway within the Defense Department to get that to the field. That could mean drafting a joint urgent operational needs request or feeding findings to the Pentagon’s Joint Counter UAS Office or a program office that might be looking for a similar capability. Air Force Col. Nate Huston, CENTCOM’s director of innovation and capability integration, said in the same interview that part of the intent behind technology sprints like this is to demonstrate a process for identifying innovative solutions to problems in the field and validating whether there’s a capability that can address it. “What we want to say is like, ‘Hey, we started at this point, we got these disparate folks together, we showed that this could be integrated,’” he said. “The other part of this is . . . we fully understand some integration will not work exactly right, and we’ll learn from that.” Courtney Albon is C4ISRNET’s space and emerging technology reporter. She has covered the U.S. military since 2012, with a focus on the Air Force and Space Force. She has reported on some of the Defense Department’s most significant acquisition, budget and policy challenges. Cpl. Igor started a new job this year, swapping the sights of a 105 mm gun on the French Army’s AMX 10 RC reconnaissance vehicle for first-person view goggles and a handheld controller. Offials are worried that drone attacks could knock out power to millions of people — as has happened frequently in Ukraine after Russian strikes. Germany plans to stand up its first dedicated drone regiment next year, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has announced. The French Air Force plans to fly crewed fighter jets in collaboration with AI-powered combat drones in 2028, under project Hypairion.

extraction.body: The Pentagon said it has delivered more than 25,000 unmanned and counter-drone systems to U.S. Central Command in 2026, backed by about $782 million in investment. More than 24,000 were counter-drone systems, fielded through Joint Interagency Task Force 401 to protect forward-deployed forces from drone attacks. The deliveries also included more than 1,300 one-way attack drones for precision strikes at longer ranges. U.S. Central Command received more than 100 uncrewed surface and underwater vessels to expand its maritime reconnaissance and strike capabilities. The Pentagon said it is expanding production on commercial lines and using modular software to get new equipment to troops faster. The aim is to give commanders lower-cost systems they can use in large numbers, reducing the need to expend munitions that cost millions of dollars apiece. “The thousands of systems operating across CENTCOM this year are just the beginning,” said Owen West, chief executive of Project Agincourt and the Pentagon’s direct reporting portfolio manager for unmanned systems. “We will out-innovate, out-build, and out-adapt any adversary on the battlefield.” The Pentagon plans to keep supplying Central Command while expanding deliveries to U.S. forces in the Pacific and Europe and across the wider joint force. The effort also lays the groundwork for Autonomous Warfare Command, a planned four-star combatant command due to be established by Oct. 1, 2027. France has finalised an order with Naval Group and MBDA to increase the Aster air defence missile capacity of its FDI frigates from 16 to 32 per ship. AIRO Group Holdings said a U.S. government customer ordered two types of drones from the company, the RQ-35 Heidrun and RQ-70 Dainn, in its first U.S. drone sale. RTX is adding production capacity for Tomahawk, AMRAAM, SM-6 and SM-3 IB missiles under four multiyear Pentagon contracts worth about $70 billion combined. The Department of the Air Force has assigned senior leaders to 15 mission areas to move what it calls “super intelligence” from testing into operational use. Canada is considering a firm order for eight Type 212CD submarines from German shipbuilder TKMS, with options for another four, CBC News reported. Rheinmetall expects Germany’s parliament to approve the Arminius Boxer armoured vehicle contract in the first quarter of 2027, with a detailed price audit likely to push the decision past year-end. Japan and the United States wrapped up Keen Sword 27 on Oct. 29 after 11 days of training with forces from seven other countries. British F-35 jets flying from HMS Prince of Wales intercepted a Russian Tu-95 Bear long-range bomber during a major NATO exercise off Norway, the Royal Navy said. Britain’s Titania military satellite is in orbit, giving the armed forces another way to observe military activity on Earth, the Ministry of Defence said. The 46,000-square-foot building will be the first at Dyess dedicated solely to the new bomber, with secure workspaces and communications networks for planning and preparing strike missions. extraction.body: Aircraft armed with advanced laser-guided rocket systems took out a little under half of the one-way attack drones the Houthis launched against military and commercial vessels during the U.S. military campaign that unfolded between March and May in and around the Red Sea, Gen. Erik Kurilla told lawmakers Tuesday. At a House Armed Services Committee posture hearing, the U.S. Central Command commander shared new details about that operation and said it underscores the military’s intensifying need for more and better counter-drone technologies and software. “We absolutely need to be putting more work into directed energy [and] high-powered microwaves, I think, are some of the innovations that have come out of this since Operation Rough Rider. About 40% of the drones shot down were shot down by something called Advanced Precision Weapon Kill System , a laser-guided 2.75-inch rocket fired off our F-16s or F-15s. That’s a $25,000 munition going against a roughly $50,000 or $100,000 drone — that is an Iranian-provided drone,” Kurilla said. Iran-backed Houthi fighters based in Yemen kicked off their attacks against vessels traversing crucial international shipping routes near the Red Sea in 2023. sources.title: US Central Command to demo integrated counter drone sensors this fall - C4ISRNet
passages: Bryan Cercy, an innovation officer at CENTCOM, told C4ISRNET the innovation team will choose sensors this summer to participate in a U.S.-based exercise in October focused on spotting UAS threats.
Early next year, it will stage a second exercise — this one at a base in the Middle East — focused on integrating those sensors into a single interface used by operators in the field.

Amid a sharp increase in one-way drone attacks on U.S. and allied forces by Iraq, Syria and Houthi rebels, CENTCOM is working with the Pentagon’s chief digital and AI office to identify sensors that can detect adversary systems and be integrated into a command and control framework.

“Our proof of concept is that there’s a world in which all of these different sensors are integrated together, and they provide the user, the operator one common picture of the threats to the base,” Cercy said June 25 during an interview at CENTCOM headquarters in Tampa, Fla.
Courtney Albon is C4ISRNET’s space and emerging technology reporter.
She has covered the U.S. military since 2012, with a focus on the Air Force and Space Force.
She has reported on some of the Defense Department’s most significant acquisition, budget and policy challenges.

extraction.body: TAMPA, Fla. — U.S. Central Command is planning a set of exercises aimed at filling key gaps in its ability to detect and track drone threats in the Middle East. Amid a sharp increase in one-way drone attacks on U.S. and allied forces by Iraq, Syria and Houthi rebels, CENTCOM is working with the Pentagon’s chief digital and AI office to identify sensors that can detect adversary systems and be integrated into a command and control framework. Earlier this month, the command’s innovation team solicited proposals from industry for the effort, dubbed Desert Guardian. Army Maj. Bryan Cercy, an innovation officer at CENTCOM, told C4ISRNET the innovation team will choose sensors this summer to participate in a U.S.-based exercise in October focused on spotting UAS threats. Early next year, it will stage a second exercise — this one at a base in the Middle East — focused on integrating those sensors into a single interface used by operators in the field. “Our proof of concept is that there’s a world in which all of these different sensors are integrated together, and they provide the user, the operator one common picture of the threats to the base,” Cercy said June 25 during an interview at CENTCOM headquarters in Tampa, Fla. “Maybe we don’t accomplish everything, but we’re inching one step closer to make the operators, on a day-to-day basis, more effective.” The command’s innovation office regularly runs technology sprints to identify operator challenges and try to find solutions. The upcoming demonstrations are part of a series of sprints the team has been running this year focused on countering UAS threats . The effort began in March with several fact-finding missions. CENTCOM’s innovation team traveled to the Middle East to observe operators and hear first hand about the challenges they face in conducting their missions. CENTCOM also leveraged its technology residency program, which temporarily embeds private sector experts within the command to help solve technical challenges. It sent its resident at the time to observe operators tracking UAS threats and better understand their capability needs. As Rinderer compiled his findings, CENTCOM conducted its own market research to find out what other organizations were doing to meet counter UAS needs and whether there was a gap for the innovation team to focus on. “Counter UAS is a very broad problem that a lot of organizations across the department are trying to solve right now,” Cercy said. “We owe the due diligence to the warfighter to really see, is there already something out there that might close that gap, even just a little bit.” It became clear through this work, he said, that while base defense operators have access to many sensors, they lack an integrated picture of the threat. “You’ve got operators that are operating on different systems that are trying to protect against threats to the base, and sometimes those systems don’t necessarily talk to each other,” he said. “They’re not integrated, and so it’s a lot of swivel chair action that’s happening . . . between the different operators to make sure that they’re all detecting a threat.” Following the two exercises, if the team identifies a capability it thinks could benefit operators, it will work to find an acquisition pathway within the Defense Department to get that to the field. That could mean drafting a joint urgent operational needs request or feeding findings to the Pentagon’s Joint Counter UAS Office or a program office that might be looking for a similar capability. Air Force Col. Nate Huston, CENTCOM’s director of innovation and capability integration, said in the same interview that part of the intent behind technology sprints like this is to demonstrate a process for identifying innovative solutions to problems in the field and validating whether there’s a capability that can address it. “What we want to say is like, ‘Hey, we started at this point, we got these disparate folks together, we showed that this could be integrated,’” he said. “The other part of this is . . . we fully understand some integration will not work exactly right, and we’ll learn from that.” Courtney Albon is C4ISRNET’s space and emerging technology reporter. She has reported on some of the Defense Department’s most significant acquisition, budget and policy challenges. Cpl. Igor started a new job this year, swapping the sights of a 105 mm gun on the French Army’s AMX 10 RC reconnaissance vehicle for first-person view goggles and a handheld controller. Offials are worried that drone attacks could knock out power to millions of people — as has happened frequently in Ukraine after Russian strikes. Germany plans to stand up its first dedicated drone regiment next year, Defense Minister Boris Pistorius has announced. The French Air Force plans to fly crewed fighter jets in collaboration with AI-powered combat drones in 2028, under project Hypairion.

extraction.body: The Pentagon said it has delivered more than 25,000 unmanned and counter-drone systems to U.S. Central Command in 2026, backed by about $782 million in investment. More than 24,000 were counter-drone systems, fielded through Joint Interagency Task Force 401 to protect forward-deployed forces from drone attacks. The deliveries also included more than 1,300 one-way attack drones for precision strikes at longer ranges. U.S. Central Command received more than 100 uncrewed surface and underwater vessels to expand its maritime reconnaissance and strike capabilities. The Pentagon said it is expanding production on commercial lines and using modular software to get new equipment to troops faster. The aim is to give commanders lower-cost systems they can use in large numbers, reducing the need to expend munitions that cost millions of dollars apiece. “The thousands of systems operating across CENTCOM this year are just the beginning,” said Owen West, chief executive of Project Agincourt and the Pentagon’s direct reporting portfolio manager for unmanned systems. “We will out-innovate, out-build, and out-adapt any adversary on the battlefield.” The Pentagon plans to keep supplying Central Command while expanding deliveries to U.S. forces in the Pacific and Europe and across the wider joint force. The effort also lays the groundwork for Autonomous Warfare Command, a planned four-star combatant command due to be established by Oct. 1, 2027. France has finalised an order with Naval Group and MBDA to increase the Aster air defence missile capacity of its FDI frigates from 16 to 32 per ship. AIRO Group Holdings said a U.S. government customer ordered two types of drones from the company, the RQ-35 Heidrun and RQ-70 Dainn, in its first U.S. drone sale. RTX is adding production capacity for Tomahawk, AMRAAM, SM-6 and SM-3 IB missiles under four multiyear Pentagon contracts worth about $70 billion combined. The Department of the Air Force has assigned senior leaders to 15 mission areas to move what it calls “super intelligence” from testing into operational use. Canada is considering a firm order for eight Type 212CD submarines from German shipbuilder TKMS, with options for another four, CBC News reported. Rheinmetall expects Germany’s parliament to approve the Arminius Boxer armoured vehicle contract in the first quarter of 2027, with a detailed price audit likely to push the decision past year-end. Japan and the United States wrapped up Keen Sword 27 on Oct. 29 after 11 days of training with forces from seven other countries. British F-35 jets flying from HMS Prince of Wales intercepted a Russian Tu-95 Bear long-range bomber during a major NATO exercise off Norway, the Royal Navy said. Britain’s Titania military satellite is in orbit, giving the armed forces another way to observe military activity on Earth, the Ministry of Defence said. The 46,000-square-foot building will be the first at Dyess dedicated solely to the new bomber, with secure workspaces and communications networks for planning and preparing strike missions. Early next year, it will stage a second exercise — this one at a base in the Middle East — focused on integrating those sensors into a single interface used by operators in the field.

Amid a sharp increase in one-way drone attacks on U.S. and allied forces by Iraq, Syria and Houthi rebels, CENTCOM is working with the Pentagon’s chief digital and AI office to identify sensors that can detect adversary systems and be integrated into a command and control framework.

“Our proof of concept is that there’s a world in which all of these different sensors are integrated together, and they provide the user, the operator one common picture of the threats to the base,” Cercy said June 25 during an interview at CENTCOM headquarters in Tampa, Fla.
Courtney Albon is C4ISRNET’s space and emerging technology reporter.
She has covered the U.S. military since 2012, with a focus on the Air Force and Space Force.
She has reported on some of the Defense Department’s most significant acquisition, budget and policy challenges.
The Pentagon said it has delivered more than 25,000 unmanned and counter-drone systems to U.S.
Central Command in 2026, backed by about $782 million in investment.

“The thousands of systems operating across CENTCOM this year are just the beginning,” said Owen West, chief executive of Project Agincourt and the Pentagon’s direct reporting portfolio manager for unmanned systems.
“We will out-innovate, out-build, and out-adapt any adversary on the battlefield.”
Central Command received more than 100 uncrewed surface and underwater vessels to expand its maritime reconnaissance and strike capabilities.

extraction.body: The 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 has already made plenty of noise with its new engine lineup. After getting a closer look at the Denali Ultimate, though, I think the conversation is going to turn to what GMC has done inside the truck. There is a lot going on here, from the materials and seats to the screens, storage and lighting. This was a walk-around of a preproduction truck, not a road test. Some functions were turned off during the demonstration, so I’m treating this as a look at the design and features rather than a verdict on how the finished truck drives or how every system works in daily use. For the broader lineup announcement, see our earlier 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 coverage . The Denali Ultimate’s grille makes a statement before you open a door. GMC showed a dark GMC badge with illumination. The grille finish prompted a little back-and-forth during the walk-around because I’m going to miss saying “Vader Chrome.” That name was fun. There are useful details beyond the grille. The engine-displacement badges move to the hood, and GMC’s team explained that the familiar external antennas have been removed as part of the new design. The Denali Ultimate shown also had 22-inch diamond-cut aluminum wheels and articulating assist steps. Its lighting includes welcome and farewell animations, which add another bit of theater when you approach or leave the truck. Inside, GMC showed an open-pore forged birch wood treatment on the console and instrument panel. The team explained that the wood is chopped and pressed to create the pattern. It has a different look from a conventional glossy wood insert, and it gives the Denali Ultimate something distinctive to put alongside its stitching, piping and topographic details. The Denali Ultimate comes with 14-way power front seats with heating, ventilation and massage. I also spent some time checking the seats. My first impression was that they felt more comfortable, especially in the area I pointed out during the demonstration. That is encouraging, but a few minutes in a parked truck is different from a long day behind the wheel. I still want that seat time before making a bigger claim about comfort. In the rear, GMC confirmed heated outboard seats rather than ventilated ones. GM also got rid of those funky storage compartments built into the rear seatbacks. The flat floor and underseat storage remain useful features for the gloves, towing equipment and other things that tend to live in a truck cab. The ambient lighting demonstration was a good example of how much customization GMC is building into this interior. The team described 143 color combinations, with separate upper and lower zones. I can already see owners sharing their favorite combinations online, especially when they can match a school or team’s colors. The cabin also needs to work as a place to charge devices and get things done. During the walk-around, GMC pointed out six USB connections across the front and rear of the cabin, along with a 120-volt outlet. The available MultiPro center console and articulating screen with hidden storage are part of the larger interior redesign GMC highlighted at the event. The follow-up screen demonstration showed a new user interface with customizable information and quick-access controls. One practical example was switching between two connected phones, which could be useful if you carry separate work and personal devices. Another was a garage-door control that can appear based on your location. Those are the kinds of features I want to try repeatedly in a production truck to see whether they make things easier. There is also an 11.5-inch passenger display, alongside the 16.3-inch center screen and 12.2-inch driver display GMC demonstrated. The passenger screen has a privacy filter, and the team walked through options for streaming, connecting a device through HDMI and choosing where the audio plays. I want to see how useful that setup is with someone riding along. GMC also confirms that wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto remain part of the new infotainment system. One change that will get truck owners talking is the digital oil-level reading for the next-generation V8s. GMC showed it in the vehicle-status app, where the display reports the oil level alongside information such as battery voltage. That is a feature I want to try myself when checking a production truck. The Sierra’s new interior gives us plenty to explore, but the real test will come with everyday use. I want to see how quickly the controls become familiar, how the screens behave in different lighting and whether the seats stay comfortable after several hours. I’m also interested in spending more time with the truck’s towing features, including available Super Cruise with trailering capability. GMC lists the Denali Ultimate’s starting price at $87,895, including the $2,795 destination freight charge. The new 6.6-liter V8 is standard, with 481 horsepower and 501 pound-feet of torque; the 3.0-liter Duramax diesel is available. GMC says the first 2027 Sierra models will reach U.S. dealers before the end of 2026. For now, the Denali Ultimate makes a strong first impression as a cabin GMC has put considerable thought into. The combination of new materials, storage ideas and configurable technology gives buyers more to consider than a new grille or a larger display alone. We’ll need a proper drive to find out how well it all comes together. His work has appeared on CBS Sunday Morning, NewsNation, MotorTrend and The Boston Globe, and he has tested hundreds of new vehicles across North America. sources.title: The 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and GMC Sierra 1500 Get Worse Fuel Economy Numbers - MotorTrend
passages: The 2027 Chevrolet Silverado 1500 and GMC Sierra 1500 are getting major updates, including new small-block V-8 engines, updated transmissions, and refreshed exterior and interior designs.
Those changes bring revised EPA fuel economy ratings, and the numbers point to a small efficiency hit for most configurations compared with the 2026 trucks.
The EPA has released ratings for the 5.7-liter V-8, 6.6-liter V-8, and 3.0-liter turbodiesel available in both trucks; final fuel economy figures for the base 2.7-liter turbo-four are still pending.
According to data from GM Authority , nearly every listed powertrain and trim combination returns lower ratings for 2027.
The exception is the GMC Sierra AT4X equipped with the turbodiesel.
The amount of the change varies by engine, drivetrain, and trim.
In several configurations, the difference is only 1 or 2 mpg, while certain four-wheel-drive diesel versions have larger drops.
Choosing a different drivetrain or trim can therefore affect the comparison as much as the engine itself.
It gains 1 mpg in city driving and 2 mpg on both the highway and combined cycle.
The V-8 changes help explain some of the decline.
Both engines have larger displacements and more horsepower and torque, which in some cases can also mean more fuel consumption.
Miguel Cortina is Mexico Editor at MotorTrend , covering the auto industry in the U.S. and south of the border.
He joined MotorTrend in January 2015 and is an avid automotive enthusiast who enjoys playing golf, surfing, and running in his free time.

sources.title: Preview: 2027 GMC Sierra 1500 Comes With Luxury, Power, and Off-Road Capabilities - Consumer Reports
passages: Like the Chevrolet Silverado 1500 , the GMC Sierra 1500 received an evolutionary redesign for the 2027 model year.
The off-road trims can handle tougher conditions, and luxury editions get luxury amenities that rival those of high-end SUVs.
GMC says the turbocharged four-cylinder has been upgraded, now producing 350 hp. (The previous version of that 2.7-liter engine produces 310 hp.)
The most extroverted trim is the Sierra 1500 AT4X.

It enhances the truck’s off-road capability with 35-inch Goodyear Mud Terrain (MT) tires, a 2-inch suspension lift, off-road shocks, front and rear electronically locked differentials to optimize traction, and a distinctive front fascia.
Like the previous model, the AT4X will again be sold with the AEV Edition package, which further fortifies the truck.
Think of the Pro as the work-centered entry point, with the Elevation scaling the trim walk with more creature comforts.
The turbo four has been changed, and the V8s are next-generation small blocks.
The outgoing Sierra 1500 is a competitive option within the full-sized truck class, and we expect the new version to be as well.
Bartlett is the managing editor for the autos team at Consumer Reports.
Consumer Reports is an independent, nonprofit member organization that works side by side with consumers for truth, transparency, and fairness in the marketplace.

GMC latest version of its full-sized pickup is set to compete with the Ford F-150, Ram 1500, and Toyota Tundra Like the Chevrolet Silverado 1500 , the GMC Sierra 1500 received an evolutionary redesign for the 2027 model year. The changes exemplify how pickup trucks, like the Ford F-150 and Ram 1500 the Sierra competes with, keep getting more upscale. The off-road trims can handle tougher conditions, and luxury editions get luxury amenities that rival those of high-end SUVs. The 2027 Sierra 1500’s exterior is new compared to last year, and the interior will have a new screen-intensive layout. The four available engines are a turbocharged four-cylinder, two new V8s, and a turbodiesel six-cylinder. The turbo four has been changed, and the V8s are next-generation small blocks. Trim options for the Sierra 1500 are the Pro, Elevation, AT4, AT4X, Denali, and Denali Ultimate. Think of the Pro as the work-centered entry point, with the Elevation scaling the trim walk with more creature comforts. Each trim separates into the off-road-focused AT4 and more capable AT4X, while the Denali and Denali Ultimate chart a luxury and tech-focused path. What it competes with: Chevrolet Silverado 1500 , Ford F-150 , Ram 1500 , Toyota Tundra Powertrains: • 350-hp, 2.7-liter turbocharged four-cylinder • 402-hp, 5.7-liter V8 • 481-hp, 6.6-liter V8 • 305-hp, 3.0-liter turbocharged diesel six-cylinder engine Each with a 10-speed automatic transmission; rear- or four-wheel drive Price: $48,500-$85,100 for crew cab 4WD Destination: $2,795 On sale: Late 2026 Final assembly point: Fort Wayne, Ind. The outgoing Sierra 1500 is a competitive option within the full-sized truck class, and we expect the new version to be as well. But like other full-sized pickups, the current Sierra 1500 has below-average reliability. Even though the 2027 Sierra 1500 has all-new sheet metal, it’s so similar to the 2026 body that you might need to look for the trapezoidal grille and more complicated headlamps to identify one. Trim-specific details distinguish various versions of the Sierra, as seen in the lower front design, wheels, and exhaust outlets. GMC says there are available welcome and farewell light animations, addressing a need you probably didn’t know existed. Trucks … with animations. The Sierra 1500 will once again be available as a regular cab/long bed, extended cab/standard bed, crew cab/standard bed, and crew cab/long bed. The most extroverted trim is the Sierra 1500 AT4X. It enhances the truck’s off-road capability with 35-inch Goodyear Mud Terrain (MT) tires, a 2-inch suspension lift, off-road shocks, front and rear electronically locked differentials to optimize traction, and a distinctive front fascia. Like the previous model, the AT4X will again be sold with the AEV Edition package, which further fortifies the truck. The redesigned cabin is simpler than the outgoing model, with screens spread across the dashboard. All combined, GMC says there’s more than 60 inches of total screen. The digital real estate includes a 12.2-inch instrument display, 16.3-inch infotainment screen, and 11.5-inch front passenger screen.
